# Changelog

Vilan is a fast-moving alpha. Minor versions (`0.X`) may change the
language, the standard library, and the wire protocol without a
deprecation period; patch versions are fixes. Each release below links
the highlights — the [book](https://vilan-lang.org/docs/) always
tracks the latest state.

## Unreleased

<!-- family: fix -->
**`std::router::link` no longer builds a drag-armed anchor: in Chrome a link drag that starts while a quick click's in-app navigation is still settling WEDGES THE TAB, and `draggable="false"` removes the trigger at no cost.** Once wedged, every drag in that tab gets `dragstart` then `pointercancel` and never `dragend`, and pointer input stays dead — hover, `:active`, clicks, native scrollbars — while compositor wheel scrolling keeps working. It is per TAB, survives a hard refresh, and only a new tab escapes it; the owner reproduced it at will by clicking back and forth between two links and dragging one (Windows, Chrome 153.0.8010.37). The wedge is Chrome's bug to fix and the arming is std's not to do: an `<a href>` is drag-armed by default, and nothing an app wants from a navigation link is a drag. **The href stays**, so middle-click, ctrl-click and copy-link-address are untouched — only the native "drag this link somewhere" gesture goes. **`View::link_to(route)` is `link`'s body without the `<a>` and the label**, so an app that builds and styles its own anchor gets the href, the attribute and the plain-left-click interception without knowing the story — and `link` is now that method plus an anchor, which is the honest relation between the two. The routing guide says so in one sentence, the gotchas page carries the mechanism, and `router.rs` pins both spellings (`b293_the_anchor_link_builds_is_not_drag_armed`). Tracker B293.

<!-- family: tooling -->
**The rpc guide's hand-wired-channel trap now names what actually makes a hand-wired mirror different — it has no ORIGIN — instead of a mechanism claim about `Unsubscribe` that the demand ruling supersedes, and `RpcError` is documented with all six of its arms.** The trap read "an `Unsubscribe` only stops the forward, because the client re-subscribes on the same id when a view remounts", which was a statement about a channel's server lifetime rather than about the thing the reader has to act on: a channel your rpc minted by hand is one nothing on the client can re-issue, so both chores it lists — revoking when you are finished, and `invalidate_on_reconnect` so a fresh session's `Waiting` mirror gets its call re-run — belong to your app because nobody else knows the call. `[expose]` gets both for free, which is the point of the bullet, and it is now the reason given. Alongside it, three sentences that went stale when A52 added `RpcError::Unavailable`: the guide counted "five variants" and the reference's `RpcError` fragment listed five, and neither named the `503` arm or the "not now, retry later" reading that distinguishes it from `Unauthorized`. Sweep of the rpc pages against `transport-rpc.md` §9 (tracker A56's lane).

<!-- family: tooling -->
**The four handshake refusals are one table in the services guide, on the line that decides between them: who made the call.** `Reject` grew a fourth arm when A52 landed `Unavailable`/`503`, and the guide kept saying `Err` answers `401`/`403`/`429` — three of four — while the client-side sentence still mapped only `401` and `403`, leaving the `RpcError::Unavailable` arm and the "not now, retry later" reading it exists for undocumented. The table names all four, and the sentence beside it says why `authorize_timeout` answers `429` and not `503`: `503` reports a judgement the APP made, from its own `authorize`; a verifier std cut off for running out of time made no judgement at all, so a `503` there would be a claim std cannot make. A48 chose `429` before there was another arm to weigh it against — the answer is unchanged, and now well-founded rather than merely chosen. Tracker A56, ruling R6 (`transport-rpc.md` §9.2).

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**`[expose(keyed = K)]` over a `SignalCell<Map<K2, V>>` whose written `K` disagrees with the map's own key is refused at the attribute, instead of the argument silently winning and the disagreement surfacing four times over as a `Keyed<K>` bound failure in generated code.** A keyed mirror is a `KeyedSource<K, T>`, and vilan has no associated types, so the `[service]` expansion reads `K` off the annotation before any type resolves. A `Map<K, V>` element names both types and takes the bare `[expose(keyed)]`; the attribute argument is for every other collection (A51). Writing both was allowed and the argument simply won — so `[expose(keyed = i32)] tasks: SignalCell<Map<str, Task>>` built the mirror, the server-side exposure and the client stub around `i32`, and the author read `'Task' does not implement trait 'Keyed<i32>'` four times, each at a call the attribute wrote and nobody typed. Neither spelling is knowably the intended one, so neither is preferred: the refusal names both, points at the ARGUMENT (the half under discussion — the field's type is not wrong), and offers the two ways out. It is the standard `check_expose_fields` already meets for a field that is no source at all (B202): said in the field's own vocabulary, in the one layer holding both spellings. The four bound failures stand down behind it, keyed on the trait application the refusal named rather than on the element, so a real `Keyed` sentence about the same type still reports. An argument written beside a `Map` that AGREES stays legal — redundant, not wrong — and keeps its contract hash. Tracker A56, ruling R6 (`transport-rpc.md` §9.2).

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**`[rpc] fun login(mut self, …)` compiled and lost the write in silence: the handler mutated its own copy, the reply carried the new value, and the very next call on that connection read the old field.** It was the receiver the `[service]` expansion admitted, so nothing said anything at all — the failure was a value that would not stick, found at runtime, in a program whose types all checked. **`mut self` is refused now, at the attribute, spanned on the METHOD's name**: `` `[rpc]` method `login` takes `mut self`, and an `[rpc]` method's `mut self` copy is discarded after the call: the handler mutates it, the reply carries the new value, and the next call on this connection reads the old one. Write `&mut self` to mutate this connection's instance, or hold the state in a `Shared<T>` field ``. Refused ABOVE the expansion, which is B117's and B266's rule applied a third time: nothing is generated, so the mistake stays one message rather than collecting the generated client's own errors on top. The span moves to the method because the receiver is the thing to change — the message this replaces was spanned on the STRUCT and recommended `mut self` itself. **Keyed on the receiver, never on the body**: a `mut self` method that mutates nothing is refused too, because the receiver is the claim being made and a body that grows one write later would otherwise turn silent again. With `&mut self` honoured by the generator (below), there is no receiver a service admits that discards a write, and the "cannot mutate immutable 'self'" message B272 recorded cannot fire for a service at all. The rpc guide gains a "mutable session state" section stating the three spellings and when each is right — `&mut self` for a write the next call must see, `Shared<T>` for state something OTHER than a method body must reach (a stored callback, a timer, a task outliving the call), `[expose]`d cells for state with a wire behind it. One new ledger row, one must-fail pin in `service_layer.rs` asserting the refusal stands alone. (tracker B272, ruling R-A38b)

<!-- family: fix -->
**`[rpc] fun login(&mut self, …)` did not build: the generated dispatcher declared `fun dispatcher(self)`, an IMMUTABLE binding, so no route could call a method that wanted a mutable receiver — and the build stopped inside generated code, spanned on the STRUCT, recommending `mut self`, the receiver that silently loses the write.** Q9 ruled `&mut self` "the idiomatic in-place receiver" for a service's synchronous session state and the generator never honoured it, so the owner's `struct S { is_authenticated: bool }` + `[rpc] fun login(&mut self, …)` sketch could not be written at all; the spelling that worked was a `Shared<bool>` field. **The dispatcher declares `mut self` now, and that is the whole fix.** Nothing about the generated closures changed: a closure captures the BINDING and not a copy of it (spec §6.9), so a `&mut self` call through any route reaches the one binding `dispatcher()` declares — and `dispatcher()` runs once per connection under `Service::factory`, so the write is the connection's, survives to its next call over the same socket, and is invisible to every other connection. **`mut self` here is not the `mut self` refused on a method** (above), and the difference is lifetime rather than spelling: this copy IS the connection's instance and lives as long as its dispatcher, where a handler's copy dies when the handler returns. **A `Shared<S>` cell was the other candidate and was not taken**: it costs a copy into the cell per connection and an import in the expansion's prelude, it puts a native container between the routes and the instance — which turns C9's resource-owning `[service]` refusal from "a closure cannot capture the resource `self`", spanned on the struct, into "`Shared` cannot hold the resource", rendered with no code frame — and the language already guarantees exactly the aliasing the fix needs. The pin `a_mut_self_rpc_mutation_is_lost_where_a_shared_field_survives`, which recorded the loss, is replaced by `a_mut_ref_self_rpc_write_survives_the_next_call_on_that_connection_alone` in `service_layer.rs` — the owner's sketch end to end over two live connections, with the `Shared<T>` field kept beside it as the control and the no-argument route exercised too; red first against the previous generator, where it takes the old struct-span error verbatim. One unrelated hygiene fix found on the way, in the reflection surface this reading passed through: a `[rpc]` method's PARAMETER rendered as a `meta::Field` with only three of its five slots written, leaving `keyed` and `key` `undefined` in the macro world — harmless only for as long as no macro read them, and now the false/empty constants they mean. (tracker B272, ruling R-A38b option (a))

<!-- family: feature -->
**An `[rpc]` method may RETURN a signal handle: the server writes `SignalCell<T>`, a plain `ChannelId` crosses, and the client's stub answers `Result<RemoteSource<T>, RpcError>` — the half `[expose]` structurally cannot do.** `[expose]` names its channels at compile time, one field per exposure, which is right for state the whole client watches and wrong for state it watches a FRACTION of: the owner's exhibit is a chat where `get_messages(conversation, amount): List<MessageId>` is cheap and `get_message(id): SignalCell<MessageBody>` must be per message. **The mapping is two rewrites and no new frame.** The stub returns `Result<RemoteSource<T>, RpcError>` (`Result<Option<RemoteSource<T>>, RpcError>` for the `Option<SignalCell<T>>` form) and the CONTRACT SURFACE names the mapped type — `get_message(str)->RemoteSource<MessageBody>;` — because the hash exists to protect the client and so must say what the client will decode; a server that turns a handle return into a plain value moves the hash and a stale client is refused at connect instead of reading a channel id as a message. The `expose:`/`keyed:` entries are untouched, so **no shipped service's hash moves** (pinned against `78bdada7`, measured at `c3ed9239`). **The reply path needed a connection, and the honest one is the `Connection` the service already holds**: `RpcProtocol` gains a connection stamp (`for_connection`, set by `Service::new` and `Service::factory` at the upgrade, `-1` for the connectionless POST leg and `local_rpc`), `RpcRequest` carries it, and `reply_source(request, source)` exports through `session_of(request.connection)` — the per-connection capability table §8 already built, which is the arena the sketch asks for and is freed whole by `drop_session`. **The mirror remembers the call that minted it** (`Origin`: the method name, the argument describers, and the seam that issues them again), which is what makes a dynamic handle rebindable and retires A41's refuse-clearly branch for every mirror a generated client holds. **R3 as ruled — demand decides, and there is no `Release` frame.** A dynamic channel's `Unsubscribe` REVOKES it (forward stopped, capability dropped, source freed) where an `[expose]`d field channel's stays demand-only (A41: it has no origin, and a remount must find it on the same id); a lease returning on a revoked channel re-issues the origin, rebinds, and paints its cached value until the fresh seed lands; and a minted mirror's `flush_close` takes one microtask hop before the frame goes out, so a dispose and a remount anywhere inside one MACROTASK — two event handlers, a route change, `bind_each` rebuilding rows — send nothing at all. **The hop is the DYNAMIC mirror's and not every mirror's**, which is where this narrows R3 as written: what it buys differs by channel kind, because a dynamic channel is REVOKED by its `Unsubscribe` (a spurious one costs a call, a capability, a `Subscribe` and a seed) where a field channel's only stops a forward the same id restarts — and widening it would cost every field mirror the promptness `remote-sources.md` §2 ratified and four A25 pins record (a write after the last dispose puts nothing on the wire; under a hop it costs one late `Update`). It also closes a hole underneath R3 for the mirrors it covers: `release` runs from the subscription's stored release hook, so the turn `at_settle` reads is the one that closure captured AT CREATION, and the shipped same-turn cancellation never applied to a lease taken outside a turn at all — the plant shows a same-TURN dispose-and-rebuild costing 2 frames up and 1 down without it. A mirror minted under an ambient owner that nothing ever leased releases when that owner disposes (owner-OPTIONAL, `defer_to_owner`'s shape: with no owner it lives with the connection, which is documented rather than diagnosed). **And a reconnect replays it**: `reattach_mirrors` re-issues each WATCHED minted mirror's origin after the positional `__attach` rebind, so `invalidate_dynamic` is retired for generated mirrors and kept for the hand-wired `ReactiveClient::source`. A method returning a source is a GETTER by declaration and must be safe to re-run — the guide says so, and the guide's new "Handles" section carries the mapping table, the lease rule, the lifetime rule and the owner sentence. Pins: the kolt-shaped exhibit end to end over a real socket with both hash halves (`service_layer.rs`); a hundred handles minted and ten leased read off the server's own tables — 101 capabilities, ZERO forwards, then TEN — with lease-zero revoking (91) and a re-acquire re-minting (92, the getter run a second time) beside the `[expose]` field control that survives its `Unsubscribe`; and the frame counts in process (`reactive_channels.rs`), where a same-turn and a cross-turn remount each cost 0 frames and the plant without the hop costs 2 up, 1 down and a re-mint. `vilan/examples/rpc` grows the method. (tracker A-handles, R3, R7; A53 closes ANSWERED — the element type is written in the method signature where the hash already reads it, and `[service]` on a generic struct stays refused)

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**A handle return's WIRE rule lands on the element, not on the source.** `[rpc] fun watch(self): SignalCell<Secret>` used to be refused as "return type ... is `SignalCell<Secret>`, which is not Wire" — true of the wrapper and useless, because the wrapper is not what crosses: the source stays on the server and its values go one `Update` frame at a time. The check now reads the handle spellings the `[service]` expansion recognises (`SignalCell<T>`, `Option<SignalCell<T>>`) and moves inward by one type argument, refusing in the return type's own vocabulary — "`[rpc]` method `watch` returns a signal handle whose element `Secret` is not Wire: ... it is the ELEMENT that crosses the wire". A Wire element in either form compiles. The RECOGNITION is the written spelling and not a `Source` reconciliation, for `[expose]`'s reason (B202): the expansion runs before any type resolves, so it maps what it can name — and a user type that implements `Source<T>` in a return position is not silently mis-generated, it falls to the ordinary `[rpc]` Wire rule and is refused by name. Three pins in `traits.rs`, one ledger row.

<!-- family: feature -->
**`KeyedCell<K, T>`: a keyed collection whose WRITES are the deltas, so a keyed channel stops paying for the size of the collection on every change.** Exposing a `SignalCell<List<T>>` keyed makes the server DIFF two snapshots per change — `keyed_diff` re-keys both and compares every retained element — and it pays that once per SUBSCRIBED CONNECTION however small the change is. It is irreducible while the source is `List`-valued, because only the MUTATION knows what changed. `KeyedCell<K, T>` is the mutation saying so: `insert`, `remove`, `update(key, |&mut T|)` and `set` each APPEND the `Delta<K, T>` op they are, to a log a subscriber's forward reads by cursor, and the log is trimmed to the laggiest live forward (a channel nobody watches keeps no history; a forward that falls behind `keyed_log_limit` is answered with a `Reset`). A position index makes `update` and `remove` a lookup rather than a scan on both ends. **Nothing on the wire changes** — the same `Reset` seed and the same element-grained `Patch` per change, whole-collection and per-key alike, the same `KeyedSource<K, T>` on the client, and the SAME CONTRACT HASH as the `[expose(keyed = K)] SignalCell<List<T>>` spelling, so a service may swap one field for the other without breaking a deployed client. `[expose] items: KeyedCell<str, Task>` is a keyed channel: the cell names both types itself, so `keyed` is redundant on it and `keyed = K` has nothing to add, and `T: PartialEq` — the diff's way of learning that an element changed — is no longer required. Hand-wired: `ReactiveServer::expose_keyed_cell(cell)`, a distinct name rather than an overload because a cell IS a `Source<List<T>>` and would otherwise satisfy `expose_keyed`'s bound and take the diffing path silently. Tracker A54.

<!-- family: performance -->
**A keyed change costs the change, on both ends: 40x cheaper at 1,000 rows and 372x at 10,000, and flat in the collection.** Two things were O(N) per change and both are gone. On the SERVER, `keyed_diff` re-keyed two whole snapshots per change per connection; a `KeyedCell` forwards the op the write recorded. On the CLIENT, `KeyedSource::apply` did `cache.get()` and `cache.set(..)` around every patch — a `SignalCell` COPIES its value on both — so applying one element-grained op to a 10,000-row mirror deep-copied the mirror twice, and `index_of` then scanned it once per op; `apply` now goes through `SignalCell::update` with `Option::take`/`replace` (the in-place path `update` exists for) and both `index_of` and `pick` read a maintained position index. Measured per change on one connection (`getrusage(RUSAGE_CHILDREN)`, loadavg 14.8-17.3, minimum of three runs, idle run subtracted): the diffing exposure 0.315 ms at 1,000 rows and 3.814 at 10,000 — 12.1x for 10x the rows — against the cell's 0.0078 and 0.0103, **1.32x for 10x the rows**. At eight connections, 0.299 -> 5.033 against 0.0048 -> 0.0148. Counted rather than timed, the same claim is exact: 20 changes over a 2,000-row collection call `Keyed::key` 240,019 times through the diff and **zero** times through the cell, at 200 rows and at 2,000 alike. Pinned as a RATIO and never as a wall bound (`a_keyed_cell_s_cost_per_change_does_not_grow_with_the_collection`). Tracker A54.

<!-- family: feature -->
**A keyed mirror IS a `Source`: `impl KeyedSource<K, T> with Source<Option<List<T>>>`, on the lease that was already there.** A52 gave `RemoteSource` its `Source` impl (`Source<Option<T>>`) and left the keyed twin bare, so a `KeyedSource<K, T>` could be observed only through its own inherent members — A49's `on_change` was not on it, `effect` and `effect_on_change` were not on it, and no generic `S: Source<…>` function could take one at all. Every observing path already went through ONE counted lease (`acquire`/`release`, `Subscribe` at 0→1 and an `Unsubscribe` deferred to the turn's settle at 1→0), so the impl adds no second mechanism: it names the one there is. `get` and `map` MOVE from the inherent impl into it — `map` as an override rather than an inherent member for B258's reason, so the strict owner law reaches a generic consumer and does not promote `status`'s own `self.cache.map(..)`. The inherent `sub(|List<T>|)` stays and still outranks the trait's `sub(|Option<List<T>>|)` on a concrete receiver, exactly as `RemoteSource`'s pair does: the two are told apart by the observer's own parameter type, `mirror.sub` reaches the shape every caller was written against, and a generic `S: Source<Option<List<T>>>` reaches the other. **The `bind_each` sibling is DECLINED** (owner ruling R5): the trait argument is the `Option` because that is the truth — a mirror has not been told anything yet — so the seam into a list binding stays `or([])`, which is the binding SAYING what an unseeded list renders as. Tracker A55.

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**Overriding a trait DEFAULT in one impl silently changed how a DIFFERENT type's inherited copy of that default read its ambient context — `self.cache.map(..)` on a `SignalCell` field ran `register_with_owner` against an `undefined` owner.** The `context` pass threads each context as a hidden parameter and gives every needs-context node a FLAVOR: strict nodes hold the bare value and keep the coverage fence, safe ones hold `Option<T>`. A dispatch site whose candidates mix the two would need two argument forms at one call, so `settle_strict` promotes the safe candidates to strict — and the candidate list it promotes over came from `dispatch_refine::candidates_of`, which is **NAME-keyed**: every override of every trait declaring that name, whatever the receiver. Over-approximating is sound for a consumer that reads an edge as a DEMAND (coverage asks for more, the const-only check refuses more) and is not sound for one that reads the candidate SET as a property of the site. So `RemoteSource`'s strict override of `Source::map` promoted `RemoteSource::status`'s own `self.cache.map(..)` — a call on a `SignalCell` FIELD, which inherits the deliberately owner-OPTIONAL default — to the override's flavor: the default's `owner_scope.get_safe()` was rewritten to `Some(<the hidden parameter>)`, `status` grew a bare-owner parameter its top-level callers never threaded, and the emitted `register_with_owner` reached `Owner::take` on `undefined`. **The fence did not catch it**, because coverage runs on `dispatch_refine`'s REFINED edges while the flavor ran on the union — the two disagreed, and the disagreement is exactly the silent-wrong-output window. **The narrowing the two now share** is the one `refined_edges` already had: an `OnType` site with a KNOWN receiver selects only the members that receiver's HEAD selects (`known_receiver_candidates`, extracted so the `context` pass and the refinement cannot drift), with every unresolvable shape — an `OnConstraint` site, a receiver-less `OnType` inside a shared default body, a generic or opaque receiver, an empty selection — widening back to the whole list. B254 is the neighbour: the same known-receiver narrowing, one pass over. **`std::rpc::RemoteSource::map` drops its workaround** — it was INHERENT with a doc comment naming the compiler limit, and is an override inside `impl RemoteSource<type T> with Source<Option<T>>` again, so the strict "a network subscription must have an owner" law now reaches a generic `S: Source<Option<T>>` and not merely a concrete `mirror.map(..)`. Two pins in `traits.rs`, the first red first (a `Mirror` whose FIELD is a `Cell` inheriting the default `Mirror` overrides: the field call answered `default(cell) under undefined` and answers `default(cell), no scope`), plus the control that the override still fences on its own receiver; A25's four owner pins are the std shape, two of which went red under the restored override. (tracker B258)

<!-- family: feature -->
**`std::router` can READ: `parse_path` takes a URL apart, `FromPath` is `Routable`'s inverse, and the query and fragment are reachable at all for the first time.** The module shipped the write direction whole — `Routable`, `to_path`, `link`, `navigate`, `current_path` — and exactly one read helper, `segments`, so every app hand-wrote index arithmetic to get a route back (kolt's `parts.len() > 3 && parts[2] == "task"` then `parts[3]`, under a FIXME asking for exactly this). **`parse_path(path): PathParts` cuts before it decodes**, which is the whole reason it is one call and not three: the FRAGMENT is delimited first (a `?` after a `#` is fragment text, RFC 3986 §3.5), then the query, then the path splits on `/`, and only then is each piece percent-decoded — so an escaped separator (`%2F` in a segment, `%26` in a value) stays inside the piece it belongs to instead of becoming one. Empty segments do not exist, so `"/w/acme"`, `"/w/acme/"` and `"//w//acme"` parse alike and no match arm names the trailing-slash case; a query key with no `=` is PRESENT with an empty value, so a flag is a `contains_key` question; a repeated key keeps the last; and `fragment` is `None` with no `#` at all but `Some("")` for a bare trailing one, because those are different URLs. Query keys and values additionally read `+` as a space, which a submitted form produces and a path segment never means. `percent_decode` is `decodeURIComponent` made TOTAL — the host function throws on `%zz`, and a URL is text a stranger chose, so a router that can crash on one is a link that takes the page down; an undecodable piece decodes to itself. `parse_query` is public beside it, because a query arrives from other places too. **`FromPath` is the inverse of `Routable`**, so a route enum states its wire format once in each direction and the pair has a law — `from_path(route.to_path())` is `route` — which is one round-trip test per route space instead of a drift nobody notices until a deep link 404s. Its member takes SEGMENTS, not a path: `parse_path` has already cut, decoded and dropped the empties, so an impl is a `match` on `len()`. It is a free generic `from_path<R: FromPath>` rather than a `from_path` default on the trait because the language admits neither half of that shape and says so in two diagnostics — `Self::` cannot dispatch inside a trait default, and an associated function with a default body is not inherited by an impl (no receiver to inherit it through). And `location_url()` (`pathname + search + hash`) is the reach for a live query; `current_path()` stays the PATHNAME deliberately, because a signal that advanced on every `#anchor` would re-render a page for a scroll and a route printing a pathname would stop comparing equal to the location. `segments` is unchanged and now documented as the RAW splitter beside `parse_path`'s decoding one. One pin in `router.rs` over kolt's own route space with its hand-written `parse` replaced by a `FromPath` impl: nine paths through parse-and-reprint (every spelling of the trailing slash, a query and fragment that do not disturb the segments), the query and fragment forms, the cut order, the decode-after-split rule, the raw/decoded pair, and a malformed escape surviving. Proven non-vacuous by dropping the segment decode. (tracker A62)

<!-- family: feature -->
**`std::dom` can MEASURE, OBSERVE and UN-SET.** kolt's `overlay.vl` carries twenty hand-written externs under a banner its owner wrote — "DOM bindings `std::dom` lacks yet" — and `views.vl` adds a twenty-first; every one of them is a binding an anchored overlay cannot be written without, and every one of them lands here. **Measurement is a VALUE**: `Element::bounding_rect(): DomRect` reads `getBoundingClientRect()` once and hands back the four numbers as a `struct DomRect { left, top, width, height }` (with `right()`/`bottom()` derived, not stored, so they cannot disagree with the pair behind them) — a fact about a moment, so it copies, compares and parks in a signal, where a live host rect keeps changing under whoever held it. `offset_width`/`offset_height` are the cheap ROUNDED pair beside the rect's fractional box, and `is_connected` is the guard both wait on, because a detached element measures 0×0 and positioning that runs too early reads as a layout bug rather than a timing one. `contains(other)` is the outside-click question a document-level listener cannot answer from coordinates, `Event::target` is what it is asked about, and `Element::query_selector_all` is the document form scoped to one subtree. **`listen_capture` is `listen` in the other phase**, on `Element` and `Window`, with the same `[must_use]` `Subscription` contract and its own raw `on_event_capture`/`off_event_capture` pair — a second pair rather than a flag, because the PHASE is part of the identity the host matches removal on. It buys the two things bubble cannot: `scroll`, `focus` and `blur` do not bubble, so an ancestor hears them only on the way down (which is what keeps an anchored menu on its element while an inner panel scrolls), and a guard that must run BEFORE the target's own listener has nowhere else to be. **`observe_resize` is the wrapper, not the raw class**: it fires once when observation starts — so a first layout and every later one run through one callback — and its `Subscription` disconnects the observer, where a bare `ResizeObserver` is a `retains` callback that leaks unless every caller remembers to. **Rule 2's last-use elision can see a `Shared` CELL: a binding fed by `cell.read()` may keep naming the cell's storage when nothing can mutate that storage while the binding holds it.** Rule 2 (§6.2) skips a copy when the SOURCE dies at the read — that is the only reason the aliasing it leaves behind can never be observed — so `is_elidable_copy` accepted a plain local binding and nothing else. A cell does not die: `let previous = row_views.read()` leaves the handle holding the same storage and every later read reaches it, which is why B256's ruling stalled on cost. So the question is asked from the other end, and every part of the answer is syntactic. **The cell's own writes are the hazard, and they come in two shapes.** `h.write() = x` REBINDS the slot — a fresh value is installed and the old one is left exactly as it was — so it can never reach back into what a read handed out; every other spelling (`h.write().push(9)`, `update`'s `mutate(self.value.write())`, a component write) mutates the storage the read shares. A cell no write mutates in place is safe outright, which is `bind_each`'s `row_views`/`row_owners`; a cell some write does mutate is safe when a rebind ORPHANS the read first, on the declaring block's own straight line with nothing that could reach a write in between — which is `drain`'s `let wave = turn.pending.read(); turn.pending.write() = [];`, where the clear that looks like the hazard is the thing that ends it. **Cell identity is a union-find over SLOTS, not a root comparison**: two slots can hold one cell (`let g = h.clone()`, `Subscription`'s `subscribers` field initialized from `SignalCell`'s, a handle passed to a parameter), and a handle moves between slots at exactly four forms — a binding's initializer, a construction slot, an assignment, and `clone()` — so unioning there and dropping every other position into one `Unknown` component covers the relation without an alias analysis. **The binding is guarded too**: it may not be mutated in place (`mut c = h.read(); c.push(10)` would grow the cell), may not sit at a value seam, and may not be one the last-use walk is opaque about — which is how a closure capture refuses, since a capture reads the binding from another region. **The base cache's 512 MiB byte budget was denominated ~24× low: it bounded a number that is a fraction of what a retained world weighs, so "512 MiB retained" was a bound on the order of 12 GB resident.** M24's budget is compared against `base_cache_retained_bytes`, which is M11's figure — the world's source TEXTS plus M41's per-`TypeId` census — and that figure is source-proportional BY DESIGN, because an eviction has to recompute exactly what the store recorded without a heap audit. What it is not is what the world weighs. **Measured**, with `world_cache_spike.rs`'s weighing harness (eight distinct keys minted through `macro_limits` over one wide-`std` closure, minus a same-key control that pays the identical per-analysis transient, the parse cache and the interner warmed first so nothing process-global is credited to a world): **4,701,037 B resident per world against 194,843 B recorded — 24.1×**, on a release build at loadavg 112, and 24.1× again in debug. **Two of the three suspects are ruled OUT, and that is half the finding**: the leaked module ASTs (`parse_clean_cached`'s immortal cache) and the interned name tables are process-global — paid once, shared by every world — so a PER-WORLD figure must not carry them, and the harness warms both before it weighs, so they are not in the 4.7 MB either. The gap is the ~229 analyzer tables the resolve fills — scopes, the entity and expression maps, the type tables, the registry clone each stored world carries — which is exactly the derived state M11's figure declines to count. **The budget is corrected, not the counter.** `BASE_CACHE_RESIDENT_BUDGET` is the bound in the currency a session actually has (512 MiB, M24's number); `BASE_CACHE_WEIGHT_FACTOR` is the measured ratio; `BASE_CACHE_DEFAULT_BUDGET` is the first divided by the second, which is the same bound in the currency `evict_to_budget` compares in. The counter itself is untouched, because it is the one figure a store and an eviction can never disagree about — and `base_cache_retained_weight()` re-denominates it for anyone reporting to a human. **`VILAN_BASE_CACHE_BUDGET_MIB` was loose in the same direction and by the same factor**: its number is mebibytes of MEMORY, which is what anyone reasoning about a language server's footprint means, and it went straight into the budget — `base_cache_budget_for_resident` is the one conversion between the two currencies now, and `0` survives it unchanged (M24's "retain nothing but the world just stored"). **M46's checked-cache budget keeps its 64 MiB and changes its derivation**: `ModuleTables::bytes` is a structural count of the rows it holds, already in the units a machine has, so it needs no re-denomination — deriving it from the re-denominated constant would have quietly divided it by 24 too. Pinned two ways: the weighing harness asserts the measured factor is within **3×** of the shipped one (a wide band on purpose — this asserts a DENOMINATION, not a byte count — and it still reds by orders of magnitude if the counter starts or stops counting the derived tables), declining rather than failing where `/proc/self/statm` is absent or the control outgrew the measurement; and the two constants are pinned as one bound in two currencies, with `0` surviving and the recorded budget asserted SMALLER than the resident one, which reds if the factor is ever inverted. (tracker M50)

**`vilan fmt` canonicalizes an element HEAD — the import and style-chain sorters' third sibling: undotted attributes lead in `id`, `name`, `type`, `for`, `href`, `src` order and then alphabetically, `on:` handlers follow them alphabetically, and a dotted chain link is a BARRIER that never moves.** The desugar is the whole argument. So the step is narrow — **the COMPILES of one tier overlap, nothing else** — and the compile is where the time is. **A mirror was not a `Source`: `RemoteSource<T>` carried `get`/`map`/`or` as inherent members and implemented nothing, so A49's `on_change` was not on it, `effect` was not on it, and no generic `S: Source<…>` function — `selector`, or an application's own — could take one.** The mirror sat outside the trait every other observable value in the estate is behind, and the only way into the ordinary reactive world was to flatten it with `or`/`map` first. `impl RemoteSource<type T> with Source<Option<T>>` now names the counted lease that was always there: `get` and `on_change` are the requirements, `sub` and `effect` are overridden onto the same `lease` the inherent members ride, `effect_on_change` comes free, and nothing is a second mechanism. **The trait argument is `Option<T>`, not `T`, because that is what a mirror holds** — `get` cannot invent a `T` before the first frame — so a `RemoteSource<List<Note>>` is *not* a `Source<List<Note>>` and `bind_each` still takes `mirror.or([])`; that boundary is pinned with its refusal ("'RemoteSource<List<Todo>>' does not implement trait 'Source<List<T>>'") beside the `or` spelling that works, so the sentence in the docs is checkable. **`on_change` attaches BEFORE it takes the lease, and the order is forced rather than chosen**: taking the lease is what sends `Subscribe`, and over an in-process transport the server's seeding `Update` comes back inside that call — acquiring first would drop the first value on a `duplex_pair` and deliver it over a socket, which is a transport-dependent contract and not one at all. Attached first, the seed is a change from the `None` the mirror held, on every transport; nothing is swallowed, because an unopened mirror already holds `None`. `sub` and `effect` are overridden for the same reason in reverse — their trait defaults are `on_change` plus one call, which on a mirror would make the immediate call twice. **The inherent `sub(|T|)` stays and still wins on a concrete receiver**: the two are told apart by the observer's own parameter type (`|T|` against `|Option<T>|`), so a caller cannot silently reach the other one, and every doc fence and estate caller is unmoved. **`map` and `or` stay inherent too, and that one is a compiler limit rather than a preference** — written as an override inside the `Source` impl, `status`'s own `self.cache.map(…)` (a call on a `SignalCell` field, which inherits the trait's default) miscompiles and `register_with_owner` runs with an undefined owner, reddening both A25 owner pins; overriding a default that the receiver's own field type inherits is the shape that breaks. Keeping them inherent keeps A25's stricter law (a mirror derivation must have an owner, statically) on a concrete receiver, at the cost that a generic `S: Source<…>` calling `.map` gets the owner-optional default. Four pins, three of them red first with "does not implement trait 'Source<Option<i32>>', required by a generic bound of this call". (tracker A52; docs `std/rpc.md`, `guide/services.md`)

It is `[derive(Wire, Debug, PartialEq)]` now: the unit arm compares by discriminant, and a payload arm compares its SENTENCE, which is what a `Transport(reason)` against a literal means. **`List::remove` and `List::insert` were hand-written shift loops over the CHECKED subscript helpers, so moving a list's tail cost a bounds check, a `__clone` and a store per element: `remove(0)` on a ten-thousand-element list was 13.9 µs, and `xs.insert(2, 3)` emitted a `while` loop where the host has a `memmove`.** Both are intrinsics now, in `pop`'s pattern — `external fun` in `std/src/list.vl`, `Intrinsic::ListRemove`/`ListInsert` in the analyzer, one emitted helper each over the native `.splice`. **The bounds panic is kept, and keeping it is the whole reason the helper exists**: `splice` CLAMPS an index past the end (`[10,20,30].splice(3, 1)` is `[]`, and `splice(4, 0, v)` appends) and reads a NEGATIVE one from the END (`splice(-1, 1)` is `[30]`), so a bare `self.splice(index, 1)[0]` would answer *exactly* the four indices `insert`'s and `remove`'s docs say a caller must be punished for — and answer them with a plausible element rather than a refusal. The helpers carry `__at`'s guard and `__at`'s wording (`index out of bounds: the length is N but the index is M`), so a caller cannot tell which of the two refused; `index == len` is still the documented append and takes a `push`. **A struct field may name a TRAIT — `struct Store { count: Signal<i32> }` — and it means a type parameter the author never writes.** The field's annotation desugars to a hidden generic bounded by that trait (`struct Store<S: Signal<i32>> { count: S }`), one per such field, appended after every parameter the declaration wrote and **grounded per literal**, not per program: `Store { count = SignalCell::new(1) }` is a `Store<SignalCell<i32>>`, and a second literal in the same scope may ground it at a different implementation. That is the per-binding rule the language already had one and two levels down — a `let` annotation keeps its initializer's concrete type (B161) and a `fun f(x: Trait)` mints one implicit generic per parameter (B186) — so ruling the field the other way would have made it the one position where a trait annotation constrains other people's code. The grammar is BARE, no `impl` keyword: both shipped positions are bare, and the editor already paints a trait annotation `interface` and a struct annotation `struct` in the same position, which is the distinction a keyword would have marked twice. **`Store` is really `Store<impl Signal<i32>>`, and the argument comes from a value**: a `fun` parameter mints a fresh implicit generic (so `fun read(s: Store)` is generic and takes both of the values above, and two mentions in one signature are two independent arguments), an `impl` subject grounds it the way `impl Store<type S>` would, a field of another struct makes THAT struct hidden-generic in turn — the virality is real and invisible — and a binding's annotation reads as B161's constraint, since the initializer is what grounds. Every position with no value in it refuses at the annotation and says which positions do: a return type, a module-level `Context<Store>`, any nested spelling; writing the argument is refused too, because the hidden parameter is deliberately absent from the written arity. **Emission is byte-identical to the written generic** — the same program spelled both ways compiles to the same JavaScript, byte for byte, two monomorphized bodies and values that are still bare arrays with no tag and nowhere for a vtable to live. **The hidden argument PRINTS**, which is a deliberate deviation from the trait-name display an implicit generic otherwise gets: reassigning a `Store<SignalCell<i32>>` to a `Store<OtherCell<i32>>` reports `Expected Store<SignalCell<i32>>, but got Store<OtherCell<i32>> instead.` with the initializer note, where the display rule would have produced the useless `Expected Store, but got Store` — the shape B211's three-way rotate and any call-argument mismatch through the sugar inherit. **Not on an attributed declaration**: `[derive(..)]`, `[service(..)]` and user macro attributes generate code from the types the author wrote, and a hidden parameter is written nowhere, so a field there keeps the refusal and its steer drops the clause it cannot honour. Two §12.2 holes the field position used to be banned for are shut by the semantics instead of the ban, exactly as B161 shut the binding's: a resource behind a trait-typed field still runs its destructor, and the route to B55's internal error through a field is an ordinary running program. 23 pins in `traits.rs` and two in the language server (the annotation paints `interface` beside a struct's `struct`; an inlay hint reads `: C<A>`), red-proved against three planted rules — the program-wide reading, a virality stopped at one level, and the trait-name display, which reproduces `Expected C, but got C instead.` twice. Corpus goldens are byte-identical. Spec §5.5 gains the field position. (tracker B184, B218; `proposal/trait-typed-fields.md` revision 2)

**A `fun` can now DECLARE what it reads: `fun render(row: Row): str context (app_ctx, turn_scope)`.** A function's context requirement has always been inferred from its body and flowed to every caller — which means it is a fact about a body, so every diagnostic about it is a fact about a body, and it surfaces wherever inference breaks rather than where the reader made a decision. One mistyped `run` argument buried the real error under three coverage fences (B229); one missing call argument produced three "can't be used as a value" refusals and five fences, four of them inside std, in code the program never touched (B241). Both are fixed at the mechanism, and both are the same shape: an inferred requirement has no boundary, so a break anywhere propagates as far as inference does. **A declared clause makes the requirement a fact about the signature**, in the spelling closure types already use (`(|| T) context flavor`), after the return type. Three rules follow, and they are one idea: **the body's strict reads must be a subset of the clause** (an error at the declaration, naming the clause the body needs); **callers are checked against the clause alone** — a call from code that is neither under a `run` of that context nor declaring it itself is refused at the CALL, naming the clause and the callee, one hop; and **the declaring body is never the site of a coverage refusal**, because its signature says the value arrives and the check moves to where that promise is made or broken. That last rule is what makes it a boundary: B241's shape with a clause reports the arity error and nothing else. **A clause WIDER than the body is a warning, not an error** — declaring a context the body does not yet read is a deliberate API surface, and adding the read later must not break callers. **Safe reads are outside the subset** (they impose no requirement on anyone), which is load-bearing rather than tidy: every `async` spawn is an implicit safe read of the standard library's ambient nursery, so a rule over all reads would force `context ambient_nursery` onto every function containing a spawn. An undeclared function keeps inference — the two forms coexist, and the clause is an opt-in boundary rather than a migration. **A clause on a trait or `impl` method is refused for now**, with a message that says why: a dispatched call selects its callee at the call site, so there is no single declaration to check against; the shape a later version needs (the clause on the trait's declaration, every override a subset of it) is written down in `proposal/contexts.md` §4. The editor shows the clause in a hovered signature and offers **Declare the inferred contexts** on the subset refusal, writing the spelling the refusal itself carries over the clause's own name list. Spec §8.6 states the rules and grammar §3.3 carries the production; eleven pins across `macros.rs` (seven: the accepted shape, the subset refusal, the wider clause's warning and its span, an undeclared caller, a declaring caller, B241's shape at the boundary, the member refusal), `parsing.rs`, `formatter.rs` and the language server (hover and the fix), every one of them red before — the syntax did not parse. (tracker B242; `proposal/contexts.md`)

That silence had a second cost: B229's context stand-down had to ask first whether the program carried any diagnostic at all, because a `run` the fixpoint never selected on an otherwise clean program would have turned a coverage fence into exactly the silent miscompile the coverage check exists to prevent, and nothing else would have said a word. **The stalled call now reports, naming the operand that stalled it** — the receiver (a method cannot be looked up until its receiver's type is known) or the first argument that never landed, with the same "could not be resolved" register its four siblings use. And **B229's clean-program guard goes**: an unselected method call means a diagnostic now, always, so the question the guard asked can no longer have the answer it was written for. Two pins in `macros.rs`, both red before the fix (the first as a silent compile). (tracker B232)

The measurement is a test rather than a claim — a cleared cache, one analysis of a wide-`std` program (cold), then the very next analysis of the same import set (the hit a second PROCESS would be served), with process CPU read off `/proc/self/stat` because wall on this box is not an instrument. The pin's bar is a third rather than a half: it exists to catch the day the floor goes to nothing, not to encode this run's figure. **The fix is not here, and the reason is stated where the measurement is.** Serving that hit across processes means writing a `World<'static>` to a file and reading it back, and the world is a graph of `&'src str` into the parse cache's leaked module texts and of `Span` offsets into them, spread over some forty maps; nothing in the tree serializes it. The design the number justifies, for whoever builds it: texts plus offsets, keyed by M21's key (the std sources' content hashes and the toolchain hash) so an edited `std` misses by CONTENT the way the in-memory cache already does; M24's byte budget and its LRU for eviction; M9's leak-soak rules for what a served world may retain; a temp-file-plus-rename write, so a killed process cannot leave a half-file behind; and a checksum that turns a corrupt or truncated file into a MISS rather than into a wrong answer. The consequence is that offering a name imported from a large module cost that module's read and its `String` allocation on every keystroke: 0.415 ms per request against 0.324 ms with the render stubbed out (M39's filing). **The paragraphs are a function of the analysis, so they are rendered where the analysis is.** `CompletionIndex` — the table M25 built for exactly this reason, derived on the server's analysis thread and on the playground's retained handle — gains every NON-ENTRY function's and external's first paragraph, one read per declaring MODULE rather than one per declaration, and a request reads a lookup. The freshness rule is the one its neighbours already keep: an entry is as old as the analysis it was built from and is replaced wholesale when the next one lands, so an edit to the declaring module is already an event that rebuilds it. **The entry's own declarations are deliberately excluded** — their text is the analyzed text the query already holds, and it is the one text a keystroke changes. **An undocumented declaration is answered from the table too**, which is the half that finishes the job: a lookup that returned "absent" for "no doc" sent an undocumented std function back to the renderer to read its module and find nothing there, and the request still paid two module reads. The third stays separate because it READS what the first fills, which is the reason it cannot join them. **`compute_view_origins` was the same shape and gets the same treatment**: its fixpoint re-derived its two candidate sets from `self.variables` and the whole expression map on every round, and a fixpoint pays at least two rounds — one to converge and one to notice — so a program with two view origins walked a 200,000-entry map twice to find a handful of `Match` legs. Neither collection is touched by the loop body (`&self`), so both are collected once, in the identical order an unmodified `HashMap` yields every time. Measured by instruction count rather than by a clock, this box having run at loadavg 50-190 all cycle with CPU on it load-dependent: `callgrind` on `vilan check src/client.vl` over the full kolt copy (browser entry, lucide included), **7,198,865,709 instructions before and 7,173,005,273 after — 25,860,436 fewer, 0.36%**, the two readings taken either side of this change alone on one pair of binaries. Callgrind counts instructions, so the figure is the same at loadavg 5 and at loadavg 190. **It is far smaller than the filing implied, and that is the more useful half of the measurement**: M37's "450 of 758 ms" came from a wall-clock probe taken at loadavg 31-166, and wall under that load is not CPU. The pass was never 60% of a `vilan check` — it was 60% of a wall reading, and the whole of it is well under 1% of the work a check does. Corpus goldens byte-identical; the whole `vilan-core` suite (4,847 tests) green. (tracker M37)

**The base cache's byte tally counted the module texts a world was built from and nothing else, so it under-reported every retained world by the size of T0's per-`TypeId` census — 25,900 B of a plain std world's 177,775 B, 17% of the figure M24's LRU budget is compared against.** `type_id_sources` is a dense `Vec<SourceId>` indexed by the id's own counter (M19 T0's dirty-bit census, which stamps the source each `TypeId` was minted in), so it costs four bytes for every type a world ever mints — instantiations included, which is a count no text length predicts. **`Source::on_change` is now the trait's REQUIREMENT and `sub` is derived from it — an implementation writes `get` and the LAZY attach, and the whole eager family arrives free.** The pair landed the other way round (A43): `sub` required, `on_change` a default that wrapped it. That default could only be honest by subscribing eagerly and then SWALLOWING the immediate call `sub`'s contract promises — a wrapper cell, a branch on every notification for the life of the subscription, and a first change that is indistinguishable from the seeding one. Building the eager form over the lazy one is pure addition instead: `sub` is `on_change` plus one call with the current value, `effect` is `effect_on_change` plus that same call, and nothing is swallowed anywhere in the trait. **The migration is one line per implementation**: rename `fun sub` to `fun on_change`, drop whatever immediate call the body made, and delegate to the inner source's `on_change`. Callers are untouched — `sub`, `effect`, `on_change`, `effect_on_change` and `map` all mean exactly what they meant, and `combine`, `map` and `selector` keep their pins. The refusal names the work — *'Stored' does not implement trait 'Source': missing 'on_change'; declare `fun on_change(self, observer: |T| void): Subscription`* — and points at the trait's declaration beside it. Migrated in the estate: nine `impl … with Source` in the shared test suites, three doc examples, and the `Stored` in the corpus program. `SignalCell` implements `on_change` as `observe` — the direct attach that always was the primitive — and keeps a `sub` override, which is now the trait's own default body with one call less indirection, because every UI binding in a program lands there. Three inference pins (the refusal, the declaration the refusal spells, an `on_change`-only source satisfying a bound and driving both members) and one behavioural pin that runs an implementation writing `get`/`on_change` and nothing else: `sub` fires once with the value already held and then once per change, and `effect` does the same under an owner. Proven red by planting a `sub` default that forwards without the call — the one immediate value disappears from the run. Three golden families move and no program's output does: `reactive-on-change.vl`'s witness is now the emitted default `sub` over a custom source (with a `witness-absent: seeded` beside it, which is the "nothing is swallowed" claim in the bytes), and `reactive-owner.vl` and the split fixture's eager bundle both take the one shape change — `effect` reaches `effect_on_change` where it used to reach `sub`, which is the same two calls in the same order one function deeper. The split fixture's chunks and its manifest are byte-identical. A `Signal` implementation that writes `get`/`on_change` in ONE `with Signal<T>` block should split it in two — `with Source<T>` for the read pair, `with Signal<T>` for `set`/`notify` — which is the shape std's own docs and tests use. (tracker A49, from lane std-27's find; docs `std/reactive.md`)

**A client refused at the handshake burned the full retry budget — ten redials over ~24 s — and then reported `Transport("could not reach …")` about a server that had answered immediately. It now gets `RpcError::Unauthorized` on the first attempt.** The cause is not in the retry loop: **no host WebSocket shows a client the HTTP status of a failed handshake.** Measured on node v24.2.0, whose global `WebSocket` (undici) is what `std::rpc` binds — a 401, a 403, a 429, a socket destroyed mid-handshake, a refused TCP connection and a server with no upgrade handler at all produce byte-for-byte the same error event ("Received network error or non-101 status code.") and the same close (code 1002, not clean). The browser API exposes strictly less, by design. So the option this was filed with — read the status off the error event, as node's `ws` package allows through `unexpected-response` — is not available at all here: std binds the host global on every platform and adds no client dependency, and it would leave the browser blind regardless. **The refusal is therefore SENT, not inferred.** A client that offered the `vilan-rpc` subprotocol is upgraded and handed one `__reject:<status>` frame — the `__conn:<id>` announcement's negative twin — before the socket closes; `dial_socket` reads it, `dial_with_backoff` ends the loop on it, and `dial_for_service` maps 401 and 403 alike to `RpcError::Unauthorized`. Everything that is not a vilan rpc client still gets the plain HTTP status line: a browser opening the URL, `curl`, a probe, a health check, a scanner, so the HTTP semantics of a refused handshake are unchanged for everything that speaks HTTP and not this protocol. **The DoS trade A40 avoided is bounded rather than paid**: a refusal that upgrades costs one 101 and one small frame where a status line costs one write, the socket is destroyed in the same turn either way so nothing is held, and `Reject::TooMany` is never eligible for the frame — which is exactly what `max_connections`, `handshake_rate` and `authorize_timeout` produce, so the refusals a flood makes are the ones that never upgrade and nobody can reach the expensive path more often than the rate limiter admits. `Client::connect` now offers `vilan-rpc` (and no credential), so the commonest refusal of all — a client with no token — is one it can be told about; `connect_with` is unchanged. `connect_socket`/`connect_socket_with` keep their `Err(str)`; the typed `dial_socket(url, protocols): Result<SocketDuplex, DialFailure>` is beside them. Three pins: the refusal frame on the wire, the status line still answering a non-vilan client, and the whole loop end to end — proven red by planting the pre-A47 server, where the same program answers `Transport("could not reach ws://localhost:44659/")` and takes 34.0 s where the fixed one takes 11.2 s, build included. (tracker A47, from lane rpc-27's find; docs `guide/services.md`, `std/rpc.md`)

<!-- family: feature -->
**`Service::authorize_timeout(millis)` bounds the verifier, and `Service::trust_forwarded_for(bool)` decides which address a limit is keyed on.** `authorize` is awaited INSIDE the upgrade handler, so a hook that hangs — a token endpoint that stopped answering, a database that is gone — holds an unanswered socket for as long as it hangs, one per client trying to connect: a denial of service the server inflicts on itself, reached without a single malformed byte from anyone. `handshake_rate` caps how fast that pile grows and nothing capped how big it gets. The bound is armed before the hook is called and answered on the timeout's own turn, not when the hook eventually returns — which is the thing that may never happen — and a hook that answers late is not raced back in, because the socket is already gone. **The refusal is 429 (`Reject::TooMany`), not 503**: the enum's distinction is judgement (401/403) against LIMIT, a verification that ran out of time says nothing about the credential and is the one refusal a client should retry, and a fourth status would mean a fourth arm on an enum whose three arms are the three answers an app's own `authorize` may give. `trust_forwarded_for(true)` reads a client's address from the first entry of `X-Forwarded-For` instead of the socket peer — for `handshake_rate`, for `Handshake.remote_addr` and for `Connection.remote_addr`, one switch for all three, because a deployment either sits behind a proxy or it does not. It is off by default and must stay off unless a proxy you control is the only way in: the header is written by whoever spoke last, so a directly-exposed server that trusted it would let any client pick its own rate-limit bucket, and its own audit trail, by writing one line. Documented alongside: **`max_connections` counts upgraded sockets on its mount and nothing else** — not the SSE or POST legs, which hold no connection to count, and not a handshake still inside `authorize`. Two pins, each red first: the slow verifier (planted at the default `authorize_timeout(0)`, the handshake reads back EMPTY, the socket held past the reader's own bound while the hook sleeps) and the forwarded key with its untrusting control (planted at the old key, "client 1 attempt 0 … HTTP/1.1 429" — the third handshake overall, from the one socket peer they all share). (tracker A48, from lane rpc-27's find; docs `guide/services.md`, `std/rpc.md`)

<!-- family: feature -->
**`[expose]` resynced the whole value on every change, so editing one message in a channel of five thousand cost the channel — `[expose(keyed)]` sends the change instead, and a client can subscribe to ONE key.** Measured over twenty channels of fifty messages: an edit goes from 123,753 bytes on the wire to **95**, a post from 6,033 (against a single channel's list, the fairer baseline) to **163**, a delete to **34** — and a subscriber holding one key is told **nothing** at all about the others, which is the column no amount of client-side filtering can produce. The three pieces, all additive: `std::wire` gains the delta vocabulary — `Delta<K, T> { Reset | Insert | Update | Remove }`, `trait Keyed<K>`, and `impl Map<K, V> with Wire` (backlog I1's gap; transport-rpc Q8 launched without map serialization and said to pull it in when a real payload needed one, and this is that payload). The reactive protocol gains `Patch(channel, ops)` beside `Update(channel, value)`, and its control frames gain an optional key — `Subscribe(channel, Some(key))` / `Unsubscribe(channel, Some(key))`, the key described inline at its own type — so **per-key demand is a property of the protocol** rather than of an application method handing out a channel per row, and the existing counted lease releases a key exactly as it releases a channel. The server keys its live forwards by (channel, key), diffs successive snapshots by key (removals, then insertions in ascending final index, then updates; a REORDER has no op of its own and falls back to `Reset`, which is rare for a collection that appends and edits and correct where a cleverer diff would be subtly wrong), and forwards only the subscribed key's changes. The client mirror is a `KeyedSource<K, T>`: `sub`/`map`/`or` lease the whole collection, `of(key)`/`sub_key(key, …)` lease one, and whole-collection demand SUBSUMES per-key demand, so holding both never doubles a delivery. `fault()` reports the first op that named a key the mirror does not hold — a server bug or a lost frame, never something application code can cause — and refuses to apply it rather than inventing an element. **The macro form is `[expose(keyed)] messages: SignalCell<Map<K, V>>`**, whose mirror the generated client carries directly, so a keyed channel no longer needs the hand-wired `ReactiveClient` A30 declined to expose; the element must be written as a `Map<K, V>` because vilan has no associated types and that is the only place the key type can come from, and a field written otherwise is refused in as many words. A keyed exposure is its own contract-surface entry, so **the contract hash moves only for a service that uses the form** — a plain-`[expose]` service hashes byte-identically to before, pinned. A keyed mirror rebinds across a reconnect like any other and re-subscribes every key it still holds, which is the protocol form A41 recorded as missing when it made `invalidate_dynamic` refuse clearly instead; its cache is cleared first, because a keyed forward reseeds only what it is asked for and an element deleted while the connection was down would otherwise survive as a ghost no later op would ever name. Four pins in `reactive_channels.rs` (the metered exhibit, the per-key lifecycle, the stray patch, the keyed rebind) and one in `service_layer.rs` (the generated client over a real WebSocket), each proven non-vacuous by planting the bug it removes. `guide/services.md` gains the keyed-mirror section with the measured table. (tracker A39; `proposal/transport-rpc.md` §8/Q8, `proposal/remote-sources.md` §2a)

<!-- family: fix -->
**A client holding both a whole-collection lease and a per-key lease on one keyed channel could make its own mirror report a protocol fault.** Found while building the generated-client exhibit above: two server-side forwards carried the same key, so every op on it arrived twice — and the second `Remove` named a key the mirror had already dropped, which is exactly the fault a keyed mirror exists to report. Demand and wire state part company in one place now: a key asks for nothing while the whole collection is held, the whole-collection 0→1 releases every key that was on the wire, and its 1→0 flush hands the wire back to whatever per-key demand outlived it. (tracker A39)

On a 58-source application at 100k entities they were still being rebuilt in full on every character typed in the entry, over bodies whose bytes had not changed and whose entity ids — by the same argument tranche 1 rests on — had not moved. **Six of them are now cached per module beside that module's diagnostics and restored, not recomputed**: `liveness::LastUse::compute` (all five of its row sets), `infer_bumps`, `compute_clone_sites`, `compute_return_clone_sites` and its returned-view reads, `compute_scalar_view_calls` and `compute_scalar_view_refs`. The seam is the same one, keyed the same way and gated on the same three terms — a base-cache HIT, a module the entry did not dirty, and a record filed under the same content — with one added term of its own: the module's table slice must have been recorded too, so a record written by an analysis that was cancelled between the two stores replays its diagnostics and rebuilds its tables, which is exactly tranche 1's behaviour. **Warm keystroke CPU, min / median of thirteen pairs interleaved in one process so both legs see the same load and the same warm world: the application's client leg 351 / 370 ms → 331 / 341 ms (loadavg 15.6), the generated view exhibit 253 / 261 ms → 226 / 236 ms (loadavg 13.5).** Against the arc's own record that is 411 ms before tranche 1, 367 after it, and 341 after this one — all three quiet-box medians on the same subject. The phase line gains a `tables n` count beside tranche 1's census, and the application reads `reused 58/58 entry-dirty 0 tables 58` on every warm analysis. **What decides the boundary is a type id.** A `TypeId` is minted per OCCURRENCE against the buffer being edited (`type_id_for_type`, B77/B95), so one minted after the world was stored names a slot the next analysis never mints, and a restored value carrying it would index a table that does not have it. **No `TypeId` crosses this record**, which is what keeps the drop planner out of the tranche: `plan_resource_drops`, `record_drop_sink_argument_types` and `build_drop_glue` fill `resource_temporaries` and `drop_owned_types_by_root` from `infer_type(..).get_type_id(..)` *inside* the checks phase, so freezing them needs the mint frozen with them — the same reason `check_hmr_transfer_bounds` was held back in tranche 1. `check_container_resource_arguments` (R10) stays live for a sharper version of its own reason: its report feeds R11 through **two** dedup sets, and the second is a `HashSet<TypeId>` of instantiations, so carrying the structure set alone would let R11 re-report what R10 had already reported. The second boundary is attribution: a row whose derivation could have been the ENTRY's is not recorded at all. The last-use walk now tracks a `foreign_touched` set — a module-level binding the entry reads is first-wins across regions, so its statement chain depends on which buffer is open — and it records the walk's OWN opacity rather than the merged verdict, because `collect_unfollowable_loans` and the view-origin closure are whole-program scans an entry's expressions can reach into and they run on every analysis regardless. **The gate is a differential of its own, and it is the emitted JavaScript that carries it**: class D writes no diagnostic, so a leg that only compared diagnostics would be blind to this tranche. Every corpus program is re-hosted as a package module with a class D probe appended — a function returning a place its frame owns, one returning a place it does not, and a `&mut` receiver whose `bumps` verdict has to be inferred — under an entry that CALLS them, so the bodies survive emission; the second analysis is then compared between a leg that restores the tables and a leg that recomputes them, with tranche 1's replay on in both, and the two must agree byte for byte on diagnostics, warnings, per-file attribution and emitted JS. It is red-first twice over. A planted **stale table** — the module's bodies skipped exactly as they are on the fast path, and empty rows served in their place — moves the emitted JavaScript of all 41 corpus modules that emit, and moves it on a dedicated fixture too; the first cut of this leg was silently vacuous without the probe, because the corpus entry imports its module and calls nothing, and the plant is what found that. |---|---|---|---|

| | sequential | 76.6 ms | 73.4 ms |
| | **parallel** | **64.3 ms** (−16.1%) | 79.4 ms (+8.2%) |
| | all members cold (measured, not shipped) | 46.3 ms | 119.3 ms (+63%) |
| | one entry alone | 40.8 ms | 37.1 ms |
| a browser application, 3 entries, loadavg 0.68–0.88 | `next` before this cycle | 916.1 ms | 910.0 ms |
| | sequential | 726.7 ms | 725.3 ms |
| | **parallel** | **677.5 ms** (−6.8%) | 748.2 ms (+3.2%) |
| | all members cold (measured, not shipped) | 522.3 ms | 824.3 ms (+13.7%) |
| | the heaviest entry alone | 580.7 ms | 577.2 ms |

**`fun check(): Result<bool, str> { let v = probe()? > 0; Ok(v) }` compiled clean and handed back `Ok(Ok(true))`, and an `Err` from `probe` came back as `Ok(Err("boom"))` — never propagated.** The `?` in it is the EXPRESSION LIFT, not a try-assert: a bare `?` lifts its whole enclosing slot (`expression-lifting.md` §2), and a `let` initializer is a slot, so `v` is a `Result<bool, str>` and `Ok(v)` builds a `Result<Result<bool, str>, str>`. The emission was right; the type check was the hole. **A generic enum variant's payload was never checked against the instantiation the position expects.** Two sites could have caught it and neither does on its own: the call-subject check reconciles the argument against the enum's still-OPEN parameter (`T` accepts anything), and the inference that fills the constructor's type arguments SEEDS them from the expected type — bidirectional inference, so `Ok(decode())` in a `Result<Option<User>, str>` context types `decode()` against `Option<User>` rather than the abstract `T`. When the argument then contradicted that seed the failed reconcile was simply dropped and the seed stood, so the constructor typed as the expectation and the payload's own type was never compared to anything. `let x: Result<i32, str> = Ok(true)` compiled, `x` reported as `Result<i32, str>`, and `[0, true]` sat behind it — reachable as a plain `i32` through any `match`. **The seed is a hint now, never an override**: a payload that contradicts it re-binds from its own type, so the constructor is the enum at the arguments its payload actually binds and the mismatch is reported where the value lands (a `let` annotation, a call argument, a struct field, a `ret`). An unknown or a diverging `panic(..)` payload says nothing and leaves the seed alone. The same hole covered `flag && probe()? > 0`, whose lift hoists above the `&&` by design — that program is a type error now rather than a wrong answer, and `!` in the same positions was correct all along (its lowering already emits the early return and yields the payload, and with B224's statement slot it short-circuits): both are pinned as controls beside the seven new pins in `generics.rs`, four red before the fix. Corpus goldens are byte-identical — nothing emitted changed, and the estate's only bare-`?` programs (`expression-lift.vl`) always spelled the container type. Spec §5.10 states where a bare `?` lands and §5.11 lists the payload check. (tracker B230)

**`if a is Some(let x) && x.on_drag_end is Some(let y) { … }` compiled clean and then threw on a `None`: `TypeError: cannot read properties of undefined`.** The emitter had no statement slot for a condition, so ANY operand that lowers to statements was walked into the ENCLOSING block and ran unconditionally — `const $a = a; const $b = $a[1][0]; if ($a[0] === 0 && $b[0] === 0)`, the second test's subject read out of a payload that may not exist, before the test that was supposed to gate it. The hoist is what keeps B187's continuation nameable: `if !(A && B) { ret; } print(y)` reads `y` after the `if`, and reaching there proves the sequence ran. An operand carrying something with no expression form — an if-expression, a resource temporary's `try`, a divergent `ret` — falls back to `let $r = lhs; if ($r) { … $r = rhs; }` (`if (!$r)` for `||`), which is `&&`/`||` exactly. So the first call to reach the parameter WROTE `any` into the shared slot, ahead of the enclosing call that actually knew, and first writer won permanently. It was never about `print`: a hand-written `fun sink(m: any)` did it identically. **The most visible spelling was every event handler**: `<div on:keydown(|event| { print(event); event.key() })>` reported `event` as `any`, so nothing about `Event` was checked inside a handler that printed — the `on:` desugar was sound all along, and the `|event: Event|` annotations applications carry are a workaround for this, not the required spelling. **`any` is now skipped, and skipped WITHOUT deferring**: the slot stays open for the call that can fill it, and a closure whose ONLY use is an `any` call gets no type from anywhere — the right answer, already covered by "type of variable could not be resolved", and the same verdict a generic `fun sink<T>(m: T)` has always given the same program. Deferring instead would deadlock that closure outright. Eight pins across `generics.rs` and `styling.rs` — the printed/print-free pair, the user-`any` twin that shows it is the type and not the function, a negative that refuses to see `any` as any refusal's subject, the handler pair, and the sole-use edge — six of them plant-proved red. A census of two real applications (`vilan check` over each, every entry) is unchanged in both directions. (tracker B227)

**`import pkg::client::SidebarTab;` at the top of the ENTRY `client.vl`, beside `[derive(PartialEq)] enum SidebarTab { … }`, made the derive vanish: "type 'SidebarTab' does not implement the `PartialEq` operator" over a type that plainly derives it.** `is_entry_module` was origin-blind — it asked only whether the module file the loader was about to read IS the entry file — and that question has two unrelated answers. One is the case it was written for, a std or dependency file opened directly in an editor, which is then analyzed *as* that module from the buffer rather than read a second time from disk. The other is a `pkg::<entry>` reference walking back into the program's own entry, which flipped the same flag and so skipped the entry-as-program walk AND the entry's own macro/derive expansion: every `[derive]` on an entry type was expanded nowhere, and a self-imported FUNCTION cost the entry its whole item table — `main` included, so the build died with "Cannot execute program without a main function". **The flag is stated as the origin gate it always was** (`Origin::Std | Origin::Dep(_)`), and a `pkg::` re-entry is answered by ALIASING the module name onto the entry's own scope instead of building a second module for it: nothing is loaded, walked or typed twice, and `pkg::<entry>::Name` resolves to the entry's own declaration, which is what the import asked for. **A direct self-import is a no-op and now says so** — "`pkg::main` is this program's own entry file, so this import brings the file into itself: everything it declares is already in scope here. Delete the import" — a warning, because the program is correct without the line. **An import CYCLE back into the entry is refused instead**, at the sibling's own import: the entry is the program, not a module, and a sibling resolves its imports before the entry walks, so there is nothing there to import; the refusal says to move the shared declarations into their own module. That construct used to "work" only by paying the price above (the entry silently ceased to be a program), and one test fixture was written in it — it now declares its shared resource in a third module, which is what the fix asks every such program to do. A non-entry module that imports its own name is untouched and stays silent, which is the latent form a real package carries. Four pins in `module_resolution` (the derive, the item table, the cycle, the non-entry control) and one end-to-end pin that builds a self-importing entry and finds its `main`; two ledger rows. **`vilan fmt` now reformats one-link chains over 100 columns.** `let selected_theme = combine((filtered_themes, selected_index)).map(|(themes, i)| themes.find(…).or_else(…));` came back from the formatter unchanged at 220 columns while the signature above it broke correctly. `is_breakable_chain` required two `.name(…)` call links — "one link is not a chain, and breaking it would buy a line and no clarity" — and the width door was gated on it, so a statement whose whole layout hung off one link's closure was exempt from the budget at any width. Two things changed, and both are narrow. A one-link chain is now a width-split candidate **when its link's last argument is a closure**: the closure's body is what can break, and when the link is the whole chain the only thing that can give that body an indentation level is the link taking a line of its own. And the split is **measured, not assumed** — the inline form prints first, with the permission handed down so the argument-tail descent still reaches inside, and the link rolls onto its own line only if the first line is still over budget. That order is what keeps `raw.map(|entry| Entry { … })` breaking at the struct literal rather than putting `raw` alone on a line. A closure body also now inherits the split permission, which it always dropped — that is what lets a chain written inside `.map(|t| …)` break at all. Six files in the tree reflow, every one of them a builder chain inside a trailing closure; three new pins, and the "one link stays inline" pins the rule was built on are unchanged and still green. (tracker E137)
