An unresolved callee is selected outright: "this signature reaches no resource" is a claim about a signature, and one nobody could read is not a claim the predicate may make. **The proof is the goldens**: all 124 corpus goldens are byte-identical and the 3,455-case inference binary is green, which is what a predicate that only ever over-selects has to produce. **Red-first, three plants**: the whole-program gate restored reds the enrolment pin (a thousand resource-free functions changed the planner's work); the predicate emptied reds all five route pins (the destructors stop running); and the callee-signature and recorded-type routes removed together red exactly the C11-temporary pin and nothing else. Recorded and not fixed: the per-request budget the gate asserts (0.2 ms) is still not met, and it was not met before this either — the remainder is a candidate's documentation, which still reads its declaring module's text once per request and is about half of what is left. **A reactive channel minted at runtime leaked its source for the life of the connection, and went silently dead — reporting `Ready` — after a reconnect.** Neither hole is on the generated `[expose]` path (static, positional, one channel per field per connection), which is why nothing pinned them; both are on the path a per-row or per-thread subscription needs, where an rpc method mints a channel with the public `session_of` + `ReactiveServer::expose`. **The leak:** `stop` disposed the live forward and left the `sources` entry, so a client that scrolled a long list accumulated one retained starter — and the source it captured — per channel it ever looked at, until the connection died. The obvious fix, dropping the entry in `stop`, is WRONG, and the pin says why in the one line that disappears under it: an `Unsubscribe` is client-local demand reaching zero (a view unmounting), and `RemoteSource::acquire` re-`Subscribe`s on the same id when demand returns, so dropping the capability there makes every remount silently dead — including a plain `[expose]`d mirror's. Withdrawal is its own verb instead: **`ReactiveServer::revoke(channel)`** stops the forward AND drops the capability. **The dead mirror:** `reattach_mirrors` rebinds the positional list `__attach` produced and nothing else, so a mirror minted from a channel id an rpc returned survived a reconnect pointing at a channel the fresh session never minted — no error, no updates, and a `status` still reading `Ready` over the old connection's value. Worse than dead: channel ids count from zero per process, so the id it still named is one the fresh session hands to something else. It cannot be rebound — asking again means re-running an application method with arguments std never saw, which is A39's protocol form — so **`invalidate_on_reconnect(socket, client)`** points every dynamically-minted mirror at nothing on reconnect: cache back to `None`, `status` back to `Waiting`, and the app re-runs the rpc that minted it. `ReactiveClient::source` is now the dynamic mint (registering the mirror for invalidation) and `attached_source` the one the generated `connect` uses for `__attach`'s own channels; the guide's traps say which is which. One in-process pin over a `duplex_pair` (`reactive_channels.rs`, plant-proved: the spec'd `stop` fix drops `second:3`), one over real processes across a server restart (`transport_robustness.rs`, unix-only like its siblings, red without the invalidation — 250 ticks of `Ready` over a connection that no longer exists). **An rpc service can refuse a connection at the handshake: `Service::authorize`, a token subprotocol, and three limits that need no auth at all.** Nothing at any layer gated a WebSocket upgrade: `accept_socket` checked that `sec-websocket-key` was PRESENT and wrote a 101 — anyone who could reach the port got a socket, a connection id, a reactive session and every mirror the service exposes, and `RpcError::Unauthorized` was a variant std constructed nowhere. `Service::authorize(|handshake| -> Result<Session, Reject>)` runs on the upgrade REQUEST, before any of that exists: `Err` answers the raw socket `401`/`403`/`429` (`Reject::Unauthorized`/`Forbidden`/`TooMany`) and destroys it, `Ok(session)` becomes `Connection.session` and feeds A38's factory — so identity arrives on the handshake and the methods lose their `token: str` parameter. The hook may await, because verifying a signature is a WebCrypto call everywhere. `Handshake { path, headers, protocols, remote_addr }` carries what the client could say, and the credential's route is the one a browser leaves open: a page cannot put a header on a WebSocket handshake, so the convention is the subprotocol list — `["vilan-rpc", "token." + credential]`, written by `std::rpc::rpc_protocols`, read back by `Handshake::token()`. The client seam is additive: `Client::connect_with(url, codec, protocols)` beside the unchanged `connect(url, codec)`, `connect_socket_with` beside `connect_socket`, and the offer is remembered on the duplex so a reconnect re-presents the same credential. **A fix rides the same seam and is independent of all of it: the server never echoed `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` at all**, and a browser closes any connection whose subprotocol offer goes unanswered — the handshake now selects `vilan-rpc` out of what was offered (the client's first non-credential choice otherwise — a `token.` offer is never selected, so the credential is never written back out) and echoes it, while an offer of nothing still produces the byte-identical 101 it always did. **A second fix: teardown rode the socket's `close` event, which node never fires for an UPGRADED socket a peer half-closes** — a lost network or a killed client emits `end` and nothing else — so every such connection's reactive session and wire entry survived it for the life of the process; `end` now tears down too (idempotently) and destroys our half. Three limits land on the same seam and work with `authorize` absent: `max_connections` (429 over the ceiling), `handshake_rate(attempts, window_millis)` per remote address, and `handshake_timeout`, which bounds the GREETING rather than idleness — the first inbound byte disarms it, so a client that is only watching mirrors is never touched. An authorized service answers only the upgrade: the connectionless SSE/POST legs carry no handshake to gate and answer 401, the rpc leg with a typed `RpcError::Unauthorized` envelope, which is where that variant finally gets a producer. `NodeSocket` gains `remote_address` and `set_timeout`. Five pins in `service_layer.rs`; the slot-release half of the ceiling pin was red before the `end` fix. (tracker A40)

**`Service::factory` mounts one service INSTANCE per connected client, so a method can finally learn who called.** `[service]` generated one `dispatcher(self)` and `Service::new` handed the protocol it wrapped to every connection, so one instance served the whole process: identity had to travel as a `token: str` first parameter re-resolved on every call, and an `[expose]`d field was one cell shared by everybody. `Service::factory(|connection| Store { … }, codec)` calls `build` once per connection — with that connection's `Connection { id, session, remote_addr }` — and every route of that connection's dispatcher closes over the instance it returned, which is `transport-rpc.md` Q9's rule made real: the struct instance IS the connection's session. Three consequences: a method reads its caller off `self`; `[expose]`d fields become per client for free (each instance its own cells, its own channels); and the instance dies with the connection, on the `on_disconnect` release that already existed. `[service]` now also implements the one-method `std::rpc::RpcService` trait (`dispatcher_for`), which is how std builds a dispatcher from an instance whose type it only learns at the factory's call site — additive, and the inherent `dispatcher()` is untouched, so **every existing `Service::new(x.dispatcher().into_protocol(codec))` still compiles unchanged**. `Service::new` is now documented as the stateless shorthand for `Service::factory(|_connection| shared, codec)`. One refusal comes with it: the connectionless `POST {mount}rpc` leg has no connection to build an instance for, so a factory service answers it `501` with the reason in the body (the WebSocket transport every generated `Client::connect` uses is the way in); a `Service::new` mount answers that leg exactly as before. The **contract hash is unaffected** — it hashes methods and exposures, and both are untouched — pinned against the value the pre-change compiler produced. `NodeSocket` gains a `remote_address` reader for `Connection.remote_addr`. Two pins in `service_layer.rs`, the per-connection one plant-proved red (a factory that builds once makes the two clients' mirrors cross-talk). (tracker A38)

<!-- family: feature -->
**The editor fades top-level code no entry of your package reaches, and every top-level item of a module no entry loads at all.** E114 shipped the fade for imports, function-local bindings and unreachable statements and stopped at the file boundary, because vilan has no visibility marker: every top-level item is module surface an unanalyzed importer might use, and a single-entry analysis cannot call it dead. A `[package]` closes that: its entries are declared, the pruner already computes what each entry reaches, and **an item no entry reaches is dead by the bundle's own definition.** Two granularities ship. The coarse one is free — the per-entry module walk that colors a file already answers "does anything load this", so a module nothing builds fades whole, with the entries it was tested against named in the message. The fine one is the union of the reachability walk across the package's entries: an item only your `probe` entry calls is used, and so is a `[platform("browser")]` item the browser entry reaches in a package whose other entries are node. **The definition is narrowed to top-level `fun` and module-level `let`, and the narrowing is measured**: a `struct`, an `enum`, a `trait` and an `impl` block compile to nothing whether they are used or not — a USED `Point { x = 1, y = 2 }` emits `[ 1, 2 ]` with no declaration anywhere — so "does the build keep it" has no answer for them, and finding an unreferenced type is a type-reference analysis with a different index. **Three exemptions landed before the first gray, because the ruled definition taken literally grayed 1,859 of a real application's 1,943 top-level items and sixteen of those were true finds.** A declared `generated` root gets nothing (1,815 of the 1,859 were one machine-written 18,198-line module that a build hook rewrites on every tag bump; the manifest key already existed and already meant "not code you maintain"). The call graph deliberately drops the edges out of a `const` module binding's initializer — right for emission, where such an initializer is data rather than code, and wrong for paint, where it grayed 27 functions whose deletion breaks the build — so those edges are now collected BESIDE the emission graph, followed only by the paint. And `context::thread_contexts` rewrites an ambient context binding out of existence, leaving `let app_context = Context<AppContext>::new();` with no readers in the graph the walk sees; the pass records what it recognized. Exempt for free: `main`, `_`-led names, `[rpc]` methods (reached through the dispatcher the analyzer synthesizes, so an UNINSTALLED service's methods still gray), and derive- and service-generated members, which carry a sentinel source and never land in a user file's range. **Trait impl members are left unpainted in v1** and said so here: whether one is reached depends on which types the program constructs anywhere, so the answer moves in blocks; inherent impl members do fade, and a twelve-member builder API nothing calls is exactly the find the fade is for. **A `[library]` gets no top-level gray at all**, workspace member or not — it has no entries, so there is no union, and every top-level item is surface a consumer may import, which is the property that saves them from forking a library that forgot to export something. `[doc(hidden)]` stays the soft tool for that, and neither causes nor suppresses a fade. **The union is computed out of band, on a per-package clock**, because the language server analyzes the OPEN file as the entry and for most files there is no `main` in the program at all — the walk has no root to start from, so every term of the union, including the one for the file's own entry, comes from a separately computed per-entry set keyed by `(canonical path, name span)` rather than entity ids, which are minted per analysis and not comparable across programs. M21's base cache cannot amortize those analyses: it revalidates by content, and the edit that evicts an entry's world is exactly an edit to a module that entry loads. **The fade is withdrawn the instant a change arrives in the package and returns only when the clock lands**, which is asymmetric on purpose: a stale fade on an item you have just started calling from another file says "dead" about live code and the response a fade asks for is deletion, while a missing fade on newly-unused code is merely late. A syntax error anywhere in the package holds the whole package's fades off, because a salvaged parse can lose a block or a file's whole tail and a smaller program reads to a reachability walk as a deader one. No suppressor marker ships and none is needed: it would have taken 1,859 of them on the application that was measured. Pinned per case rather than per example — eight definition pins in `vilan-core` (the two exemptions proven non-vacuous by planting the bug each removes), eight paint pins over real manifests, a withdraw-on-edit pin driven through the real notification handlers, and a union-walk cost pin on a generated three-entry exhibit sized like the application, with nothing copied from it. (tracker E124)

**A keystroke no longer re-checks every module of a program it did not touch.** The one seam that skipped module-local checking was restricted to `std`, because std's diagnostics are pinned ABSENT by the differential gate and a package module's are not. That restriction cost the whole of a warm keystroke's module checking: on a 57-source application the analyzer re-derived every sibling's move checks, view checks, readonly and mutable-argument checks and deprecations on every character typed in the entry, over bodies whose bytes had not changed. The seam is now sealed over **every source of a base-cached world**, beside std's rather than merged into it, and a reused module's own diagnostics are **replayed** — recorded per source by the analysis that derived them, spliced back before the order normalization by every later one, spans and per-file attribution intact, because a span is a byte offset into text the cache has already re-validated. Three terms gate it and all three must hold: the world came from a base-cache HIT (which is what makes the module id prefix byte-identical), the entry moved none of that module's type slots, and a record for it exists under the same content. The dirty bit is new too — every `TypeId` now carries the source that minted it, and `write_type_slot` files the writes it already calls world-changing against that source — and it answers the question the whole design rested on: on the measured application a keystroke dirties **0 of 57 modules**, every time. Reuse is all-or-nothing per world by design: editing any loaded module throws away every module's record for that world, which needs no dependency graph and stays sound in the presence of whole-program impl visibility, where an import-closure key could not. **Warm keystroke CPU on the 57-source application: 399 / 411 ms → 358 / 367 ms (min / median of eighteen, three interleaved passes, loadavg 15-22), and the `checks` phase 188-205 ms of wall → 153-155 ms (-21%).** The generated 1,791-function exhibit does not move (25 → 24 ms): it matches the application's function count and nothing about its shape, which is the finding E121's gate already carries. The gate is a differential: every corpus program re-hosted as a package module under a dependent entry, each carrying a planted refusal or deprecation, analyzed warm both ways — replayed and re-derived — and required to agree byte for byte on diagnostics, warnings, their per-file attribution and the emitted JS. It goes red under a no-op splice. Replayed notes carry `SourceId` INDICES into the world's source vector, so a fingerprint of that vector is asserted on every replay rather than commented; a module whose diagnostic reaches into the entry is not recorded at all and re-derives forever. The table builders and the drop planner — a third of the phase, and the half that feeds the emitter rather than the diagnostics — are not in this tranche, and neither are the two checks whose "module-local" answers turned out to carry whole-program state (R10's report doubles as R11's dedup set; the HMR transfer bound re-infers through `&mut self`).

**`Style::when(condition, delta)` — the conditional merge, as a chain instead of a pile of `if`s.** A style that depends on a handful of independent flags had one spelling: rebind a `mut` style once per flag, `+`-ing a delta in each arm. `base.when(is_selected, selected).when(is_disabled, disabled)` is that, folded, and it is five lines of std with no new machinery — `when` never CONSTRUCTS a style, it selects between two that were already built and already emitted their rules inside their own `const` expressions, so the construct-in-const rule is untouched with a runtime flag in the middle. Chain order is **precedence**, exactly as with `+`: when two links both fire, the later delta wins whatever properties they share. The guidance the ruling asked for is in the doc comment and both guides: the chain reads best when each condition mentions its **own** flag, and a condition that has to mention another link's flag (`!selected && !disabled`) is the tell that the states interact and that a `match` should state the exclusivity structurally — guidance, not a prohibition. Pinned as an EQUIVALENCE over the 015 exhibit's shape: at all four cells of two independent flags, the chain's rendered class list is byte-identical to the `+`-and-`if` spelling it folds up, and the shared-property cell resolves to the later delta's class — proven red by merging in the other direction. A corpus program carries the same exhibit through the byte gate. (tracker A36; style-variants.md §6/§8 Q3; docs `guide/styling.md`, `std/style.md`)

**`view("input").autofocus()` — an element mount hook, replacing the uuid-plus-timer dance a custom modal needs otherwise.** HTML's `autofocus` attribute fires only on a document's initial parse, so it does nothing for anything mounted later, and `std::ui` offered no hook at all: attachment happens at six unrelated places in the module (`mount`, `Slot::place`, `children`, `bind_each`'s order pass, `when`, `swap`) and none of them was reachable from a view. The workaround, written character-identically three times in one app: mint a uuid, set it as the element's id, start a 1 ms timer, look the element back up, focus it — with a private `focus` extern of its own, because `std::dom::Element` had no binding for it. **`View::on_mount(action)` hands the callback the element itself**, once it is IN THE DOCUMENT, and `View::autofocus()` is that with `element.focus()` in it; `Element::focus` is now a std binding, so the private copy goes. The hook is a **microtask**, which is enough for every site: the whole synchronous build, and the `mount` that finishes it, run to completion before any microtask does — and a `when` body or a `bind_each` row that appears in a *later* drain wave is synchronous too, so its append still lands before the microtask it queued. That last case is the one that could have forced a heavier at-settle-then-microtask shape; measured under a DOM, it does not. The SSR twins accept and drop, like the event binders — there is no document to be in. Pinned by a DOM harness that walks from the element to the document root inside the callback, at all four attachment sites, plus the focus itself and the SSR markup; proven red by running the action inline, where every site reports the element detached. (tracker A45; docs `guide/ui.md`, `std/browser.md`)

**`bind_each` asked for a key AND a `PartialEq`, and most lists only have one of the two to give — so there are three forms now, each dropping a bound.** The double demand was doing real damage: an item type carrying a closure cannot derive `PartialEq`, so a caller hand-wrote one comparing the very field it also passed as the key — the same decision written twice, and a `Theme` whose variables changed compared equal, was Kept, and never re-rendered. **`bind_each_values(source, render)`** is the identity-keyed form — `bind_each(source, |x| x, render)` written once, which is what every `|x| x` key in the estate was spelling by hand. **`bind_each_by(source, key, render)`** is Solid's `<Index>` beside `bind_each`'s `<For>`, and asks nothing of `T` at all: a row whose key survives keeps its element, its owner and its bindings, and std writes the new item into that row's own `SignalCell<T>`, so the row updates *through* the bindings `render` already made instead of being disposed and rebuilt. The trade is stated in the docs rather than hidden: `set` never compares, so every kept row's cell is rewritten on every change of the list. The three-argument `bind_each` is untouched — 10 call sites across the estate keep compiling, and renaming it was never on the table, which is why the new forms take new names. Underneath, `reconcile` is parameterized on `same: sync |T, T| bool` and has no `T: PartialEq` bound: the key decides identity and whether the row moves, `same` decides reuse against rebuild, and they are two questions rather than one. `bind_each` passes `==`, `bind_each_by` passes "always the same" and therefore never emits a `Refresh`. `render` receives the row's cell as a concrete `SignalCell<T>` because vilan has no trait objects — a closure PARAMETER cannot be typed by a trait — and the docs say to treat it as read-only. SSR twins for both, read-once like every binding there. Pinned in a DOM harness by running all three forms over one pair of edits: a changed value re-renders under the two value-checked forms and only those, a reorder rebuilds nothing anywhere, and `bind_each_by`'s row keeps its element IDENTITY across a value change while its text follows — proven red by planting a dispose-and-rebuild into the kept arm. (tracker A42; analysis-reuse.md; docs `guide/ui.md`, `std/browser.md`, `std/reactive.md`)

**`selector(source)` answers "is this row the selected one?" for a thousand rows in two writes, not a thousand.** The obvious spelling derives a boolean per row off the selection signal, and every one of those derivations recomputes on every change — moving a highlight one row down a list costs `n` notifications, and the linear dedup scan inside the turn queue made the whole wave O(n²) on top. `selector` is Solid's `createSelector`: **one** subscription on the source and a cell per key, so a change writes exactly the key that left and the key that arrived, whatever `n` is. Measured over a thousand live rows, each holding its own cell: 2 notifications per change against 1000 for the derived spelling. `of(key)` creates the key's cell on first ask (seeded against the current value) and hands the same cell back after, so it drops straight into `show`/`when`/`bind_class`/`bind_styled` from inside a row's render body — and the entry's removal is the AMBIENT OWNER's, which inside a `bind_each` row is the row's own, so the map stays the size of the live list rather than of every list the session ever showed. It is a handle with a method rather than the bare closure Solid returns, and that is forced rather than chosen: a vilan closure captures its context at creation, so a closure built inside `selector` would defer every key's cleanup to the owner ambient where `selector` was *called* — the component, never the row. **The turn queue's dedup is keyed now too**, because the O(2) win does not survive an O(n²) queue: `enqueue` tested membership by scanning the pending list, inside `notify`'s own loop, and its comment had been inviting a keyed set since it was written. Same semantics — one entry per subscriber per wave — measured 80 ms → 229 ms across a 4x growth in observers where the scan went 696 ms → 9630 ms. Pinned by the thousand-row notification count and by a scaling RATIO taken in one process (a number of milliseconds is a claim about the machine; a ratio is a claim about the algorithm), both proven red by planting the derived-per-row selector and the scanning dedup back. (tracker A44; docs `std/reactive.md`)

**`source.on_change(observer)` subscribes WITHOUT the immediate first call — the lazy half of the pair `sub`/`effect` had no spelling for.** `sub` fires once with the current value and then on every change, `effect` is the owner-registered form of the same thing, and both are eager by design: every one of `std::ui`'s fourteen bindings relies on that first call, because it *is* the initial paint. The lazy primitive existed and was std-internal (`observe`), so an effect that must not fire on the state the program starts in — a "you have unsaved changes" prompt, an analytics ping, a derivation that already seeded its own first value — had nothing to reach for. Solid's opt-out is an option (`on(deps, fn, { defer: true })`); vilan has neither overloading nor optional parameters, so the opt-out is a **name**: `Source::on_change` and its owner-registered twin `Source::effect_on_change`, beside `sub` and `effect`, which are unchanged in every respect. Both are trait members, so a `Source` of your own gets them free: the default `on_change` wraps `sub` and swallows the one immediate call — honest against `sub`'s documented contract, and overridden by `SignalCell` with a direct attach that never makes the call at all. **The member the reactive-traits paper's Q5 was waiting on is this one, so `map` widened with it**: the derivation combinator moves off `SignalCell` onto `Source`, and a storage-backed cell or a mirror of your own now derives exactly like the canonical cell does (`stored.map(|value| i"n={value}")`). `combine` moves onto `on_change` too and stops re-setting its derived signal once per input at construction — it seeds itself from the snapshot and then only listens. Pinned by a corpus program carrying the eager/lazy pair on one signal, the owner-registered form across a disposal, the trait default over a hand-written `Source`, and the widened `map`; `combine`'s redundant writes are invisible from vilan code (nothing observes the derived cell at construction), so that half is pinned at the declaration. (tracker A43; reactive-traits.md Q5; docs `std/reactive.md` and `guide/reactive.md`)

**Two spellings of one unsaved file agree again in the editor's containment tests.** `canonical_path_of_unwritten` gave up at a `.` or `..` in the unwritten tail (a component with no file name) and answered the whole path lexically, while the plain spelling of the same file resolved through its deepest existing ancestor — so under a root whose canonical form differs from its spelling (Windows's 8.3 temp directory; a symlink anywhere) `same_file` said two spellings of one buffer were different files. **`let present = x is Some(let n); print(n);` compiled, and read the payload slot of a value that may have no payload — `undefined` for a `None`, `NaN` where the program's own type said `i32`.** Every capture rule vilan has is about a CONDITION, because a condition is the only thing that selects on a test's answer; the analyzer could not say so. `condition_polarity` was `None` in two different situations — outside every condition, and inside one that installs no frame (a `while`-shaped `for`, a `match` guard, which never did) — so an `is` written as a plain expression fell through to B171's answer and its capture ran to the end of the scope. B199 fixed the sibling conflation one layer in; this is the outer one. **The rule: a capture bound in expression position reaches the rest of THAT expression and nothing after it.** There is no narrowing that could make the later read work — vilan has no flow typing, so "`n` where `present` is true" is not something the language can say — and admitting it emits a payload load the test never proved. The `&&` half is deliberately kept, because `&&` short-circuits wherever it is written: `let big = x is Some(let n) && n > 1;` still binds `n` for its own right operand, and only the read past the statement is refused. **The refusal quotes the author's own test back**: "'n' is bound only inside the `is` test that captured it: outside a condition that test is an ordinary `bool`, and nothing after it proves the payload is there. Put the test where a branch depends on it — `if x is Some(let n) { … }` — and read 'n' inside." A second half was needed to reach module scope, where B33 keeps no positional record at all because module bindings are order-independent: a declaration with a real END is the exception, since an end is meaningless without positions, and without it `let present = slot is Some(let n);` at module scope handed `n` to `main`. **Two corpus programs were written in the refused shape** — `derive-enum.vl` and `derive-json.vl` both did `print(r is Err(let e)); print(e);` — and are rewritten to read the capture inside the branch the test selects, with byte-identical stdout. **`fun main() { if flag { ret; } … }` compiled clean and then died at load: `SyntaxError: Illegal return statement`, the whole module refused before a line of it ran.** `main` is INLINED at module scope — that is what makes a vilan program a flat ESM file rather than a function call wrapped around one — and a `ret` in it lowered to a bare `return` out there, which no JS parser accepts. Every spelling was affected: a guard clause, a `ret` nested in a loop, a valued `ret` in a `main(): i32`. **The lowering is a labeled block**, not a function: `main`'s body is wrapped in `main: { … }` and each of those `ret`s becomes `break main`. A `ret` in a loop breaks the LABEL, not the loop, which is the distinction a bare `break` could not make; a valued `ret` assigns the exit-code temp on its way out so the `process.exit` after the block still sees it; a `main` that owns a resource keeps its `try`/`finally`, and the break runs the teardown on the way out. **`semanticTokens/range` answered in the ANALYZED snapshot's coordinates while `semanticTokens/full` answered the live buffer, so a viewport request after an unlanded edit above the window painted every token in it one line off until the next analysis landed — on the request an editor sends most.** E121's keystroke path re-serves the landed token capture through a two-sided edit anchor, which is what positions `full` against the buffer on screen; E122 moved `range` onto the same capture but sliced it by ANALYZED line and encoded it against the analyzed index. One capture, two pictures — and the drift the keystroke path exists to remove, reappearing in the viewport. **`range` now answers through the same anchor**, and is by construction the window of `full`'s own stream: an `Exact` verdict re-maps the window's landed spans and paints the edit window from syntax exactly as `full` does, and `Stale`/`Unusable` degrade to whole-file syntax exactly as `full` does. **The cost still follows the window**, which is what E122 bought: the capture is indexed by analyzed line and the anchor moves an analyzed line by a constant — zero through the head, the tail's own line shift through the tail — so the analyzed lines that can carry a token into a live viewport are at most two contiguous stretches of that index, merged and read as slices rather than scanned, and the edit window is lexed only when its own lines meet the requested ones. The existing cost pin (a twenty-line viewport at 0.003× the whole file, against a 0.25 bound) is unmoved. **Pinned with the old mechanism computed beside the answer**: a line typed into a function body above a twenty-line viewport, the answer asserted equal to `full`'s window byte for byte AND asserted to DIFFER from the capture sliced by analyzed line — so if the anchor ever became a no-op there, the non-vacuity assertion reds before the equality does. The salvaged-adoption pin next to it gains the one line that makes its document the state a server is actually in (buffer and analysis agreeing), since with E125 a viewport is a claim about the live buffer and comparing one to an analyzed-space filter is a question about the anchor, not about the salvage fold it is there to hold. (tracker E125)

**The release differential is one test per corpus program now, and the 600 seconds it was really spending turn out to be one program that never exits.** `the_release_preset_is_observationally_neutral_over_the_corpus` ran the whole corpus behind an 8-way loop inside a single test, and at **607.3 s of a 698.7 s union** it WAS the union's critical path — a straggler nextest could not schedule around, because the leg was one unit of scheduling that could not use more than its own eight threads however idle the box was, and whose static chunking made the slowest chunk the clock. It is now a `corpus_programs!` declaration, one line per program, writing a test each: 124 independent processes across every core there is, a regression that names its program in the test id rather than in a message, and one bad program re-runnable on its own. **The split named its program on the first run.** `watch.vl` blocks on `flat.next()` for a filesystem change that never comes — "a watch never ends on its own", as the program's own comment says — so both builds ran to `NODE_TIMEOUT`, both were killed at 300 s, and the gate then compared two identical `Err("node did not exit within 300s")` strings and passed: **600 s for a verdict that could not come out any other way**, and 600 s nobody could see while every program shared one clock. It joins `NOT_RUN` with that reason (still compiled both ways, only the node leg skipped), and the binary's longest remaining member is **9.6 s**. Shortening the deadline instead was the other direction and is E32's disease exactly — the observation would become "what had it printed when we gave up", which load decides. The corpus-wide claim survives as the SUM of the parts: `every_corpus_program_has_a_test_of_its_own` holds the declaration to `vilan/test/` in both directions and re-asserts the old loop's two non-vacuity bounds, `every_program_not_run_is_still_a_corpus_program` reds on an exclusion that names nothing, and `release_differential` leaves `.config/nextest.toml`'s straggler priority, whose reason is gone. (tracker N49)

**Two rules from Order 25's seal, which was green locally and red on Windows CI.** A `#[cfg(windows)]`-only pin is compiled by the cross-check and verified only by CI, so a report that lands one must say so by name rather than let a green union imply it was exercised; and a pin that waits on a process — a watcher, a hook, a server — is a race until its ordering is proven by the harness's own sequencing, never by a sleep. Both are in `CLAUDE.md`'s Testing section, where the next lane will meet them.


<!-- family: fix -->
**A `--watch` round decides each leg's freshness at that leg's own turn, and compiles a leg that writes another leg's input first.** Both watch loops — `vilan build --watch` and the HMR round — decided "fresh" for every leg BEFORE any leg compiled. When one leg's recorded sources include another leg's `dist/` artifact (a server leg inlining the client bundle it is built beside), the consumer was measured against the producer's OLD artifact, judged fresh and skipped; the producer then rewrote that file, and the consumer's own artifact went on shipping bytes that no longer existed until some unrelated edit happened to reach its own modules. A round now orders its legs so a producer compiles before the leg that reads its output, and a leg downstream of one that recompiled recompiles with it (`watch_leg_reuse::a_leg_that_reads_another_legs_artifact_recompiles_in_the_same_round`). Reuse is unchanged everywhere else: the ordering is stable, so a workspace with no artifact dependency between its legs compiles exactly as it did.

**The language server's containment test resolves both sides the same way, so an unsaved buffer under a symlinked project root keeps its project.** `canonical_path` never fails — where resolution fails it degrades to the path as spelled — so a buffer that is not on disk yet was compared, lexically, against a layer root that had resolved through its links, and the editor answered that a file plainly inside its own package was foreign: no package root, no platform, every `pkg::` import unresolved. Both sides now go through `canonical_path_of_unwritten`, which resolves the deepest ancestor that exists and re-attaches the tail as spelled. Identical for a path that is on disk, so nothing about a saved file changes.

**One file reached under two names is collected once.** The project walk's cycle guard keyed on DIRECTORY identity, which is the whole question for a cycle and half of it for a link: a file symlink beside its target (`src/alias.vl -> real.vl`) handed the same file to the collector under both names, so `vilan fmt --check` printed two `would reformat` lines for one file and counted it twice, `vilan fmt` formatted it twice, and the watch round's manifest fingerprint hashed one `vilan.toml` twice. The guard now keys on entry identity — `(device, inode)` on unix, the resolved path elsewhere — for files as well as directories. Both spellings stay valid layout; a file that cannot be identified is still visited, because a duplicate line is cheaper than a source file nobody formats.

**`VILAN_WATCH_LOG` traces what a `--watch` session SAW and what it DECIDED.** Set it to a file (or `-` for stderr) and the loop records, with a clock and a pid: the baseline and every recorded input seeded into it, every poll that found a difference — naming each path added, removed or moved, with both timestamps — a heartbeat for the polls that found none, and every round's start, verdict and duration. A watch session's whole observable surface used to be one line per round, which is enough to say a round happened and nothing at all to say why one did not; the two watch harnesses now turn the trace on and print it when a wait times out, so the family's recorded strike ("round 1 in 0.6 s, then nothing for 300 s") is a verdict rather than a mystery. Off unless asked, and a path that cannot be opened disables it with one warning.

**A self-call bound by a `let` and read in an unannotated recursive body's return position resolves.** `fun g(n: i32) { if n == 0 { ret 1; } let x = g(n - 1); x + 1 }` failed "type of variable 'x' could not be resolved", on the binding and at every call, where the direct-tail form `g(n - 1) + 1` had always worked. It was a deadlock: `x`'s constraint waits on `g(n - 1)`, which waits on `g`'s inferred return, which reads the tail `x + 1`, which read `x` — and a binding whose type slot is still `Unknown` answered "not yet" instead of looking at what it was bound to. Deferring is right when someone else is going to land the type and wrong when this ask is what that someone is waiting for, so an UNANNOTATED binding with no type yet is now read through its initializer, which is the hop B185 gave `unfilled_closure_parameter` for closure parameters. The re-entrant ask then answers `never` — evidence that constrains nothing — and the other return evidence decides, exactly as it does for the direct-tail form. Two guards ride along and are pinned: an annotated binding is not followed (its annotation is its own answer and outranks the initializer), and the existing cycle guard ends a binding cycle (`let p = q; let q = p;`, writable because module bindings resolve in any order), which stays the ordinary refusal. Mutual recursion and a chain of rebindings are pinned beside the exhibit; the spec's return-type-inference paragraph says a binding in between changes nothing. B126's residue, orphaned since 2026-08-22, closes with it (B191).

<!-- family: feature -->
**The guard clause: `if !(slot is Some(let n)) { ret; }` binds `n` for the rest of the block.** The owner's ruling off B171's scope question — "`if !(x is Some(let y)) { return }`, would the binding be accessible after?", yes. B195 already knows which captures a condition binds on its FALSE path, because that is the set it hands an `else`; when the `if` has no `else` and its then-branch provably diverges, that false path is the *only* way past the `if`, so the same set is published into the enclosing scope from the end of the `if` onward. They land there as ordinary declarations, so a later `let` of the name shadows them and the scope is the block the `if` was written in, not the function. All three conditions carry weight and each has its own pin: an unnegated `if x is P(let n) { ret; }` reaches its continuation exactly when the pattern did *not* match; a then-branch that can fall through reaches it on a miss; and an `if` with an `else` reaches it through whichever arm did not diverge, which is a wider rule nobody has ruled. Divergence is the type checker's own analysis (`Divergence::checker` — `ret` and `jump` are its leaves, `jump break`/`continue` inside a loop included), so the guard and the editor's unreachable-code paint cannot disagree about what "dead" means; `panic(..)` is a leaf for the paint and not yet for the checker, so a panicking guard is pinned `#[ignore]`d against B204 and the spec carries the gap as an implementation note. The spec's `is` section, the tour's control-flow page and the "cannot find" entry in the error appendix all state the shape (B187).

**An `is` capture reached through a call argument is unbound in both branches.** `if always(maybe is Some(let n)) { print(n); }` compiled and printed `undefined` — a read of a payload slot the subject does not have — because the branch bookkeeping travels the condition's boolean spine (`!`, `&&`/`||`, the `is` test) and *dropping* it for anything else meant falling back to the plain then-branch default. A call's truth proves nothing about a test inside its argument, so the capture now reaches neither branch: stepping off the spine narrows the capture's visibility to the subtree it stepped into rather than clearing the frame. The one rule that survives the step is `&&`'s, and only inside that subtree — `always(maybe is Some(let n) && n > 1)` still binds its own right operand, because `&&` short-circuits wherever it is written. The same cap closes `always(maybe is Some(let n)) && n > 0`, which read the missing payload from the `&&` written around the call. The spec's `is` section states the spine rule (B199).

<!-- family: performance -->
**A superseded analysis now STOPS. A keystroke burst used to run one whole whole-program analysis per debounce window and throw all but the last away at `land`; ten keystrokes on kolt's `views.vl` cost 989 ms of CPU each and now cost 127 ms — one complete analysis and nine cancelled, measured through the real notification handlers.** E117 stamped every analysis with the world revision it read and taught `land` to DROP a result the world had moved past, which closed the ghost-diagnostic hole — but it closed it at the end: the superseded analysis still ran to completion on its 128 MiB thread. The analysis now carries a cancellation token, installed on that thread and read at the phase boundaries the `VILAN_PHASE_TIMING` line names (the entry walk, `build()`, the check sequence, and the post-passes' `contexts+graph` and `const-pass`), plus per call site inside `check_generic_bound_satisfaction` and per function inside the move scan — the two loops the `checks` phase is mostly made of, which is what bounds the cancel latency at one call site rather than one whole-program sweep. Measured on the generated 1,791-function exhibit at loadavg 87: a token set 10–75% of the way through a 249 ms analysis stops the thread in 13–69 ms. **Every checkpoint sits downstream of every process-global store** — the base world cache is written before the entry tail begins, the parse caches hold one complete module each — so no cancel can leave a shared cache holding a partial value; a macro world's nested compile is exempt outright, because its world is cached for the process and a half-built one stored there would be read back by a later analysis as whole. **The cancelled analysis answers `None` rather than a truncated program**, which is not a nicety: a checkpoint that fires before `build()` leaves type slots the constraint fixpoint would have filled, and the extraction tail reads them by hard index. Nothing here is what correctness rests on — `land` and `plan_publish` keep their revision-stamp checks unchanged, an analysis that outruns its own cancellation is dropped exactly as before, and removing every checkpoint changes what the editor shows not at all, only how long it took. **`did_open` registers its generation like an edit does.** E123 routed the open through the same scheduling but it registered nothing, so an edit arriving before the open's analysis finished did not supersede it — the two ran side by side and the revision stamp decided which landed last; the edit now cancels the open. **The dependency sweep supersedes each dependent** instead of awaiting one full analysis per dependent with no supersession check between them, and it abandons itself when the world moves under it, which on a shared module is worth an entire analysis per stale round. The dependents it schedules are marked `dependency_moved` for the window between the module's edit and their own re-landing, which fills the seam the keystroke path shipped with a hard-coded `false`: inside that window the verdict is `Stale` — whole-file syntax-only tokens, hints still served (Q1/Q4). The session trace grew a line to say what the scheduler did — `analyses: started= landed= cancelled=` — and it is a diagnosis, not a counter: cancelled climbing with started while landed does not is a session typing faster than it can analyze. Numbers, release, loadavg 85–87, ten keystrokes a debounce window apart: the generated exhibit 80 → 13 ms of CPU per keystroke (6.0x), kolt's `views.vl` 989 → 127 ms (7.8x), against a warm complete analysis in both cases so cancellation is not credited with M21's saving. **`diagnostics_budget` holds and is now CPU-clocked**: 59 ms of process CPU (310 ms of wall) on the 1,791-function exhibit at loadavg 92, against the 500 ms mandate the paper measured at 925 ms — it stays behind the same `#[ignore]` its sibling gate has, for its subject's size rather than its verdict. Backlog M26.

<!-- family: performance -->
**The language server's base-world cache has a byte budget and evicts least-recently-used, instead of growing for the life of the session.** The cache retains one resolved pre-entry world per distinct key shape, and since M21 the key includes the entry's package root and its sibling set — so an N-file package can mint N keys from one editing session, and the only eviction the cache had was per-key overwrite. The retention was already measured (`base_cache_retained`, and the `BaseCacheWorld` leak-tally site); it is now bounded. Worlds carry the bytes the store recorded and the tick of their last store or HIT, a store evicts least-recently-used worlds until the total fits the budget, and the world just stored is exempt — so a single world larger than the budget bounds the cache at one world rather than turning it off. The default is 512 MiB, generous on purpose; `VILAN_BASE_CACHE_BUDGET_MIB` overrides it in mebibytes, read once at server start, with a value that does not parse reported on stderr and ignored. An evicted world gives back everything it was holding: its recorded bytes, and the claims it held on analysis-owned overlay copies.

<!-- family: performance -->
**Editing a file that imports an OPEN sibling no longer rebuilds the whole pre-entry world on every keystroke.** The language server caches the resolved world every analysis starts from, and since M21 a `pkg::`-importing entry is eligible for it — but a world that had loaded a module served from the open-document overlay was refused the store outright, because those copies are owned by the analysis that parsed them and freed when it is superseded (`leak-soak.md` §7.9.4a; §7.9.2 proved the naive form unsound — a stored world borrowing analysis-owned text is a use-after-free reachable by pressing ctrl-Z). That is exactly the shape a real session has: kolt's `client.vl` imports `pkg::views`, `views.vl` is an open buffer, and every `client.vl` keystroke paid `base` 1,357–2,713 ms while its two siblings, which import no open file, paid `base 0.0 ms`. Ownership is a reference count now: every party that holds a reference derived from an overlay-served copy holds a *claim* on it — the analysis that parsed it, and any stored base world built over it — and the copy is freed exactly when the last claim is released. A stored world takes its claims inside the analysis that still holds the originals; a cache hit hands the world's claims to the receiving analysis under the cache lock, before the clone escapes; an analysis with nowhere to keep a claim (the CLI, the wasm front end, a transient reader, a macro-world compile) is served a miss rather than a borrow nothing keeps alive. Per-keystroke growth stays zero, and an unchanged open buffer is now parsed once for a whole run of analyses instead of once per analysis.


<!-- family: fix -->
**A trait-conformance refusal now advises a signature the author can actually write. `impl P with PartialEq { }` said ``declare `fun eq(self, b: PartialEq): bool` `` — and `PartialEq` is a trait, so that line names a type no value can have; the advice was unfollowable at the one moment the reader most needs to follow it.** The cause is the `= Self` default. `trait PartialEq<B = Self>` resolves `B` to the very same type as `Self` — both are `Type::Trait(PartialEq, [])` — so a signature rendered from the RESOLVED types cannot tell a declared `b: B` from a declared `Self`, and printed the trait's own name for both. `function_signature_label` now renders FOR the impl, by the WRITTEN name, which is the rule B29's own conformance check already applies (`ambiguous_position_expectation`): `Self` is the impl's subject, and a parameter's own name is the matching `with`-clause argument, falling back to the subject when the clause supplied none — precisely what `= Self` means. So `impl P with PartialEq` advises `fun eq(self, b: P): bool`, `impl Meters with Combine<Feet>` advises `fun merge(self, b: Feet): Meters`, and an ordinary `name: str` is untouched, because only a position resolving to the DECLARING trait's own abstract type is ambiguous at all. **B197's arm rendered its own signature to route around this, and that duplicate is gone**: one rendering serves both arms, so an operator trait whose shape is not `fun m(self, b: B): Self` can no longer be described wrongly by a template that assumed it was. Hover is deliberately unchanged — there is no impl in hand there, and `Self` is what the author typed. Five pins (`PartialEq`, `Add`, a user trait's `= Self` default, a written `with`-clause argument, and the ordinary-parameter control); the two B197 pins that read the signature go red without the fix too, which is the routing under test.

<!-- family: fix -->
**`self.add(self)` written out in a trait default over a supertrait resolves. `trait Doubler with Add { fun twice(self): Self { self.add(self) } }` was two errors on a program with no mistake in it — `Expected Doubler, but got Add instead.` at the call and `Expected Add, but got Doubler instead.` at the argument — while the OPERATOR spelling of the same thing, `self + self`, has dispatched since B193.** Inside a default body `self` is the trait's own abstract type (`Type::Trait(Doubler, [])`), and a member reached from a SUPERTRAIT is declared in that trait's terms: `Add::add` is `fun add(self, b: B): Self` with `B = Self`, and both of those resolve to `Type::Trait(Add, [])`. So the argument was refused against a parameter naming a different trait, and the call's type was refused by the enclosing default's own declared `Self` return. A supertrait's `Self`, reached through a sub-trait, IS the sub-trait's `Self` — the lookup now records the pair, and both halves rebind it: the argument check, which reads a parameter type straight off the declaration, and the `Self`-return specialization, which already substitutes structurally for a concrete receiver and simply did not count a sub-trait receiver as one. **The rewrite has to be structural rather than a substitution entry, and that is the interesting constraint**: types are not interned, so a member's `b: Self`, its `Self` return and the trait's own `Self` binding are three distinct ids for the one type, and no id-keyed context can reach all three. **It applies only to an argument-less `with` clause**, which is the whole rule rather than a convenience: with no argument written, every `= Self` position and every `Self` mean the sub-trait and a blanket rewrite is exactly right, where `with Add<i32>` parts them — `b: B` is `i32`, the `Self` return is still the sub-trait — and nothing in the resolved types tells them apart. That shape is untouched. Four pins: both spellings side by side in one trait, two impls proving the default dispatches per specialization, a two-level `Base`/`Middle`/`Top` chain on a user trait (whose chained call also proves the CALL came back as the sub-trait), and the control that a method no supertrait promises is still refused.

**A refused `[expose]` now generates NOTHING — no contract entry, no client mirror, no `session.expose` call — so `[expose] tasks: i32` is ONE diagnostic instead of five. B189 took the pile from six to four; the residue was two `cannot infer 'T' … ': Wire'` and two `cannot find type '_'`, and `_` is not a type: it is the `service` expansion's own placeholder, handed to an author who never wrote it.** The expansion reads an exposed field's element off the field's SOLE type argument — it runs before any type resolves, so the `Source` impl the compiler reconciles against is not there to read — and when it could not read one it pushed the literal `"_"` and carried it into all three places the element is named. The field's curated refusal already stands alone and says the actual thing (`its type 'i32' does not implement 'std::Source'`), so the expansion writes nothing for a field it cannot read, in BOTH channels that write one: std's `service` macro in `rpc.vl`, and `service_impl_source`, the Rust generator a fixture std falls back to. The skip is per FIELD — a good exposure beside a refused one still gets its surface entry, its mirror and its `expose` call, which is pinned by a program that names the mirror's type. **Generating nothing left the compiler owing a sentence, and that is the second half of this change.** The two rules were never quite the same rule: the analyzer reads the element off the `Source` impl (A32's ruling, so a source whose element is not its first type argument is read correctly), the expansion reads it off the written annotation. A type implementing `Source<Note>` with no written argument satisfied the analyzer and defeated the expansion, which used to make it fail loudly and wrongly (`cannot find type '_'`) and would now make it compile with the exposure silently not happening. It is refused instead, at the field, naming why: the mirror's element is read from the annotation's sole type argument, so spell the source with its element there. The accepted set is exactly what it was — that program never compiled — and the message is now one an author can act on. Five pins, red-proven in two halves (the placeholder restored; the refusal removed), plus the `Feed<Note>` control that A32's own shape still exposes.

**A `[derive(..)]` on a type declared inside an inline `mod` now generates its impl INTO that `mod`, where the type it names is in scope. `mod shapes { [derive(PartialEq)] enum Kind { .. } }` was four diagnostics on a program with no mistake in it — `cannot find type 'Kind'; import it first` twice, plus a follow-on per variant raised inside a body the author never wrote.** Expansion is unified, so a derive rides the same channel a macro attribute does, and every generated list walked into the FILE's module scope whatever scope the deriving item was written in. That placement is only ever right for a top-level item: the impl a derive writes names its subject by the bare name the author wrote, and a `mod`-nested type's bare name resolves in exactly one scope — the `mod`'s. **The fix is placement, not spelling**, which is what keeps B188's rule intact: the template is untouched, so a diagnostic raised inside generated code still re-anchors at the `[derive(..)]` that produced it, where qualifying the subject by its module path in the template would have rewritten the code the author is shown. Each generated list now records the inline-`mod` path it was written under, and the walk steps that path down from the file's scope before placing the list; a segment that names no module falls back to the enclosing scope, which is both the old placement and the right answer for a path no walk created. **The Rust generators' fallback channel had the same bug for a reason of its own** — it accumulated one file-wide text buffer and flushed it as a single list — and a backed enum reaches it whether or not anything is derived, so `mod shapes { enum Kind { Flat = "flat" } }` reported `'value' is already defined for 'unknown'` on top of the missing type. Those buffers are now bucketed per declaring scope, each with the prelude imports its own text needs. Six pins — an enum and a struct inside a `mod`, a nested `mod` proving the path is a repetition, two `mod`s deriving the same trait on two types that share a name (one shared bucket would put both impls in one scope), the backed-enum channel, and the top-level control — five of them red against the tree with the placement removed, the control green. B190's fixture drops the hand-written `impl Kind with PartialEq` it had been standing the derive up with.

**A generic parameter is rigid inside its own body.** `reconcile_type`'s `(_, Generic)` arm bound a generic wherever it reconciled — including inside the function that DECLARES the parameter, where the caller has already chosen it. Two garbage runs on 0.40.0, both reproduced with written generics (bounded and unbounded), so neither was the parameter sugar's doing: `fun swap(a: X, b: X) { mut c = a; c = b; c.who() }` called as `swap(A { tag = "aa" }, B { n = 7, label = "bb" })` printed `A/7` — `A`'s `who` reading field 0 of a `B`, an `i32` out through a declared `: str` — and `fun f(x: X) { need_a(x) }` for `fun need_a(a: A)`, called with a `B`, printed `9` through the same declared `: str`. An impl binder leaked the same way (`impl Box<type T> { fun leak(self) { need_a(self.value) } }`). A parameter an enclosing `fun`, `impl` or `trait` owns is now RIGID: it unifies with itself and nothing else, and only the parameters a site is inferring — a callee's at a call, a struct's at a literal, an enum's at a constructor, a declaration's own at an `impl` head — are open. A bounded parameter still SATISFIES a trait-typed position through its bound (satisfying is not binding), and an identity mapped type `(U in T: U)` now reduces to its source instead of being bound to it. **One module declares a name once, and a bound names a trait.** Two `struct N`, two `trait N`, a `struct N` beside an `enum N` or a `trait N` were all accepted with no diagnostic: the scope's lookup index keeps one entry per name, so the LAST declaration won and `x: N` resolved by declaration order — `trait N` first made `N` the struct and ran; `struct N` first made it the trait and failed at a struct literal with `cannot initialize a non-struct: N`, which names neither declaration. A duplicate top-level declaration of any sort is now refused at the second site, with a note at the first; two *modules* may still each declare `N`, a module being a namespace. Separately, `fun f<T: S>(…)` with `S` a struct was accepted and surfaced only as `cannot access field 'v' on type T` somewhere downstream; a struct or enum in bound position is now refused where it is written, naming the sort and steering to a similarly named trait when one is in scope.


<!-- family: fix -->
**A tuple receiver resolved NO method at any arity — not an inherent impl, not a trait impl, not `impl (i32, i32) with Add`'s own `add` — so `(1, 2) + (3, 4)` ran and answered `4` / `6` while `(1, 2).add((3, 4))` was "cannot call method 'add' on (i32, i32)".** One impl, two spellings, and only one of them reachable. B170 made a tuple reachable as an impl SUBJECT and the operator path has dispatched through it ever since; the METHOD path never looked at a tuple receiver at all. **Nothing about the lookup needed teaching, and that is the shape of the bug.** The operator path finds a tuple impl by scanning the implementations and comparing the receiver against each `implementation.subject` with `compare_type`; the method path's candidate collector scans the by-member index and compares with the *same function* over the *same table*, using the same identity (arity, then elements structurally). What was missing was one level up: method resolution dispatches on the receiver's SHAPE, its arms are the nominal types, a bare trait `self` in a default, and a bounded generic — and a tuple fell to the catch-all "not callable", so it never asked. Adding the shape to that arm is the whole analyzer fix; everything the arm does is already shape-agnostic, including binding an impl's generics by reconciling its subject against the receiver, which is what types `impl (type T: Display, T)` at both `(i32, i32)` and `(str, str)`. **Three more nominal-only receiver sets sat below it on the way to a running program, and each was reachable only once the one above was fixed.** The transformer's re-dispatch — how a trait default specialized for a concrete type finds the impl that provides its requirements — admitted nominal receivers only, so `impl (i32, i32) with Tagged`'s inherited `label` walked past the impl to the trait's *bodyless* `tag` (caught by the emitter's never-silent check rather than shipped as an empty function). And the arm that lets a value satisfy a trait-typed slot listed the nominal shapes too, which is exactly how `PartialOrd<B = Self>` declares `lt`'s operand when an impl writes no argument: `(1, 2) < (3, 4)` ran while `(1, 2).lt((3, 4))` was "Expected PartialOrd, but got (i32, i32) instead" — the operator/method asymmetry again, one level below the fix that removed it. A tuple's own trait membership was never in doubt at any of these sites: `smaller<T: PartialOrd>((1, 2), (3, 4))` already ran through a bound. **What does not change:** a tuple's arity is part of its type, so an impl answers only for the arity its subject names (`impl (i32, i32)` gives `(1, 2, 3)` the ordinary "(i32, i32, i32) has no method 'first'"), and a tuple has no member surface of its own — `(1, 2).len()` is still refused. The operator path is unmoved and travels with its method twin in the same pins. This is what the tuple-comprehension paper measured when it found "the suite as methods" blocked one level BELOW variadic generics: the block was not the generics, it was that a tuple had no methods to be variadic over. (tracker B210, from `proposal/tuple-comprehension.md` revision 2 §R1.2; docs `spec/types.md` §5.7)

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**`for x in tuple` compiled, ran, and bound `x` to `any` — so `for x in (1, "two", true) { print(x + 1) }` printed `2`, then `two1`, then `2`, and a `&mut` walk over a tuple silently discarded every write. The loop is now refused.** It was never designed: it was a fallthrough. A flat tuple IS a JS array at runtime, so the native `for...of` lowering ran, and the element-type lookup — which has arms for `List`/`Set`, `[T; n]`, a type declaring `next(&mut self): Option<T>`, a trait default's `Self`, and a trait-bounded generic — had **no tuple arm**, so a tuple fell to the give-up default written for an empty, never-pushed list: `any`. The spec produces `any` at host boundaries only, and a tuple literal is not one, so this was a conformance hole rather than an ergonomic gap. It was unsound three ways and the guards around it were inconsistent, which is the tell that nothing decided any of it: native binary operators went through (`x + 1` at three types, no complaint — and NOT a case the generic-left-operand rule can see, since `any` unifies with everything in both directions by spec), an ordinary annotation laundered it (`let s: str = x` was **accepted** and printed `undefined`), and the lending walk `for e in &mut xs { e = e + 1 }` compiled to `__replace(e, e + 1)` with `e` bound to a JS number — `Object.assign` on a primitive coerces to a wrapper, so the tuple slot was never touched and `xs.0` was still `1` afterwards, with no diagnostic anywhere. Meanwhile *field* access and *method* calls on the same binder were already refused ("cannot access field '0' on type any"), so a nested-tuple loop reported the one broken loop twice. **The refusal is the conservative half of two answers, and it is the forward-compatible one.** The other is to UNROLL the loop — check and emit the body once per element, each at that element's own type — which is the same elaboration the tuple comprehension's concrete arm needs and would deliver fold, reduce, any, all and for_each with no new syntax; that question is open, and every program this change rejects is one an unroll would accept, so it can replace the refusal without a migration where `any` could not. The message names the rule and then the spelling that works, which differs by which tuple you wrote: over a **concrete** tuple, positional access and destructuring work and the comprehension does not (`(x in t => e)` over one answers "must be a mapped tuple"), so it says so rather than steering at a form that would refuse the reader again; over a **mapped** tuple `(U in T: F<U>)` it is exactly inverted — `t.0` is refused while `T` is abstract and the comprehension is the shipped form for that source — and that half was a live miscompile of its own, printing `[ 0, 1 ]` and `[ 0, 'two' ]` for a pack of `Option`s. The binder's give-up type is narrowed with the refusal so the reader gets ONE diagnostic: `any` absorbs inconsistently and restated the same broken loop in the body, where the analyzer's own "no answer here" stands down. **The estate census found exactly one site**, and it was a test asserting the bug: a pin listing the deliberately-native iteration forms ran `for item in (5, 6)` beside `List`, `str`, `[T; n]`, `Set` and `Bytes`, and checked only that it *ran*. Being natively iterable is a fact about the emission; having one element type is what the loop's typing asks, and only `[T; n]` answers it — the tuple line is gone and the array's is pinned in its place. Zero hits in std, macro_std, the corpus, the docs fences, the examples, the benchmarks or the templates. (tracker B209, from `proposal/tuple-comprehension.md` revision 2 §R1.1; docs `spec/grammar.md` §3.5, `spec/types.md` §5.9)

<!-- family: feature -->
**`panic(…)` evaluates to `never`, and `never` ERASES: it yields to whatever it meets in every join — `if`/`else` arms, `match` arms, a block's tail against the type expected of it, an operator's operands (`never + i32` is `i32`), a call's argument against its parameter — so a body that ends in a `panic`, or in a `for { … }` nothing breaks out of, owes no return value, and programs the compiler used to refuse now compile.** The bottom type was already in the solver and `panic(..)` already had it; what did not agree was the checker's DIVERGENCE analysis. E114 gave the editor's unreachable-code paint two leaves it deliberately withheld from the checker — a `panic(…)` call, which lowers to a `throw`, and an endless `for { … }` — because widening the checker is a language change and not a paint lane's to make. It is made: `Divergence` has ONE constructor now, so the statement the editor grays and the statement the checker treats as dead are the same statement by construction rather than by two walks agreeing. Return-position checking and R4/R7's diverging-leg exemption gain both leaves with it, so `fun f(): i32 { panic("x"); }` and `fun serve(): i32 { for { tick(); } }` check without an unreachable value after them (std's `rpc.vl` carried `0 - 1 // unreachable — the panic throws` for exactly this; N48, beside this entry, deletes it). **Erasure removes the diverging participant and nothing else** — `let v: str = if c { 1 } else { panic("no") }` is still a mismatch, reported at the `1`, because the arm that survives still has to agree — and `never` never reaches emission as a value, since the expression that had the type leaves before anything can read it. **The endless-loop leaf is conservative in the direction that matters**: a `jump break` binds to the nearest enclosing loop by span, so an inner break leaves the outer loop endless, while an unspanned (desugared) loop and a `for cond { … }` — the `while` — are left out of the set and their tails still owe their value. Both leaves are settled ONCE per resolution phase, from facts the WALK banked rather than from the call table, which fills in as calls resolve: reading a callee from there made "does this body diverge?" depend on fixpoint order, and a return-type constraint that resolved before the panic call it sat after saw a body that did not. Twelve pins, each red-proven against a planted tree — four different plants, because the erasure half and the divergence half fail in different places — and the three controls (a plain void tail, a loop with a break, a `while`) are pinned red-side too. The type system chapter states `never` and the erasure rule where it lists the types, the return-position rule where it lives, and the memory chapter's R4 names what a diverging leg is.

The inputs are now digested before the run and the outputs after.

Latent today, and deliberately so: the route partition cannot produce such a reference at all, so every artifact of the split fixture is byte-identical and the change is inert on every plan v1 can make.** The shipped chunk preamble reads `const panel = __vilan_chunks.fn.panel;` and that is safe for exactly one reason: anything two route arms reach is eager, so a chunk's non-std dependencies are all eager, and the eager registrations run in the entry's own module evaluation — strictly before any chunk can be fetched (`bundle-boundaries.md` §1.6, fact 2). The fix is the one `bundle-boundaries.md` D5 recommends and is the form the eager forwarder has always carried — `__vilan_chunks.fn.docs_double(3)` at each use — so arrival order stops mattering entirely and no dependency graph is needed. **`shapes::Dot { x = 1 }` parses. Its own lane felt it: two of B172's pins construct through a `make()` helper because they could not write the literal they meant. **The literal now reads the same production, character for character** — the head is `parse_path_type`'s loop, a `::` continuing the path only when a NAME follows it — so one, two or any number of segments work for the reason `std::reactive::SignalCell<i32>` works as a type, and generic arguments still belong to the last segment. **The disambiguation needed no new rule, which is the point of reusing the production.** A condition parses through the no-struct mode, and that mode does not reach the literal rule at all, so `if k == shapes::Kind::Flat { … }` reads its `{` as the block exactly as `if Foo { … }` does; parenthesising is the same escape it always was. **A PARTIAL generic-argument list is now what it reads as — a PREFIX. `tag<Dog>(a, b)` on a two-parameter `tag` binds `T` and lets the arguments infer `U`, where it used to leave `U` abstract all the way into emission and stop the compiler with an internal error asking the author to report their own program; and an OVER-long list, which used to be accepted with the extra argument silently dropped, is refused.** Supplying none worked (inference from the arguments) and supplying all worked; supplying *some* did not, which is the shape B186's implicit-generic sugar walks into by construction — `tag<Dog>(label, subject: Greet)` writes one argument for a list the sugar has just made two long. **The family is worth naming precisely, because it is two different failures under one root.** The partial case is not a silent wrong answer: it is a hard stop in the emitter (`internal: a call resolved to `Greet`'s requirement `greet`, which has no body … please report this program`) on a program the analyzer had fully typed and accepted — codegen reading a binding channel wrongly, which is the miscompile family's own defect even where the outcome is loud. **An editor keystroke no longer rebuilds the standard library's world just because the file imports a sibling module. What is true is that sibling modules LOAD INTO the world, so a world built for one sibling set is not a world for another — and that is a KEY, exactly as the entry's `std::` reference set and its dependency seeds already are. **A generic bound is now evaluated once per (type, trait, arguments) instead of once per call site, which takes the whole-program bound check off the per-keystroke curve it was on.** `check_generic_bound_satisfaction` walks every recorded call site of the whole program on every analysis — including every site in every module the edit never touched — and asks, per bound, whether the value's type satisfies it. On kolt with its 636 KB generated icon module that is 1,791 unchanged functions re-asked on each keystroke, and the check is 63% of the `checks` phase they dominate. The answer depends only on the resolved types involved, never on which call asked, so it memoizes — and the key has to be the resolved `Type`, because ids are minted per OCCURRENCE and an id-keyed memo memoizes nothing (the same finding, and the same fix, as the `refined_edges` selection memo one cycle earlier). Both memoized calls read their subject only as a resolved type plus a trait id, so equal keys have equal answers by construction. Pinned by a counter, not a clock, for the reason its neighbour is: the memo changes no diagnostic, so no behaviour test can see it, and a timing assertion on a shared machine is not a test — sixteen extra calls at one type add sixteen evaluations without it (12 → 28) and ZERO with it (12 → 12). This is the first tranche of backlog M19; what remains — reusing an UNCHANGED module's analysis across analyses — needs a cache keyed on module content that one `Analyzer` over the whole program has no seam for, and is the paper's to sequence.

Paint asks for two leaves the checker does not have, and the asymmetry is deliberate and one-directional: a `panic(…)` call, which lowers to a `throw`, and an endless `for { … }` (the language's only endless-loop form — `for cond { … }` is the `while`) that nothing breaks out of. Paint may see MORE divergence than the checker safely, because paint decides nothing; widening the checker the same way would be a language change, since `expr_diverges` gates the diverging-leg exemption and return-position checking, and a body ending in `panic()` would newly satisfy a declared return type. A `jump` carries no label, so it binds to the nearest enclosing loop by span, and a loop whose nesting is ambiguous is simply left out of the endless set — the conservative direction, which paints the statement after it as live. One faded range per dead block, not one per statement, because what died is the REST of the block and N grayed lines say that N times. Both inherit the imports third's conservatism whole: nothing fades while the buffer is ahead of the analysis, nothing fades in a file carrying a diagnostic — which is also what makes the platform-colored case safe, since a browser-only file analyzed under the wrong color is a file full of diagnostics, and the fade is already off. **Seventeen pins, eight of them watched red against the live implementation** (eight of the nine unreachable pins failed before the synthesized-tail rule landed — a `fun f() { ret; }`'s trailing `Void` records the closing BRACE as its span, passes every span test, and is not code at all), with the exemptions proven non-vacuous by removing them one at a time and watching the `_`-led, top-level, and diagnostic-gate pins go red. **Cost, measured, because E114's neighbour E121 sets a 10 ms keystroke budget**: both producers are called from exactly one place, `publish::diagnostic_groups`, which is the debounced diagnostics path — nothing on the keystroke path pays for them — and no reachability walk was added, the emission pruner's answer being a whole-program question the honest scope above turned out not to need. The first cut was still too expensive and the measurement caught it: `entity_map` is whole-program, so asking it for the open file's blocks scanned `std` and every dependency, and then ran the divergence walk over every `std` body — on kolt's `views.vl` (the E121 exhibit) 118 ms, and enough to push the package-recolor pin past its ten-second settle deadline on a loaded machine. Ids are assigned per file in contiguous blocks, so the new `Program::entities_of` FETCHES a file's rows by id range instead of scanning for them, and the same inversion (`id_ranges_of`) replaces the per-row `source_of` linear scan that the local walk was paying once per variable. After it, on the same file and the same loaded machine: 2.8 ms for the locals and 6.2 ms for the unreachable walk, against the already-shipped import third's 65 ms in the very same run — a 19× drop on the walk that mattered, and the recolor pin back inside its deadline. (Absolute figures are from a machine at loadavg ~90 and are worth only the ratios in them; the ratio is the claim.) Both found real things on their first corpus run — `rpc.vl` carries a `let (channel, subscription) = entry;` whose `channel` is never read, and an expression its own author labelled `// unreachable — the panic throws`. Found and NOT fixed: an unused top-level item in a single-entry `[package]` genuinely is dead (that entry's analysis IS the whole program), and could be faded behind an entry-count gate plus exemptions for `main`, `[rpc]`, `[expose]` and derive products — recorded on the item rather than built, since the gate is narrow, a false gray is the worst outcome paint has, and none of it is decidable for a `[library]` at all. (tracker E114, owner-proposed — the declarations and unreachable thirds)
