<!-- family: breaking -->
**An operator trait's method is now required at impl time: `impl P with Add { }` was accepted, `check` reported no errors, and `P { n = 1 } + P { n = 2 }` threw an uncaught `not implemented yet` naming no type, no method and no span.** `std::operators`'s ten traits carry `panic("not implemented yet")` bodies — deliberately, so the declarations type-check — and a body is a body, so the conformance rule "a member with a default body is inherited" let the empty impl through. Meanwhile the refusal a type with NO impl gets reads "add `impl P with Add` providing `add`": advice this program had followed to the letter, minus the providing half. The panicking default is not a default anyone can mean, because its only behaviour is to throw, so the rule for the ten operator traits inverts — the method is required, and an impl that provides none refuses at the impl rather than at the first operator. **The bodies stay, and `+=` still derives from `+`**, which is what they are for; the refusal says so, so nobody reads the requirement as an oversight to work around. It also names the exact signature to write, rendered rather than read off the trait — the trait's own `b: B` renders as `b: Add`, which is not a signature anyone can write, and an `impl Meters with Add<Feet>` gets `fun add(self, b: Feet): Meters`. Reached through a supertrait (`trait Doubler with Add`, then `impl Money with Doubler {}`) the requirement comes from a trait the impl does not name, so the message says whose it is and names the separate `impl Money with Add` that satisfies it too. **Migration**: an empty operator impl was already a runtime panic waiting to happen, so the census across std, the corpus, the docs fences, the examples and kolt found none — 63 operator impls, every one of them providing its method. (backlog B197, audit run 7's F12, ruled)

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**A trait default's `self <op> self` now dispatches to the type the default is specialized for: `trait Doubler with Add { fun twice(self): Self { self + self } }` made `Money { cents = 21 }.twice()` print `2`.** The emission was the host's `+` over two lowered structs — `[21] + [21]` is the string `"2121"`, and slot 0 of that is `"2"` — a plausible wrong answer that never looked like a failure. Not `+` alone: `self - self` and `self * self` over the same pair were `NaN`, so their fields read `undefined`, and `self == self` was a reference compare that ignored the impl entirely, printing `true` for a `PartialEq` whose `eq` answers `false`. **Both halves of the defect were one missing dispatch.** `self` inside a trait DEFAULT body is `Type::Trait`, and the operator check skipped that shape: with nothing dispatching it, the anything-goes native emission survived, which over an aggregate is JavaScript's own coercion. B175 could not close it, because the refusal it would have written was advice nobody could take — and the reason for that is the same missing case: the binary emitter demanded a CONCRETE receiver, so a default body's operand matched nothing. The answer was never a refusal. A default body's operand now dispatches on the SPECIALIZED type, through the channel a `self`-CALL in a default body has used since B55 — the emitter reads its own `current_self_type` where the recorded type is absent — so one default body over two impls gives two answers, and a native specialization keeps native JS (dispatching a native back into std's `impl i32 with Add` would recurse forever). **The analyzer stops skipping the shape, which makes a real error visible for the first time**: `self + self` in a trait with no `Add` supertrait would reach the host's operator at every specialization, and now refuses — with its own sentence, not B175's bare-trait one, whose steer ("hold the value in a generic bounded by the trait") is nonsense inside the trait's own body. The declaration that works there is a supertrait, and the message names it. (backlog B193, the residual B175 filed and audit run 7 widened)

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**`-` and `!` now hold their operand to an admitted set: `let flipped: bool = -true` compiled and held `-1` — truthy, and equal to neither `true` nor `false` — while `-Point { x = 1, y = 2 }` was the host's `NaN` and reading a field of it printed `undefined`.** The binary family closed a release ago; a unary is typed somewhere else entirely — `Expr::Unary` in the inference walk simply returns its operand's type — so it reached no operand rule at all, and the same defect survived at the site with only one operand to blame. `-"12"` was `-12` typed `str`, on which `.len()` is undefined; `-Level::High` was `-5` typed `Level`, matching no variant, so `== Level::High` and `== Level::Low` both answered false. **The admitted sets are stated rather than read off an impl, because there is no impl to read**: vilan has neither a `Neg` nor a `Not` trait, so nothing at a unary ever dispatches — `-` admits the numeric primitives, `!` admits `bool`, and each refusal names the set it is holding the operand to. On a native non-numeric operand (`bool`, `str`, a backed enum) the message is the binary family's, retold for one operand: a unary takes its type from its OPERAND, the host operator returns a number, so the expression is a number wearing a type it is not. On an aggregate it says the thing that is actually true there — no trait exists that could give `-` a meaning — and steers to the number inside (`-value.field`). **`!` never miscompiled a type and is refused anyway**, because its defect is the other half of the same sentence: the result was always `bool`, but the host's `!` is a truthiness test that admits every value, so `!5` was `false`, `!"hi"` was `false`, and a struct — an array once lowered — was always truthy. That is a question nobody asked, compiled silently; it is B28's `if`-condition rule at the operator that produces the `bool`. **A type parameter is refused whatever its bound**, for the reason the whole family turns on: membership in an admitted set is provable by bound only where a trait names the set, and no trait names "the numeric primitives" or "`bool`". `fun negate<T: Sub>(value: T): T { -value }` compiled, and the one declaration printed `-5` for `negate(5)` and `undefined` for a struct. **A trait-typed operand is refused for a sharper version of the same reason, and it is the one shape the binary site can rescue and this one cannot**: `self + self` in a trait default now dispatches on the specialized type, because a supertrait can promise `Add` — but nothing can promise `-` or `!`, so `trait Flipper { fun flipped(self): Self { -self } }` printed `undefined` for every specialization and `!self` printed `false` for all of them. The two ways of arriving get different steers, because only a default body has a trait to add a method to. Census across std, the corpus, the docs fences, the examples and kolt: zero — every unary minus in the estate already had a number under it. (backlog B200, the twin B196 found and left)
<!-- family: performance -->
**Semantic highlighting, inlay hints and completion now describe the buffer on your screen instead of the last finished analysis, and their cost stopped tracking the size of the codebase. On a generated 1,791-function exhibit the whole-program walk every request used to pay costs 1.104 ms of thread CPU; the keystroke path that replaced it answers semantic tokens in 0.004 ms — 276× less — and inlay hints in 0.001 ms, with the whole three-provider burst at 0.828 ms against the 10 ms budget (release, 50 requests per window, loadavg 41.9 on 16 cores; wall 2.926 / 0.004 / 0.001 / 1.632 ms beside it and asserted on nowhere). On a read-only copy of a real 1,791-function application the same request went from 12.2 ms of wall and 10 ms of CPU to 0.30 ms and 0 ms, and from 12.3 ms measured from the keystroke to 1.8 ms — at loadavg 45 against the earlier reading's loadavg 11, so the four-times-busier machine makes those a floor rather than a ceiling.** The measurement that motivated it is `proposal/editor-latency.md` §1.4a: hold a file completely fixed and grow the codebase around it, and the cost of serving that file's semantic tokens grows 6.4× — 4.2 to 27.0 ms of CPU for one unchanged 468-token file as its import closure goes from 4 to 5,000 functions — because every request re-walked `program.functions`, `structs`, `enums`, `traits`, `variables`, `parameters` and the whole `entity_map` from scratch. The 10 ms budget was spent at roughly 490 reachable functions, and kolt's `views.vl` is at 1,791. The fix is to stop recomputing: an analysis now captures its own token stream, hint list and symbol index once, when it is built, on the analysis thread — and a request re-serves that capture through a byte-identical anchor plus one lex of the open file, whose result is used only inside the window being edited. The cost that remains is proportional to the file, which is what the mandate asked for, and independent of the program it belongs to, which is what it was not. Mechanically the path is three pieces in a new `crates/vilan-lsp/src/keystroke.rs`, and none of them type-checks, resolves a project context, or touches the filesystem. Positions come from a *two-sided anchor*, which generalizes B38's `compute_retained_tail`: everything before the first differing byte and after the last differing byte is literally the same text, so the landed answers there map onto the live buffer by a constant shift and are exact — B38's own honesty argument, now applied to the larger half it threw away. The middle window between the anchors is the region you are editing, has no image in the analysis, and is painted from *syntax alone*; a landed span that straddles a window edge is dropped rather than clamped, because half of it describes bytes that are gone. Whether the classification outside that window is still true is decided by a *declaration-shape stamp* — a hash of every token the lexer produces outside a function body, which is exactly the text that binds a module-scope name. An equal stamp means no top-level declaration was added, removed or renamed, no `import` line moved and no signature changed, so the landed names still resolve where they did; a changed one degrades the whole file's tokens to syntax-only until the next analysis lands. It is computed off the lexer rather than the parser, so it costs one linear pass and survives the mid-keystroke syntax error that would fail a parse, and every ambiguity in it resolves toward *changed*, which is the safe direction. Completion gains a *per-module symbol index* of declared names, kinds and signature labels, built from the landed analysis and grouped by `Program::source_of`, with the edited module's own entry rebuilt from live syntax on any keystroke that moves its stamp and skipped on every keystroke that does not — so a `fun` typed one keystroke ago completes, which no answer drawn from the last analysis can do. The three combine into three verdicts, and they are the honest vocabulary for what a mid-keystroke answer is worth: *exact* (an anchor exists and the stamp matches) re-maps the landed tokens and paints the window from syntax; *stale* (the stamp moved, or a module this file imports did) paints the whole file from syntax, because syntax is never wrong; *unusable* (a paste replaced the file, leaving no byte-identical line) paints from syntax and withholds every hint. Two owner rulings are wired in exactly as ruled. Tokens take the yes: the region your eyes are in is syntactic and therefore always right, and a briefly mis-coloured identifier outside it is cosmetic and corrects itself on the next landing — which is what makes the owner's own exhibit work, since the lexer emits no token at all for a comment, so commenting a line out removes its semantic colours on the very next keystroke instead of holding them for the 409 ms–1.1 s staleness window §1.5 measured. Hints take the split: withheld inside the edit window always, because a hint on the line you are typing is simultaneously the most likely to be wrong and the least useful, and a wrong hint is not a cosmetic error but a lie about a type; served unchanged outside it rather than flickered off, because the only "mark" VS Code offers is removal and a display that strobes across a typing burst is the larger harm. The gate is a pin family under the thread clock (M15), on a subject this repository GENERATES rather than borrows: kolt is never integrated into this codebase, so the exhibit is a synthetic module of one repeated shape sized like kolt-with-lucide, written by a generator in the test and not checked in. Its non-vacuity is structural rather than promised — every run measures the whole-program walk the path replaced, in the same process on the same subject, and asserts that the path beats it, so the planted regression §6.2 asks for is the code compiled beside the answer. A seconds-long smoke pin exercising every seam runs in the ordinary gate; the 1,791-function budget pin is `#[ignore]`d, as is the 500 ms diagnostics pin, which does not pass and is not this change's to meet — one keystroke still costs about 925 ms of CPU to diagnostics at that size, and M21/M19 are what close it. Found and NOT fixed, and the gate now says exactly where the remaining budget goes: with tokens and hints down to microseconds, essentially the whole 0.828 ms burst is completion, and it is the landed engine's own per-module `name_to_id_map` sweep and per-request `read_dir` that the index is built to retire and has so far replaced only for a `module::` path prefix. The scope arm's shape was settled by measurement rather than by taste — offering every loaded module's declarations there turned a 125-candidate scope completion on a real application into a 3,144-candidate one, so the index contributes the edited module's own declarations and nothing else, and reaching a name that needs an import stays auto-import's job, with the ranking tiers and the edit that inserts it; the arm now answers 124 candidates where the old engine answered 125, plus whatever the buffer has declared since the last analysis. What that leaves is worth stating as a number rather than a hope: on the same application copy the five-provider burst an editor fires is 12.0 ms measured from the keystroke, against 15.3 ms before and a 10 ms budget, and every millisecond of the remainder is now completion. One older pin is rewritten rather than kept: `semantic_tokens_answer_the_analyzed_snapshot_while_typing` claimed the whole token stream comes back byte-identical while you type, which is precisely the staleness the ruling overturns; it now holds the sharper and true property, that the anchors hold still and the window tracks the buffer, with nothing lost and no classification changed. (tracker E121 §2.1/§6, from Order 25's keystroke-path lane; `proposal/editor-latency.md`)

**The viewport semantic-token request now costs the viewport: `semanticTokens/range` computed the WHOLE file's token stream and then filtered it by line, so twenty visible lines cost 9.0 ms of wall and 10 ms of process CPU on kolt's `views.vl` against the whole file's 8.9 ms — a ratio of 1.01, which is the defect stated as a number (measured before E121's keystroke path landed, at loadavg 8.2–11.9).** It is the request an editor sends most and it was the one paying most: `Document::semantic_tokens` re-walks `program.functions`, `structs`, `enums`, `traits`, `variables`, `parameters`, the whole `entity_map`, `member_name_spans` and `type_references`, re-parses the file raw for the markup and CSS spans, then sorts and de-overlaps — and the range handler ran all of it before discarding everything outside the window, plus one line-index lookup per token in the FILE to do the discarding. **E121's keystroke path, which landed between this item's measurement and its fold, did not reach this request.** It moved `semanticTokens/full` and its delta onto the analysis's own capture — a walk paid once, on the analysis thread — and left `range` on the per-request walk, so the defect survived it intact: re-measured on the merged tree, a twenty-line window still cost **0.851×** the whole file (1752.71 ms against 2059.89 ms of thread CPU over forty rounds of a 12,000-token stream, loadavg 1.29). The window is now a SLICE of that same capture. E121's `LandedSnapshot` carries a `token_lines` table beside its tokens — the first token index at or after each line — so a window is a clamp and two indexes rather than a walk, and the answer comes from **one capture per analysis rather than a second memo of the same tokens**, which is the shape this fold chose over the standalone `SemanticTokenStream` memo the item was originally built with. **The invalidation rule is the whole safety argument, and it is a one-place rule.** The capture is a pure function of the analyzed snapshot — the `program`, the `analyzed_index` its spans point into, and B38's `retained_tail` — and those three move together in exactly one place, `Document::adopt_analysis`, which is where the capture is replaced and its line index rebuilt. A live edit deliberately does NOT invalidate it: `set_text`/`apply_change` move the LIVE snapshot alone and these tokens describe the analyzed one (S1), which is the same reason the answer was already allowed to be one analysis stale, and the reason `range` stays in ANALYZED coordinates while `full` answers the live buffer through E121's two-sided anchor. **B38's salvage tail is folded into the capture at that same point, and that is a repair rather than a translation.** The capture is built on the analysis thread, where the tail does not exist yet, and nothing folded it in afterwards — so since E121 the capture and the walk disagreed exactly on the salvaged region, and `semanticTokens/full` painted nothing below a parse break that `Document::semantic_tokens` would have salvaged. One rule (`fold_retained_tail`) is now applied at both moments the tokens exist, and after an adoption the capture is byte-for-byte what the walk answers. Three pins, gating three claims. The answer is unchanged — a window's bytes are compared against the filter-the-full-stream form they replace, over windows that start mid-file, end past the end, land on a line with no tokens and cover everything; planting an ignored end bound reddens it. The answer is unchanged across a salvaged adoption too, at both the capture and the handler; removing the fold reddens both of those and leaves the two older B38 pins green, which is what says they could not have caught it. And the cost follows the window — on a 1,500-function, 6,000-line synthetic module with a 12,000-token stream, forty rounds each of a 20-line window and the whole file, on M15's thread clock: **0.003×** (0.98 ms vs 286.26 ms) against a bound of 0.25, where planting the pre-fold mechanism reads the **0.851×** above. The bound sits between two mechanisms, not two tunings. Tracker E122, the editor-latency paper's §1.6 find; folded across the keystroke path in Order 25.

**Opening a file no longer parks a tokio worker for the length of its first analysis: a `semanticTokens/full` issued the instant after `didOpen` answered in 1270.7 ms before this change and 7.9 ms after, on kolt's `views.vl` at loadavg 8.2–11.9.** `did_open` called `Document::analyze` inline on the async handler, and that call joins a 128 MiB analysis thread — so the notification handler held its worker for the entire first analysis and every request behind it waited, which the server's own session trace had been reporting all along as `slow request: didOpen took 1252 ms`. Nothing else in the file does this: `analyze_and_publish` has always gone through `spawn_blocking`. The open now does what an edit does. It inserts the buffer synchronously — a new `Document::unanalyzed`, the text and its line index and nothing an analysis produces — so a query arriving immediately still finds the document and `land`'s invariant that a missing map entry can only mean *closed* is untouched; then it schedules the analysis through the same `analyze_and_publish` every other path uses, sampled and stamped with the world revision it read (E117) and landed only if it is still the newest view of the live text. `Document::internal_error`, the degraded document a panicked analysis lands on, is now that same constructor plus its one honest diagnostic. The trade is real and stated: the first token or hint request after an open answers EMPTY instead of waiting, which is the state the debounce window between an edit and its analysis has always had, and a `semanticTokens/refresh` pair follows the landing so the empty answer is transient. Measured over interleaved rounds per binary: the open-then-request latency **1270.7 / 1058.9 ms → 7.9 / 1.5 ms**, the `slow request: didOpen` trace line **two occurrences → none**, and the open's diagnostics still publish at the same magnitude (1270 / 1059 → 1408 / 1051 ms) because the analysis is unchanged work on a different thread. Pinned two ways on a current-thread runtime, which is what makes the ordering exact rather than statistical: a request issued while a fresh open's analysis is in flight is ANSWERED and the analysis has demonstrably not landed when it is — planting the inline analyze reddens that assertion by construction — and the open's diagnostics still arrive afterward; and an edit arriving during a fresh open is the analysis that settles, so the supersession the scheduling brings with it is guarded too. Three existing pins had to be told to wait for an open now that one does not block: the two package-recolor pins read a diagnostic straight after `didOpen`, and the session-leak loop went from tens of seconds to **88 ms** the moment its twelve opens stopped analyzing — a gate quietly becoming vacuous, so it now waits for each and costs 8.9 s again. Tracker E123, the editor-latency paper's §1.6 find.

**`[derive(..)]` on a GENERIC type now generates a real generic impl — `impl Handle<type T> with Wire` over `Handle<T>` — instead of an erased one that named the subject bare in every role, and the arity rule generated code was exempted from now applies to it.** Every generator spelled its subject by its bare NAME wherever a type was wanted: `[derive(Wire)]` on `std::arena`'s `struct Handle<T>` emitted `impl Handle with Json`, `Result<Handle, str>` and `fun rebuild(..): Handle`, and `[derive(Debug)]` on a `struct Pair<T> { a: T }` emitted a body calling `.debug()` on a parameter nothing bound. Those are under-supplied applications, and B188's erasure — the very hole B188 closed for written code — was precisely what let them type-check, so B188 shipped its arity refusal GATED off `DERIVED_SOURCE`: total over what a program writes, exempt for what a generator writes. The exemption is gone and the gate with it. **The macro reflection surface now carries the subject's own generic parameters.** `macro_std::meta`'s `StructItem` and `EnumItem` each gain `generics: List<GenericParameter>` — name, written bounds, and the default AS WRITTEN — plus the two spellings every generator needs from them: `subject()` renders the subject as an application of its parameters (`Handle<T>`, `Either<L, R>`), and `binders(trait)` renders the impl header's binder list. Both are used by the vilan derive macros (`Json`, `Wire`, `Debug`, `Default`, `PartialEq`, `Hashable`) and mirrored in the Rust fallback generator, because two backends that disagree about a subject's spelling are worse than one that is wrong. Path heads (`Handle::from_json_value(..)`), struct-literal heads and display text keep the bare name: each of those names a namespace or a word, not an application. **THE RULE is the derived trait on every REACHED parameter, and a bare binder for a phantom one** — a parameter is reached when some field type or variant payload is written in terms of it, at any depth, so `value: T` and `held: Option<T>` both reach `T` and `Handle<T>`'s `T` reaches nothing. That is a deliberate DEPARTURE from the default this was ruled with, which was Rust's rule: bind the derived trait on every parameter, reached or not. The census is what changed it. Exactly one derive over a generic subject exists in std — `Handle<T>` — and its parameter is phantom by construction, because a `[derive(Wire)]` type whose field is typed by a parameter is refused at its own declaration by the Wire boundary check. C7 rules that a handle is sendable whatever it names ("a name is not the thing it names"): the entity stays on the server, only `{ index, generation }` crosses, and `docs/std/cells.md` and `docs/guide/services.md` both say in so many words that a handle names entities whose type is not itself Wire. Rust's rule would emit `impl Handle<type T: Wire>` and make `Handle<Session>` un-sendable for any `Session` that is not Wire — refusing a program the compiler has a passing pin for. So for `Wire` the every-parameter bound is pure cost: the reached case is unreachable, and the bound buys nothing while breaking C7. Reachability is also EXACT in vilan in a way it cannot be in Rust, where `PhantomData<T>` mentions `T` and the compiler therefore cannot tell phantom from reached: a vilan phantom parameter appears in no member type at all, so "mentioned by a written member type" IS the test. A type form the reflection surface cannot decompose — a tuple, a closure, a reference — is read as reaching every parameter, which falls back to Rust's rule rather than to a bare binder over a body that will not compile. **What this buys is that one derive now serves every instantiation.** `[derive(Json)] struct Box<T> { value: T }` encodes and decodes at `Box<i32>` and `Box<str>` from a single impl; `[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Default)]` over a generic works the same way. All of that was a compile error before — `cannot call method 'to_json' on T`, reported inside code the author never wrote — so nothing ran wrong and nothing changes meaning; this is a capability, not a correction. An unmet bound is refused at the USE site, naming the concrete argument and the trait (`'Opaque' does not implement trait 'Debug'`), not at the `[derive(..)]` and not inside the generated impl. Nine pins, seven of them red against the live compiler before the change, including a MIXED subject whose reached parameter binds and whose phantom one does not, both directions pinned so the bare binder cannot quietly disable the check. **Two `DERIVED_SOURCE` gates deliberately stay**, because this rule does not make them redundant: B189's covered set suppresses a generated `[service]` subscription call restating an `[expose]` refusal already reported at the author's own field, which is diagnostic dedup on a different axis entirely and has nothing to do with derive bounds. B174's operator exemption is the one this DOES make redundant — it exists because `[derive(PartialEq)]` emitted an `eq` over an unbounded `T`-typed field, and that field's parameter is now bound `T: PartialEq` — and it IS lifted, in this same unreleased section: the b194-landing lane removed it once b174 had merged, so the derive surface passes the operator rule rather than skipping it. (tracker B194, from b188's STOP; `macro-engine.md` §3/§10, `claims-and-epochs.md` §6)

**A negated `is` test now scopes its capture to the branch that actually matched: `if !(x is Some(let n)) { … }` no longer binds `n` in its then-branch — the branch reached only when the pattern FAILED — and does bind it in the `else`, which is reached only when it matched. The program this stops compiled, ran, and printed `undefined`.** B171 ruled the scope of an unnegated capture a day earlier — then-branch yes, `&&`-right operand yes, `||` arms no, `else` no — and a negation is the case that sentence does not reach. `if !(maybe is Some(let n)) { print(n); }` emitted `if (!($a[0] === 0)) { console.log($a[1]); }`: the payload slot read exactly where the subject has no payload, which JavaScript answers `undefined` and prints, so the program produced a plausible wrong answer and reported nothing — the same shape and the same silence as the `||` arm B171 closed. **The rule is B171's then-branch rule MIRRORED, and it is ruled here rather than restated**: a `!` swaps which of the two branches the capture is bound in, so the then-branch of a negated test refuses and the `else` accepts — and on down an `else if` chain, since each `else` in it is still the previous condition's false path. Two negations cancel, because a swap applied twice is the identity. The `&&` rule is unchanged *inside* the negation — `!(x is P && use(n))` still binds `n` for the right operand, which the short-circuit reached by matching — but a negated capture does not cross an `&&` it sits to the LEFT of: `&&` carries only its left operand's true side, and a negated capture is bound on the false one. That last case is the one a naive parity counter gets wrong, and it was live unsound too: `if !(!(x is Some(let n)) && n > 1)` compiled and read the missing payload before this change. A capture under a `||` stays unbound in both branches, exactly as B171 left it. **The mechanism is B171's visibility range, extended rather than duplicated.** The walk carries the answer for a capture at even negation parity and the answer at odd parity as a PAIR, which is what makes `!` a plain swap of the two halves and what lets `&&` cut the half its short-circuit does not carry while leaving the other alone — no depth counter, and the nesting cases fall out instead of being enumerated. The `else` branch is a sibling scope the capture was never declared in, so the negated captures a condition binds are handed to the `if` walk, which declares them into that scope from its start; an ordinary `let` of the same name inside the `else` still shadows from its own point on, since the positional rule does not care where a declaration came from. The bookkeeping travels the condition's boolean spine (`!`, `&&`/`||`, the `is` itself) and stops there: a capture inside a call argument is bound by an evaluation the condition's truth says nothing about, so it gets neither a negated cut nor an `else` declaration and keeps precisely the answer B171 gave it. No new diagnostic — the refusals are the ordinary "cannot find" error, which the errors appendix now steers under, since a capture that is visible in the branch three lines down reads as a compiler mistake. Fifteen pins beside B171's, nine of them red against the live compiler before the change; B171's seven are untouched controls and stay green. **`if !(x is P) { ret; }` binding the continuation past the `if` is still NOT part of this** — the then-branch is refused by the rule above and the read after the `if` stays refused too, both pinned; B187 rules that shape. Found and NOT fixed, a B171-era approximation this change deliberately leaves alone rather than widening its scope: a capture reached through a call argument (`if always(x is Some(let n)) { print(n); }`) is still visible in the then-branch and still reads the missing payload — off the boolean spine the condition's truth proves nothing about the test at all, negation or no negation. (tracker B195, from Order 24's rulings-smalls lane; docs `spec/types.md` §5.7, `tour/control-flow.md`, `appendix/errors.md`)

(2) **Two bounds raised to 300 s**, the value E39/E40 settled `WATCH_LIVENESS` on and for the recorded reason: `settled`'s 10 s (200 × 50 ms) is not too large for a healthy sweep when the sweep is a real re-analysis of a real package and the whole pin costs 13.8 s idle — measured here at 9.58 s for `removing_the_import_colors_the_file_back` on a quiet box, grazing the old bound — and `release_differential`'s `NODE_TIMEOUT` of 30 s is a fixed clock around running a corpus program, which is E32's disease exactly. (3) **`priority = 100` for the stragglers**, the idiom the leak plateaus already use: `dependent_edit_measurement` was the sole survivor of a 5455-test union at 246.6 s, holding the run open about four minutes after everything else had finished, and `style_chain_order` and `release_differential` were the other >120 s members. **The CPU-time direction — M15's shape — was measured against every one of these and fits none.** For the watch rounds the subject is an EVENT delivered by a 300 ms poll loop that sleeps in between, not a computation: at loadavg 79 a watcher with nothing to do burns **0.030 s of CPU per 30 s of wall — 1.0 ms/s, set by the poll rate and not by the load** — against 0.33 s for round 1 and 0.02 s for round 2, so a CPU deadline is a wall deadline in different units and makes *starved* and *stuck* less distinguishable, not more. The Windows pin `a_product_the_generator_has_not_written_yet_is_still_covered` flips from `#[ignore]`d to live and asserts the same property through NTFS's fold; it is **unverified locally** — no unix host can run it — and CI's Windows leg is its instrument, with `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` the compile proof that it and the new helper build for that target. If that leg disagrees, the ruling reopens with its evidence. (tracker B198, ruled 2026-09-01; audit run 7 hazard (c); `const.md` §9.2's G17 symlink doctrine)

**Windows' own link spellings — junctions, case folding, the `\\?\` verbatim prefix — are now measured by CI instead of inferred from the unix run, and `vilan fmt`'s cycle guard can finally say "I do not know what this directory is".** Order 23 shipped the symlink doctrine (`const.md` §9.2: a link is a supported spelling of project layout, resolved honestly, with every fence applied to the resolved tree) with every pin `cfg(unix)`, because creating a symlink needs a privilege Windows does not grant by default. Audit run 7 read the non-unix half and found the cycle guard's stop arm UNREACHABLE. `TreeWalk`'s identity for a directory was `util::canonical_path`, which never fails: where it cannot resolve, it degrades to a lexical normalization — the right answer for a comparison KEY over a path that may not be on disk, and the wrong one for an IDENTITY. `Some` was therefore the only value the arm could produce, so the `else { return }` that stops the walk on unix could not run at all. It is the failure case that this costs, and it is worth being exact rather than dramatic: while resolution SUCCEEDS the two helpers agree and an ordinary junction cycle is caught either way, but the moment it stops answering, the lexical fallback mints a distinct key at every level of a cycle — `src/l1`, `src/l1/l1`, `src/l1/l1/l1` — `visited` never collides, and the walk fans out with nothing behind it, since `TreeWalk::walk` has no depth cap and there is no ELOOP on that side. The fix is one call, `fs::canonicalize(path).ok()`, so that a resolution failure STOPS the walk instead of minting a fresh key — the same sentence the unix arm already says when `fs::metadata` fails — and the reasoning is written beside it, because the two helpers differ in precisely the property this one call site depends on. **Eight pins land with it, all `cfg(windows)`, and CI's Windows leg is the only instrument that can run them**: on a unix host they compile away, so a green local suite says nothing whatever about them. Four are built on JUNCTIONS, which need no privilege and which `fs::metadata`, `fs::symlink_metadata` and `fs::read_link` treat as links exactly as they treat a unix symlink (`cmd /S /C mklink /J`, where `/S` is load-bearing — without it `cmd`'s own quote-stripping pass mangles a quoted temp path): the cycle itself, under a 60-second timeout that asserts exactly one `would reformat` and kills-and-panics on a hang, since a pin proving a hang is gone must not be able to pass by hanging the harness; a junction inside a declared tree digesting UNFOLLOWED, re-pointed at a byte-identical tree so that following and not following disagree; a declared directory input reached through a junction staying fresh across three builds; and a product under a junctioned `generated` root surviving both of the exclusion's ladders across the `\\?\` seam. A fifth needs the privilege — a RELATIVE directory symlink is the one shape a junction cannot express, because a junction stores an absolute target resolved when it was made — and SKIPS with a printed note when the machine does not grant it, rather than failing or quietly passing. Three more pin hazards with no link in them at all: a generated root covering its products through a case-folded spelling (NTFS folds case and nothing in the predicate does, so the answer rests entirely on `fs::canonicalize` handing back the on-disk spelling), and the reopen caveat `strip_verbatim_prefix` documents itself out of — its doc justifies stripping unconditionally on the grounds that "the result is a comparison key, never a path we reopen", and three callers reopen it, so a path past `MAX_PATH` is now round-tripped through the stripped spelling and reopened in all three of their shapes. **One measurement is RED and lands `#[ignore]`d rather than fixed.** A product its generator has not written YET has no on-disk path to canonicalize, so a case-folded spelling keeps its case while the declared root canonicalizes to the one NTFS holds; `covering_from`'s `resolved.starts_with(&root)` compares components byte-for-byte, answers None, and the formatter would rewrite a product — §12.1's fmt↔hook loop, reached by a spelling instead of by a link. Neither repair is obviously right, which is why it is a ruling and not a patch: folding case inside `covering_from` makes a deliberately platform-independent predicate platform-dependent in the one function whose whole point is that two front ends answer alike, and resolving the nearest EXISTING ancestor instead changes what `canonical_path` promises every caller it has. (tracker B198; audit run 7's F6, Order 24 charter item 4)

**Every native operator now checks its LEFT operand, not just `+`: `true - 3` typed `bool`, `"12" - "3"` typed `str` and `Level::High ^ Level::Low` typed `Level` were each a number wearing a type it was not, and all three compiled clean in v0.40.0.** b148 gave `+` an admitted set on the native path and gated the check on `+` alone, arguing the gate in a SCOPE note: the other native operators "emit arithmetic on numbers, where `+` emits a rendering". That is a statement about a NUMERIC left operand and it is true of nothing else. Three native types are not numbers — `bool`, `str`, and a backed enum — and for those the argument inverts: the host operator returns a number, a binary takes its static type from the LEFT operand, so what comes back is a number wearing a type it is not. Same miscompile `+` was fixed for, entered by the other nine operators. **The three shapes, as they ran before this landed.** `let c: bool = true - 3` held `-2`, so `if c` took the TRUE branch while `c == true` printed false — a `bool` that is neither of its values, and a `fun takes_bool(c)` accepted it. `let s: str = "12" - "3"` held `9`, and `s.len()` on it was `undefined`. `Level::High ^ Level::Low` was `4` typed `Level`, a value matching no variant at all: `== Level::Low` and `== Level::High` both false, silently — its `-` sibling was louder only by luck, panicking in a `match` with "Level: 4 is not one of its values". The bitwise arm was the quietest of the three: `true & 3` is `1`, which prints as `1` and looks like nothing until something compares it. Compound assignment inherits through the desugar (`c -= 3` is `c = c - 3`), so it inherited the bug and now inherits the refusal. **The rule is that the carve-out is "the left operand is a number", never "the operator is not `+`".** The numeric MIXING b148's SCOPE note deferred is a different question and stays deferred: `f64 * i32` computes a correct answer of the declared type, and refusing it is a numeric-strictness change with an `as_f64()` migration of its own. `+` keeps a block of its own because its admitted set is not this one — `str + x` concatenates, the one thing a non-numeric native left operand legitimately does with an arithmetic symbol. **The comparisons needed nothing, and were checked rather than assumed**: `bool` has no ordering (B24 already refuses `<` on it), a string backing is not an order (§3.6 already refuses that), and `str` and an integer backing both order correctly — replaying the audit's 216-program operator matrix confirms it, with 48 programs flipping from running to refused and **zero flipping the other way**, no output of a still-running program moved. **The refusal names the admitted set of the left operand it refuses**, in the operand-role family the `+` rulings settled: "`-` on `bool` has no meaning: `bool`'s admitted operators are `== != && || !`", `str`'s are `+ == != < <= > >=`, an integer-backed enum's are `== != < <= > >=`, and a string-backed enum's are `== !=` because §3.6 takes its ordering too. Each shape gets the steer that is actually its own — a bitwise operator on a `bool` is nearly always the logical one mistyped, so `&` names `&&`, `|` names `||` and `^` names `!=`; a `str` is pointed at `.repeat(n)` for `*` and at `.parse_i32()`/`.parse_f64()` otherwise; and a backing value is a lowering detail, not a number to compute with, so the enum is pointed back at its variants. Every steer the refusals name is compiled and run in a pin, because a rule with no legal spelling is not a rule. **The estate census found zero spellings the refusal takes** — 293 `.vl` files across std, `macro_std`, the corpus, the examples, the benchmarks, the CLI templates, the compiler's own fixtures, kolt and the website, each checked with the shipped compiler and this one; 390 fenced examples across 47 docs pages, through the docs gate; and a text sweep for a literal `bool`, `str` or enum-path left operand of the nine operators over every one of those surfaces plus the markdown, whose only hits are inside string content and the spec's own EBNF. There is no intended `str - str` and no backed-enum arithmetic idiom anywhere in the world. Thirteen pins, ten of them proven red against the shipped compiler before the change, covering the three shapes on `-` and on a bitwise operator, both compound forms, all twenty-seven squares of nine operators against three left shapes, the admitted-set wording including the string backing's narrower set, the steers, and three controls — the `f64 * i32` carve-out, every operator each refusal names as admitted, and `str + str`/`bool == bool` unchanged. **Found and NOT fixed, pinned `#[ignore]`d**: the UNARY `-` is typed at a different site and reaches no operand rule at all, so `-true` is `-1` typed `bool`, `-"12"` is `-12` typed `str` and `-Level::High` is `-5` typed `Level` — the same miscompile, owing a census and a refusal family of its own. Also noted and deliberately out of scope, because it is coercion rather than unsoundness: a NUMERIC left with a `bool` or `str` on the right (`12 - "3"` is `9`, `12 << true` is `24`) still coerces, and that belongs to the deferred strictness family with `f64 * i32`. (tracker B196, audit run 7's F1 — a released miscompile, present at v0.40.0)

**A trait on a PARAMETER is now an implicit generic: `fun f(x: Trait)` reads as `fun f<T: Trait>(x: T)`, monomorphized per call like any generic you write out.** This is the reactive paper's §7.3, the half of B161 that did not ship with the `let` position — and it is a surface, not a semantics: the desugaring is exactly the spelling the language already has, so there is nothing new to check, emit, or explain beyond where the `<T: …>` went. Parameters are the bulk of the estate's trait-annotation sites (the paper's §5 census), which is what makes it worth a surface at all. **The two readings are one family and they are not the same reading, which is worth stating because the difference is invisible in the spelling.** A `let`'s annotation is a CONSTRAINT: one initializer, one concrete type, the binding keeps it, and the body reads the impl's own surface — `let d: Greet = Dog { name = "rex" }` still lets you read `d.name`. A parameter is QUANTIFIED: one type per call site, so the function is checked ONCE against the bound and the body reaches the trait's members and no others — `fun describe(subject: Greet)` refuses `subject.name` exactly as `fun describe<T: Greet>(subject: T)` always has. Both are "no widening, no `dyn`, static dispatch"; only one of them has a `for all` in front. **Three consequences, each pinned.** Each annotation is its OWN generic, so `fun pair(a: Greet, b: Greet)` accepts a `Dog` and a `Fox` together and a function needing them equal must write the generic and use it twice — more permissive than the concrete parameter it replaces, so no call anywhere breaks. A parameterized trait binds the trait's arguments (`cell: Holds<i32>` is bounded by `Holds<i32>`, and a `Cell<str>` is refused at the call). And the implicit parameter is APPENDED after every generic the declaration writes, so the positional generic-argument spelling this language has — `tag<Dog, Fox>(..)`, no `::<>` — keeps binding what it always bound; prepending would have silently re-pointed every explicit argument one slot left. **The paper's honest cost concern is answered by measurement rather than argument.** A silently-generic function changes its emission shape, so the census took three sites shaped like `std::ui`'s A33-widened bindings (`fun bind_text<S: Source<str>>(self, source: S)`) — one whose body resolves per impl, one whose body never mentions the bound, one more of the first kind — and compiled each estate at two types, written out and sugared. Naively that is six emitted copies; five land, because M16's emitted-body sharing merges the T-independent one, and **the sugared and written spellings emit byte-identical output** — the same 683-byte file, the same five bodies for the three sites. The sugar costs what writing the generic costs, to the byte, which is the negative A33 carried and now has an answer for. **Everything else stays refused, with a steer that now names the position that works**: a return type, a struct field, a generic argument (`List<Greet>`), and a CLOSURE parameter — a closure has no generic list for an implicit parameter to be appended to, so the one position that cannot carry the sugar keeps the error. `&Greet` is deliberately NOT in that list and is now pinned so it cannot drift: `&` is a call convention that `walk_type_node` erases, so there is no `Reference` type for a trait to be nested inside, and the annotation the reading sees is the trait's own. That is B161 as shipped — `let seen: &Greet = & dog` has always been the constraint form, keeping `Dog` — and the parameter now reads the same annotation the same way, which is what "reuse B161's machinery" has to mean if the two positions are to agree. The refusal keeps its single error identity and reads "a trait names a parameter's bound, not a value type; write `fun f(x: Trait)` for a parameter, or a generic for a field/return". Seventeen pins in the sugar's own section, nine of them red against the live compiler before the change, including a `View` extension bound on `Source<i32>` against the real `std::ui` — the shape the estate will be written in. Three of B72's parameter-position REFUSALS invert into acceptances here, which is that arc closing rather than a regression: B72's steer said to write `<T: A>`, and the parameter now means it. What B72 established is untouched where it still applies — the rule fires at the declaration with no call in sight, it is one rule rather than a per-position message, and its pins now read at a field or a return. Found and NOT fixed on the way through, pinned `#[ignore]`d: a PARTIAL generic-argument list (`tag<Dog>(..)` on a two-parameter function) leaves the unsupplied parameters uninferred and reaches emission abstract; supplying none works and supplying all works, and it reproduces on two written generics with no sugar in sight. (tracker B186; `proposal/reactive-traits.md` §7.3; docs `spec/types.md` §5.5, `tour/data-and-traits.md`)

**`Optimistic<T>` gains a second type parameter — `Optimistic<T, S: Signal<T>>` — so the cell wraps any signal, not only the canonical one.** A field must name a real type, which is why `Optimistic::over` asked for a concrete `SignalCell<T>` while `optimistic`, `bind_value` and the rest of A32's write-back class had already widened to the trait. Widening the cell means NAMING the signal's type, and `S` is that name. **The census is the whole break, and it is small**: `Optimistic` appears as a TYPE in exactly four places in the world — `struct Optimistic<T>` and its field `value: SignalCell<T>`, the header `impl Optimistic<type T>`, and `fun over(signal: SignalCell<T>): Optimistic<T>` — all four in `std/src/reactive.vl`, plus their transcriptions in `docs/std/reactive.md` and one prose mention in `docs/guide/reactive.md`. The moved spellings are `Optimistic<T>` → `Optimistic<T, S>` wherever the type is written out, and the field `value: SignalCell<T>` → `value: S`. The corpus, the examples, the benchmarks, the CLI templates, kolt and the website contain **zero** occurrences of either spelling; the compiler's own eight `Optimistic::over` fixtures needed no edit at all, because inference binds both parameters from the call. **Migrating your own code**: nothing changes at a call — `Optimistic::over(title)` is unchanged and still infers. You only spell the second parameter where you write the cell's type out, which is a struct field or a return type: `Optimistic<str, SignalCell<str>>`. **Making that true required a real fix in the solver, which is the interesting half.** A generic that appears ONLY inside another generic's parameterized bound is recovered from the concrete one's impl — `f<T, S: Source<T>>(source: S)` learns `T` from `S` — and that recovery ran over a callee's OWN generic list alone. An IMPL's binders have the identical shape and the identical single channel, and `impl Optimistic<type T, type S: Signal<T>> { fun over(signal: S): Optimistic<T, S> }` declares no own generics at all, so the derivation ran over an empty list: `S` bound from the argument, `T` stayed abstract into the return type, and `let cell = Optimistic::over(title)` was refused with "the type of 'cell' is never fully determined". The recovery now runs over the whole set a call may bind — own generics, the declaring impl's binders, the declaring trait's parameters — which is the set B102 already established a call's substitution keys on, so nothing new is recorded and no instantiation splits. Worth knowing that the old behaviour was only VISIBLE across a module boundary: the leaked-residual check that reports it fires when the parameter is declared in no file the binding's own file is, so the same shape written in one file left `T` silently abstract and said nothing. One documentation defect fell out of the census and is fixed in passing: `docs/std/reactive.md` had been transcribing the free `optimistic` as `<T, E>(signal: SignalCell<T>, ..)` since A33 widened it to `<T, E, S: Signal<T>>(signal: S, ..)` — a fenced signature the docs gate compiles but cannot check against the source it describes. (tracker B186 / A32 §9.3; docs `std/reactive.md`, `guide/reactive.md`)

**An import nothing uses is now FADED in the editor rather than left looking live — the first of the three gray-out classes, and it is paint: a hint carrying `DiagnosticTag::Unnecessary`, out of the Problems count and out of every gate.** "Graying out dead code generally looks better to me" — the owner, on the treatment other languages get in VS Code. The protocol's door for it is the `Unnecessary` tag on a hint-severity diagnostic, which dims the range and touches neither the error badge nor anything that reads a diagnostic count, so the severity is pinned rather than trusted: an unused import arriving as a Warning would enter exactly the tally it was asked to stay out of. The detection is not a second opinion — it is the ORGANIZER's, the same leaf walk and the same usage test Organize Imports already prunes by, so what fades is precisely what the offered fix would remove, which is the only honest relationship between a mark and its remedy. That inherits the honesty the organizer had to earn: a type-only import counts (a `[derive(Json)]` alone is a use of `Json`), so does a struct constructor, so do references from code generated out of this file, and a RE-EXPORT is not a leaf at all — `export import` binds a name for somebody else, so this file not using it is the point rather than a mistake. It also inherits the conservatism, deliberately, because a mark that lies is worse than no mark: nothing fades while the buffer is ahead of the analysis, and nothing fades in a file carrying a diagnostic, since a half-typed name might be about to use the very import in question. Five pins, all proven red — the unused leaf faded beside a used one, the re-export exempt, the type-only import exempt, a broken file fading nothing, and the wire shape (hint, tagged, over the leaf and not the statement, with no squiggle beside it). **The other two classes in the item are not shipped and stay open**: unused private declarations (which should reuse the emission-time reachability pruner rather than walk a second time) and unreachable statements after a diverging expression. (tracker E114, owner-proposed — the unused-imports third)

**The language server's line-index cache no longer answers for text that is gone: an entry is served only while the file still matches the length and modification time it was built from.** `line_index_for` caches by path for any file that is on disk and not buffered, and it had no invalidation at all — documented as safe because it was "written for `std`, whose files do not change". Stability was never a property of the KEY, only of std, and the map holds whatever a cross-file definition or reference asks for. A workspace file is exempt from the cache only while a buffer is registered for it, so one that was cached before it was ever opened kept its pre-edit index through the whole open/edit/save/close cycle, and every later reference into it converted spans through line breaks that had moved: a wrong position, published, with nothing to correct it for the rest of the session. The fix makes the documented invariant true rather than assuming it — a hit must match the file's current `metadata`, and anything else re-reads. That is strictly more than the two remedies the report offered: a did-close hook would not have seen a `git checkout` or a generator's rewrite, and restricting the map to `std` would have gone stale on anyone editing std itself. It also keeps the win the cache exists for, because a stat is orders of magnitude cheaper than a read plus an index build — pinned in both directions, a changed file re-indexed (proven red against the stamp comparison removed) and an unchanged one answering with the very same `Arc`. The entry is stamped with what was read BEFORE the read, so a file that changes mid-read looks stale next time and is read again; the cache can waste a read, never answer a wrong one. (tracker E112, Order 23's editor-health lane)

**The formatter breaks after `|| ` when a closure's element body has to split, so the opening tag, the children and the closing tag are all measured from one column.** The owner's exhibit — `overlays.attach(submenu, || <div .styled(example_padded_style)>`, the children below it, `</div>);` back at the statement — has three anchors that answer to nothing in common: the opening tag starts wherever `|| ` happened to end, the children indent one level from the STATEMENT, and the closing tag sits at the statement's column, so the open and the close are at different columns and the wider the head the further apart they drift. The element now takes a line of its own, one level in, and its children and close hang off THAT line: `overlays.attach(submenu, ||` / `<div …>` at one tab in / `<button>…</button>` at two / `</div>);` back at one. This is the rule a BLOCK body has always followed — `print_block` puts its statements one level past the line the `{` opened and its `}` back on that line — which is what makes an element body read like every other closure body instead of like a special case. Width still decides and decides first: the element is printed inline and only a rendering that actually broke is rolled back, so `|t| <li>{t}</li>` keeps its line and the pins holding an expression-bodied closure argument inline keep holding. Four pins, all proven red against the break removed — the exhibit verbatim, the one-child form (an element child forces a split with no help from the budget), nested children each aligning to their own open tag, and a closure argument nested inside an element head (`.bind_each(items, |t| t.id, |t| …)`), which takes the same rule at that depth. The formatter's own gates are unmoved: same tokens out, no silent bail, canonical in one pass, idempotent. (tracker E118, the owner's exhibit)

**An element head's closing `>` keeps its highlight when it lands on a line of its own: the parse now records the element's angle brackets and the language server paints them, so the shape a head is written in cannot change what it looks like.** Spread a wide head's attributes one per line and the `>` that closes it ends up on a line with no `<div` in front of it — where it lost its color entirely, or rather gained the wrong one. Both suspects the report named were real and only one of them was the bug. The TextMate grammar's element rule is a single-line `match` (`(</?)(tag)\s*(/?>)?`), and a TextMate `match` is applied one line at a time, so a `>` that has left the tag's line is out of its reach by construction — it fell through to the operator list and painted as a comparison. The semantic-token pass could not compensate because it never covered element punctuation at all: `ElementBody` carried the tag NAME's span and the close tag's, and nothing said where the brackets were, so `<`, `>`, `</` and `/>` were the grammar's alone. **The parser now records them** — the opening `<`, the `>` or `/>` that ends the head, and a close tag's `</` and `>` — at the four places it consumes them, which is the only place their positions are known; the editor paints all four as the tag they belong to. That is a property of the parse rather than of the line, so a one-line head and a multi-line head produce the same tokens, in the same order, with the same kinds, which is exactly what the new pin asserts (proven red by dropping the emission). The grammar gets the narrow companion rule for the case it can still see — a `>` or `/>` alone on its line is a head terminator, and the formatter breaks after a binary operator and never before one, so no formatted line begins with a bare comparison `>` — because the grammar is what colors the file when the server is not running. (tracker E115, the owner's report from kolt's multi-line heads)

The edge found nothing to sweep, forever. An analysis now records which package modules it reached, and when that set MOVES the whole package is re-analyzed and re-published — every open document under the same `pkg::` root, dependency edge or not. The gate stays narrow where it should: a body edit, a rename, a new `std` import all leave the reach identical and take the old path, so the sweep does not widen for the typing that makes up nearly all of it. **The manifest half was worse and is fixed in the same stroke.** `vilan.toml` is in no program's `canonical_sources`, so once the sweep was gated on the edge a manifest SAVE re-analyzed nothing at all — a changed `target`, a new `[entry.…]`, a `default-entry` moved, a dependency finally fetched: none of it reached the editor until a restart, and the code comment promising that a manifest save "re-analyzes every open document" had quietly become false. A saved manifest now sweeps every open document whose package root lies beneath it. Three pins, the two handler-driven ones proven red against the widened sweep removed: the import is added and the error clears, the import is deleted and the process color comes back (a fix that only ever re-colored toward browser passes the first and fails the second), and the decision itself — an edit that does not move the graph re-colors nothing. (tracker E116, the owner's report; E113's follow-up)

**A ghost diagnostic no longer flashes back after a comment/uncomment round trip: every analysis now carries the world revision it READ, and a result older than the one already landed is dropped instead of published.** Comment an important line, uncomment it, and an error from the commented state reappeared for a moment — the owner's report, and the class is an ordering hole rather than the slowness that made it visible. The server had two guards against an out-of-order result and both were text comparisons: the debounce generation, checked before an analysis starts, and `land`'s "is this analysis of my own current text", checked after it finishes. Text is exactly what the affected document does not change. An edit in one file re-analyzes every OPEN file that imports it, and a DEPENDENT's own buffer never moves — so its two in-flight analyses, the one that read the module commented out and the one that read it restored, are byte-identical to the live text, both pass the guard, and both land, in whichever order the CPU finishes them. The loser published last. The fix is the standard remedy the report names: a monotonic world revision, bumped by every notification that changes what an analysis would read (an open, an edit, a close, a save), sampled BEFORE an analysis starts and stamped onto its result. `land` then drops a result whose stamp is older than the adopted one, whatever its text says, and the publish planner drops a plan whose stamp is older than the last one it accepted for that owner — neither recorded nor sent, so the superseded view cannot even merge into a shared module's union. Older strictly: an equal stamp is a second look at one world, which is what a dependents' sweep legitimately does, and dropping it would leave the dependent stale. One further seam was closed at the same time — the planner is a mutex, so plan ORDER was always well defined, but the `publish_diagnostics` awaits that follow could still interleave and deliver the older plan last; plan and send now happen under one gate, and the analyses themselves stay fully concurrent. Both pins were proven red against the fix removed: the `land` pin lands two text-identical analyses of one document in the losing order and asserts the older is dropped, and the planner pin publishes a clean analysis and then the superseded broken one and asserts the ghost is not what the editor is left showing. (tracker E117, the owner's report; E106's slowness is what widened the window)
<!-- family: miscompile -->
**A generic type named with no type argument — `fun read(h: Holder)` for `struct Holder<S>` — is refused instead of having its parameter silently erased. The erasure was a live miscompile: it let a `Holder<str>` satisfy a `Holder` parameter and print `seven1` through a declared `i32` return, on a clean compile.** The hole was one arm in the drain that resolves a written type name. A name with arguments attached them to the nominal type (`Option<i32>` → `Enum(option_id, [i32])`); a BARE name fell through to whatever the reference resolved to, which for a generic declaration is that declaration's own type — argument vector **empty**, the parameter erased rather than bound. Downstream, an empty argument vector reads as "nothing to check", so every later comparison was vacuous: `read(Holder { inner = "seven" })` unified, `h.inner` typed as the unbounded parameter, and the emitted `console.log("seven" + 1)` printed `seven1` with `n` declared `i32`. **The same hole had an internal-error twin.** Where the erased parameter carried a trait bound (`struct Holder<S: Get<i32>>`), the field typed as the abstract BOUND, so `h.inner.take()` resolved to `Get`'s body-less requirement and the transformer — which cannot emit a signature — bailed with "please report this program". One erasure, two symptoms; refusing the annotation removes the abstract receiver that put an unimplementable call there at all. **The rule is that an under-supplied application is refused in every position an annotation can occupy** — parameter, return type, `let` annotation, struct field, a nested generic argument (`List<Holder>`), an `impl` head subject, a trait-bound argument — naming the arity and handing back the spelling that fixes it: `` `Holder` takes 1 type argument, 0 given — write `Holder<S>` ``. Inference from context is deliberately not attempted: annotations are checked, never inferred (B161's family), so a missing argument has nothing to come from. A parameter with a **default** supplies itself, so `struct Holder<S = i32>` written bare is complete and still type-checked on the default — the refusal fires only where a missing argument is genuinely missing. **Over-supply is the same check's other direction and was never actually checked**: `fun read(h: Holder<i32, str>)` reported nothing at all unless some *use* happened to force a mismatch, so an annotation nothing used passed silently. One arity check now owns both directions, at the annotation, where the fix goes. **The estate census found zero hand-written spellings that relied on the erasure** — 223 `.vl` files across std, the corpus, examples and benchmarks, every docs fence, every `.vl` fixture and inline snippet in the Rust tests, the website and the playground: every bare use of a generic name turned out to name a non-generic type of the same name declared in the same program. Two spellings are exempt and both fall out of the word *written*. A path **head** (`Option::None`, `List::from_json_value(..)`, `math::min(..)`) names a namespace to look a member up in, not a type, so its arity is nobody's to supply. And **generated** code is not written by the author: today's derive generators spell a subject by its bare name in every role, so `[derive(Wire)]` on `std`'s own `struct Handle<T>` emits `impl Handle with Json` and `Result<Handle, str>`, and the erasure this change removes is exactly what let those type-check. Refusing them would report a *generator's* defect at a `[derive(..)]` the author cannot edit — and making the generators generic-aware is a ruling rather than a fix, because the reflection surface a macro sees (`macro_std/src/meta.vl`'s `StructItem`/`EnumItem`) carries no generic parameters at all, and a derived impl over a parameter needs bounds nothing computes (`impl Box<type T: Json> with Json`). So the rule is total over what a program writes, and the generator half is filed rather than half-shipped. Twenty pins cover the miscompile, the internal-error twin, each annotation position, the two-parameter and partially-supplied forms, both exemptions, and the four controls that keep the refusal honest — a correctly-supplied application, a defaulted parameter, `Self` inside a generic impl, and a plain non-generic struct. (backlog B188, found by the papers lane on B184's path; the same substitution-hole class as reactive-traits §8.1/§8.2; docs `spec/types.md` §5.6/§5.11, `tour/memory-model.md`)

**The playground's buffers get a real prelude, chosen by mode: the WEB set in the browser mode that runs your program, the base set in the server check mode, and a toggle that turns the ambient scope off.** A pasted single-file program has no `vilan.toml`, so B156's weakest-scope rule had no `[package]` to hang the key on — and the playground therefore taught the spelling the prelude exists to delete, while `vilan init`'s scaffolds demonstrated the ambient idiom. `vilan-wasm` now carries the missing half as a **synthetic package context** rather than as synthesized imports: `compile_program_with(source, platform, prelude)` sets `Workspace::entry_prelude`, the same field a manifest's `[package] prelude` lands in for every other front end, and the existing `seed_preludes` pass does the rest. §9.2's mandate is what makes that the only acceptable shape — the prelude binds at the weakest layer, so a pasted `enum Signal` still wins over the web set's ambient one and an `import std::style::style;` still beats the ambient module `style`, both silently, both pinned. **The defaults are per mode and the browser's is the web set, deliberately.** The playground's browser mode is not a program that happens to target the browser; it is a web app, which is the one corpus §3.3 showed the base seven never empty an import block for — so `Signal`, `SignalCell`, `view`, `View` and the modules `style`/`ui` are ambient there, and a counter or a view tree pastes in with no import block at all. The server check mode is a process program and takes the base set, exactly what `vilan init` would give it. **The wire is `compile_with(source, platform, prelude)`**, with `prelude` absent for the mode's recommended set, the word `"off"` for none, or a module path to pin one; the page feature-detects the export, so a glue built before it existed keeps calling `compile_for` and takes the same recommended defaults. The base cache already keys on the entry prelude, so flipping the toggle or the mode never serves the other one's world. **One thing the work found that the filing had wrong**: the BASE set was already reaching manifest-less buffers, because `Workspace::default()`'s `entry_prelude` is `PreludeSpec::default()` — bare `print` compiled in the playground at v0.40.0 and the examples' `import std::io::print;` was redundant rather than required. What was genuinely missing was the web set and the toggle. **One thing it found and did not fix**: the B4 import steer and its web-set arm are both silently dead in the playground, because the std module inventory they read is a `read_dir` (`analyzer.rs`, `std_module_files`) and there is no filesystem behind the wasm — so an absent `Signal` in server mode reports plainly and names no repair. That silence is currently the honest answer, since `web_prelude_steer`'s repair is a `vilan.toml` line a pasted buffer cannot write, and it is pinned as such: an overlay-aware inventory would light up exactly that misdirection and has to deal with it. (tracker K14, ruled door 1 with a toggle; proposal/prelude.md §5.3, §9.2)

**An operator that dispatches to your impl now checks the right operand against the `B` that impl declares — until this landed it checked nothing at all, and passed a foreign struct straight into a body typed for another one.** `impl Counter with Add { fun add(self, other: Counter): Counter }` resolved for `Counter { n = 1 } + Point { x = 1, y = 2 }`, handed the `Point` to a body reading `other.n`, and printed `2` — the `Point`'s first slot, read under the wrong type, from a program that compiled clean. B179 ruled the operand roles for a NATIVE left operand a day earlier: the operator belongs to its LEFT operand, so the right one must be a MEMBER of what that operand's `add` accepts. A nominal left operand is exactly where an impl gets to SAY what that set is, and the dispatch site never read it — so the rule B179 wrote held only for the half of the language that does not dispatch, and the half that does was wider open than the one it closed. Every operator the dispatch serves had it, all measured before the fix: `-` gave `7` and `*` gave `30` off the same slot, `/ % << >> & ^ |` all computed, `==` answered a plausible `true`, `<` answered `true` through `PartialOrd`'s inherited `lt` default, and `counter += Point { .. }` rode the desugar's second registration site into the same body. The check is one general reconciliation at the dispatch site rather than a rule per trait, because the `B` it has to read is the IMPL's, and that is three different things: a type the impl wrote (`impl Meters with Add<Feet>` admits a `Feet` and, this is the point, refuses a `Meters` — which used to read `other.f` off the `m` slot and answer `6`); one of the impl's OWN parameters, substituted through what the subject bound (`impl Bag<type T> with Add<T>` at a `Bag<i32>` wants an `i32`, and stored a `str` there before); or `Self`, whether spelled in the impl or reached through `Add<B = Self>`'s default, which interns as the trait's own type and would have left the check with no `B` at all for the overwhelmingly common impl had it not been resolved. A binder the subject does not decide is a hole the operand fills, which is acceptance rather than refusal, and the bound it carries is then what the operand is checked against. **A GENERIC right operand refuses here for B179's reason one level along**: a bound promises a trait's methods, never that the parameter IS the declared `B`, and a declaration is checked once for all of its instantiations — so `fun bump<T: Add>(counter: Counter, value: T)` is refused even though `Point` satisfies `Add` and the call type-checked (it printed `8`, `1 + 7`). The comparison had to be the RIGID one conformance uses, because the ordinary one treats a parameter as a hole and answers true to whatever is asked — which is how two unrelated parameters in the two positions passed each other. This is also what makes B179's second steer truthful: "put a left operand there whose `Add` declares a `B` that admits `T`" named a route that was broken while every nominal left operand accepted every parameter, and the spelling it means — the left operand's own type carrying the parameter, so its `Add` declares `B = T` — is now pinned green and running at two instantiations. Sixteen pins over thirty cases, twelve of them red against the live bug and four of them controls that were green before and after — because half of this fix is refusing what was wrong and half is not refusing what was right. Census clean: every corpus golden byte-identical, every docs fence still compiling, std's own `impl List<type T: PartialEq> with PartialEq` unaffected. (tracker B180, found by lane b179 the day B179 closed; docs `spec/types.md` §5.7 and `appendix/errors.md`, ledger row 346)

**A type can be named through the module that declares it — `style::Style`, `ui::View`, `std::reactive::SignalCell<i32>` — in every position a type is written.** Until now a `::` path resolved in value position and nowhere else: `style::style()` and `style::Display::Flex` ran, and `style::Style` was a PARSE error as a return type, a `let` annotation, a parameter, a struct field and an `impl` subject, with an explicit `import std::style;` in the file making no difference — the type grammar's nominal form was a bare `IDENT`, so the `::` never belonged to the type and whatever the position wanted next found it instead (a parameter reported `found '::' expected ',' or ')'`; a `let` cascaded into a bogus `cannot find 's'`). **That made the web prelude half a prelude.** `prelude = "std::web"` carries `style` and `ui` as MODULE names — the ruled spelling, since a module contributes exactly one name — so a web-set user could reach every VALUE in `std::style` and no TYPE in it, and both web templates carried a forced `import std::style::Style;` with a comment explaining why. The type grammar now has one nominal production, `type-path`: a name, optionally qualified by the modules that declare it, optionally applied to generic arguments. It is reachable from every arm of the type cycle, so a qualified path composes like any other type — `List<style::Style>`, `(style::Style, i32)`, `[style::Style; 1]`, `&style::Style`, `|style::Style| i32`, a trait bound, a generic argument, an `impl` subject. **Resolution is the path machinery that already existed, not a second one**: the spine folds into the same `StaticAccessor` nodes an expression path builds, and the member is looked up in what the namespace DECLARES, so `pkg`-local modules, nested `mod`s and any depth of std path work by construction. Generic arguments attach to the last segment, the only one that names a type; the earlier segments are modules and take none. **A path addresses exactly one namespace, so a segment naming a non-type is refused where it stands** — `let s: style::style` (the function, not the struct) now says `'style' in module 'style' is not a type` instead of quietly annotating the binding with a closure type and surfacing, if at all, as a mismatch at some later use. The unqualified form keeps its own rule, which is the opposite one and stays right: a bare name in type position may skip a value binding and keep looking outward, because it has somewhere to look. **The templates lose their workaround**: `crates/vilan-cli/templates/browser` and `fullstack` drop `import std::style::Style;` and write `fun card_style(): style::Style`, which the init pins build and run. **A second, independent defect closes with it.** The return-type failure reported `found 'fun' expected an expression` anchored at the item's own first column, naming a token the reader had written correctly. `fun` + a name + `(params)` commits — nothing else in the grammar starts that way — but the body's opening `{` was a silent head-check, so a function that parsed to its return type and then met something that was not a body backtracked whole and left the farthest failure with the `expression ;` alternative tried before it, which declines on the `fun` keyword. The body is a located demand now: `fun f(): i32 Bar { … }` reports `found 'Bar' expected '{' or ';' for a bodyless declaration`, at `Bar`. Pinned on its own, since the grammar fix subsumes the spelling that found it. Fifteen pins across the parse, analysis and formatting layers: one per type position, the nested and multi-segment forms, the generic tail, the web prelude reaching a style type with no member import, the three refusals (a missing member, a non-type member, a non-module segment), a formatter round trip (the type printer BAILS on a form it does not know, which silently stops formatting a whole file), and the diagnostic anchor. (backlog B172, found by Order 23's templates lane; docs `spec/grammar.md` §3.9, `spec/types.md` §5.1, `spec/names.md` §4.5)

**`T::default()` under a bound now types as `T`, not as the bound — which makes `List::sum` over a struct element actually add: it printed `4` for a wallet holding 40 and 2.** A trait's associated function has no `self`, and the specialization that makes a trait member's `Self` return concrete is driven by the RECEIVER — read off the member's first parameter. That is the one shape the check skipped, and a skipped operator keeps the anything-goes native emission, so `sum` over any element type with its own `Add` emitted the host's `+` over two lowered structs: `[40] + [2]` is the string `"402"`, whose slot 0 is `"4"`. A plausible wrong answer, never a visible failure. The fix is the same structural substitution the receiver branch already performs, applied where the path named a BINDER instead of a receiver — the accessor records both halves when it resolves through a bound (the constraint, and the trait that provided the member), so nested occurrences of `Self` specialize with the bare one. **The `Trait::func()` path is deliberately untouched**: its subject is the trait itself, not a bound binder, so its `Self` stays abstract exactly as B162 ruled. **And the operator check's skip list loses `Type::Trait` with it** — the carve-out existed solely to keep std's own `sum` compiling over this wart, and with the wart gone a value typed as a bare trait gets a verdict like every other shape. One trait-typed shape still skips and is filed rather than refused: `self` inside a trait DEFAULT body, where `self + self` over a supertrait `Add` still emits the host's `+`. Refusing that one would be advice nobody can take — the explicit `self.add(self)` does not resolve there either — so it is pinned `#[ignore]`d until both halves close together. (backlog B175, closing the hole B170 left open)
