**An `is` capture is in scope exactly where its test is known to have PASSED — the then-branch and the rest of the condition after an `&&` — and the spec sentence that said it was "scoped to nothing" is gone. The fourth did not, and it was the worst of the four to get wrong: `if maybe is Some(let n) || n > 1 { … }` compiled and emitted `$a[0] === 0 || $a[1] > 1` — a read of a payload slot the subject does not have, which JavaScript answers `undefined` and compares `false`, so the program ran, produced a plausible wrong answer, and reported nothing. `||` short-circuits: its right arm runs precisely when the `is` test FAILED, so nothing is bound there. The corpus program that exercises `args()` had been in exactly that state, byte-identical to its golden and unrunnable; one golden moves (`process-env.mjs`, `arguments` → `arguments2`) and the program runs. **A native operator whose LEFT operand is a generic parameter now needs a bound that PROVIDES the operator's method — `+` needs `T: Add`, `-` needs `T: Sub`, `==` needs `T: PartialEq`, `<` needs `T: PartialOrd` — and the estate's whole migration was one `<T>` → `<T: Add>`.** This is the deferred breaking generics change, taken. B169 and B179 closed the operand-role frame's RIGHT half and B181 closed the logical pair's right half; each left the LEFT, on the stated ground that refusing it is a bound requirement on every trait default written over the trait's own parameter — a migration, not a miscompile fix. What escaped meanwhile ran and answered: `fun bump<T>(value: T): T { value + 1 }` compiled, and `bump(Point { x = 1, y = 2 })` emitted the host's `+` over the struct's lowered tuple and printed **`1,21`**. The comparisons were worse than the arithmetic, because `-` and `*` at least produce a visible `NaN` while `==` and `<` produce plausible booleans: `same<T>(M { n = 7 }, M { n = 7 })` was **`false`** (JavaScript compares the lowered structs by reference) and `less<T>(M { n = 10 }, M { n = 9 })` was **`true`** (lexicographic `"10" < "9"`). Sixteen operators, one root: a `Type::Generic` left operand recorded a dispatch when its bounds provided the method and otherwise fell through to the same native emission a grounded value gets. **The migration was priced before it was taken, and the breaking surface is ONE site.** The census swept std, macro_std, the corpus, examples, benchmarks, every docs fence, the crates fixtures, the project templates, kolt, the website and the playground for a trait default applying a native operator over its trait's own unbounded parameter, and found a single one — `crates/vilan-core/tests/inference/macros.rs`'s `trait Doubler<T>`, a compiler test fixture, re-derived independently by this lane. Zero in std, zero in the corpus, zero in the docs, and the applications declare no traits at all. The only other unbounded-left-operand sites in the estate were the two `#[ignore]`d pins asserting the refusal, which the change turns green rather than breaks. That fixture worked by luck at `i32` and printed **`abab`** for `Holder { value = "ab" }.twice()` — one type argument from demonstrating the bug it was silently relying on; it now reads `trait Doubler<T: Add>`, still prints `42`, and the bound is orthogonal to what it asserts. **The rule is adequacy, not merely a bound, and that is the ruling's own refinement over the item as written.** `T: Display` promises `to_string` and not `add`, and before this it left the shape exactly as broken as `<T>` — the check that asked whether a bound provided the operator's method only ever *recorded* a dispatch and never refused its absence. The right operand already checked adequacy, so the two sides disagreed about what a bound has to prove; they no longer do. A bound reached through a **supertrait** counts, which is what keeps std's own `math::minmax<T: Ord>` (`a <= b`, whose `le` comes from `Ord`'s `PartialOrd`) compiling, and is pinned. The refusal follows the operand-role family's wording and names the bound that would admit the operand, because the left operand is exactly where a bound works: `` `+` on `T` needs `T: Add` — a parameter promises only what its bounds promise, and `T` is unbounded, so there is no `add` to dispatch to ``, closing with where to put it. When the parameter is a **trait's** own it says so — ``declared on `trait Doubler` `` — since that bound cannot be added locally: it moves the trait, and every `impl` of it and every bound that names it. **`&&` and `||` are the one family where "add a bound" is not the fix, so they refuse outright on either side.** They admit `bool`, they model no operator trait at all, and no trait names that set — so B181's shipped sentence serves the left operand unchanged, and the left half it deferred to this step is simply the same check with the side condition dropped. `both(Point { x = 1, y = 2 }, true)` printed the struct: JavaScript's `&&` yields its right operand when the left is truthy. **One boundary is deliberate, and it is B188's, drawn on the same generators for the same reason.** `[derive(PartialEq)]` on a generic struct emits an `eq` comparing a `T`-typed field, so the rule would refuse the derive surface wholesale — and the diagnostic anchors at the `[derive(..)]`, which is not where the bound goes, so it would name a fix from a span that is not the declaration. Generated code was exempted, the rule total over what a program **writes** (which is what the census counted), and the generator half filed rather than half-shipped. B194 shipped that half in this same section — a derived impl binds every parameter its body reaches, so the `eq` above compares a BOUNDED `T` — and the exemption is gone again with it: the derive surface now passes this rule instead of skipping it, and an instantiation that cannot supply the bound is refused at the author's own call site. Bounding the struct yourself works as it always did, and every half is pinned. The spec needed no new rule, only an exact one: `spec/types.md` already prescribed `<T: Add>` for a left-operand parameter and the compiler did not enforce it, so this is a conformance fix — the section now says the bound is required, that it must provide the operator's method, that a supertrait's counts, that inside a trait default it goes on the trait, and what the author of a generic `&&` is told instead. (tracker B174, ruled 2026-09-01, from Order 23's operators lane via audit run 7 and `proposal/generic-left-operand-census.md`; docs `spec/types.md`)

<!-- family: feature -->
**A server can call functions the CLIENT declared.** Until now the wire went one way: a browser called an `[rpc]` method and a server answered, and a server with news — a session revoked, a job finished, another user moving something on the screen you are looking at — had no way to say so that was not the client asking a hundred times to hear once. `[client_service]` on a struct in the browser half declares what the server may call; `[service(KoltClient, client = KoltHandlers)]` names it on the service; `connection.client()` hands the factory a typed `KoltHandlersProxy` the service holds as a field and reaches as `self.client.session_revoked(reason)`. The generator is direction-agnostic — `[client_service]` produces the SAME dispatcher a `[service]` does, because `Dispatcher`, `RpcProtocol::respond` and the whole `arg`/`reply` foundation never knew which end of a socket they sat on — so the browser half is generation, not runtime. The wire grows ONE LANE and no flags: text `s:<id>:<payload>` and binary tag `0x73`, carrying requests the SERVER minted, in the server's own id namespace. Reusing `r:` would have collided two `fresh_id()` counters and made `r:7:` ambiguous on both ends; with a lane per direction each side reads its role off the prefix and nothing has to carry a direction bit. **This version is notifications only.** A `[client_service]` method declares no return type: fire-and-forget needs no pending table, no correlation id and no reverse reply lane, it cannot deadlock a handler's turn, and it covers what a server actually wants to say to a browser. The handler still runs inside `turn(FlushPolicy::AtEnd, ..)` exactly as a server-side one does, so a notification that writes a signal three times publishes one wave. The contract hash covers BOTH directions — a service declaring `client = …` appends the handler surface to its own, so the two ends agree about the reverse direction or the connection is refused at `__contract`, before any `s:` frame could be sent — and a service declaring none hashes byte-identically to what it always did. Both attributes on one struct is peer-to-peer, one dispatcher, no new spelling.

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**Two refusals for the reverse direction, both at the attribute and both in its own vocabulary.** A `[client_service]` method that declares a return type is refused: v1 is notifications only, so there is no reverse reply lane for a value to travel on and no pending table to correlate it with, and the message says to drop the return type or have the handler call back on the connection it already holds. And `[service(.., client = X)]` where no `[client_service] struct X` is declared in the same module is refused too — the reverse surface is read off X's `[rpc]` methods AT EXPANSION and folded into this service's contract hash, so a handler the expansion cannot see would hash as no handler at all and both peers would agree about nothing. Same-module is the constraint the message states, because same-module impls are the reflection the compiler does.

<!-- family: fix -->
**Two rpc frames that TCP coalesced into one read were serialized by the receive loop, so a handler awaiting anything the SECOND frame would have delivered waited for a message the loop was holding.** Frames arrive as chunks, and the socket's `data` handler parsed each chunk into events in a loop that AWAITED each event's `respond` before parsing the next. Across chunks there was never a problem — node calls the handler again whether or not the previous call's promise settled — but within one chunk two requests were a queue rather than two handlers in flight, and on a fast local link coalescing is the common case, not the rare one. A handler that suspended on state the next frame of its own chunk sets waited for it forever. The loop now STARTS each handler's turn and lets the event loop interleave; per-handler turns settle independently, exactly as they always did across chunks. **Reply order within a chunk is not promised** — replies carry their request id and arrive when their handler is done, so a slow first frame no longer holds a fast second one behind it. Nothing in the protocol ever depended on the order; this makes it visible. The pin drives the server from a raw socket, so the coalescing is the test's rather than the kernel's: two masked frames in one `write_all`, the first handler waiting on a flag only the second sets, and its wait bounded in retries rather than in wall time.

**`std::print` is gone, and so are the fifteen other alias-only re-exports that lived in `std/src/lib.vl`. Each name is now spelled at its real home — `std::io::print` — and the prelude carries the ergonomics the aliases existed for.** Every entry in std's package root was there for one reason: to let a caller write `std::print` instead of `std::io::print`. That is import brevity, and a package root is the wrong place to sell it — a re-export whose only job is to be shorter is a second spelling of a name with no rule for which one is canonical, which is exactly what the estate then split down the middle. With a prelude in the language the ergonomics are served properly, so the alias layer goes. **The census is the whole surface**: `lib.vl` is the only `lib.vl` in std and `export import` appears elsewhere in the package only in the two prelude modules this same order added, so six statements and sixteen names is all of it — `print`, `panic`, `assert`, `Default`, `str`, and the eleven numerics `BigInt`/`f32`/`f64`/`i8`/`i16`/`i32`/`i53`/`u8`/`u16`/`u32`/`u53`. Two findings from counting: **thirteen of the sixteen had ZERO uses in the entire estate** — nobody, in std or the corpus or the docs or the examples or kolt or the website, ever wrote `std::Default`, `std::str` or any of the numerics, and the numerics were doubly dead because they are §4.7 primitives that have been ambient with no prelude at all since before any of this; and **std never used its own aliases**, spelling every internal import `pkg::io::print`, so migrating std itself was a null change and `lib.vl` was the only std file that moved. **Each old spelling gets a curated diagnostic rather than the generic failure**, because `std::print` will be typed from muscle memory for a long time and "cannot find 'print' in the imported path" names neither the removal nor either way forward: `` `std::print` was removed: `print` is in the default prelude (no import needed), and its module path is `std::io::print` ``, with the prelude clause dropped for `panic`/`assert`/`Default` (in neither std set, so claiming no import is needed would be false) and replaced for the primitives with "is a primitive and is always in scope — delete the import". The arm fires only directly under `std`'s root, so a typo inside a real module (`std::io::prnt`) keeps the ordinary message. **The migration took two shapes and the split was deliberate.** The fixture corpora — 200 files of Rust test sources, the `vilan/test` corpus, the benchmarks — were **rewritten** to `std::io::print`, a pure textual substitution that preserves every fixture's meaning exactly and cannot depend on the prelude reaching that fixture's package; the corpus goldens are byte-identical, which is the negative this half is checked against. The teaching corpora — 47 files of doc fences, the examples, `README.md`, the CLI templates — had the import **deleted** instead, 159 lines of it, because a doc fence that imports what the prelude supplies teaches the wrong thing, and the docs gate compiling every one of those fences afterward is the prelude's best end-to-end proof. Hello-world now opens with `fun main`. Two things the sweep exposed and fixed at the root rather than around: the transformer looked `print` up in std's PACKAGE-ROOT scope, which only ever worked because the alias put it there, and now reads a `print_fn_id` the analyzer captures from `std::io` beside `panic`'s — a lang-adjacent function should say where it lives rather than ride a convenience re-export; and `std::number` and `std::string` were being loaded only as a side effect of `lib.vl` re-exporting their members for the `std::i32` / `std::str` short names, so they join `boolean`, `list` and the rest in the always-loaded core list, where the primitives they host say so themselves. **Migrating your own code**: delete `import std::print;` outright if your package uses the default prelude (the compiler will tell you, and Organize Imports now strips it for you); otherwise respell it `std::io::print`. `panic`, `assert` and `Default` are a respelling either way; the numerics and `str` are a deletion, since they were never needed. (backlog B156; proposal/prelude.md §10.2; docs `spec/names.md` §4.7, `appendix/errors.md`)

**A `let` or `mut` REBINDING of a closure parameter waits for the parameter's type the way a mention of it does — so it keeps a container whole, and keeps the copy it owes.** `s.set_with(|values| { mut next = values; next.push(2); next })` refused with "cannot call method 'push' on unknown", and the copy-update-return idiom is precisely what `set_with` is FOR. The cause was one resolver out of step with every other. An unannotated closure parameter reads `Unknown` until the call site infers the closure against the callee's signature and fills its slot (B13's channel); every consulting resolver — a method call, a subscript, a `for`, a `match` — recognises that `Unknown` as a "not yet" and defers on it. The VARIABLE resolver did not: it took the `Unknown` for an answer and ground the binding on it, permanently, because the fill lands afterwards. So the rebinding was `unknown` for the rest of the closure while the parameter itself typed fine — which is why the direct spelling (`values.push(2)`) always gave the right refusal and the rebinding never did. Rebindings now count as mentions: the walk that answers "is this an unfilled closure parameter?" follows a still-ungrounded binding to its initializer, and the variable resolver defers while its value is one. That is the whole fix, and it is general — nothing about `set_with`, about traits, about default bodies, or about `mut`, all of which the discrimination had pointed at. A plain `let` lost the type identically; so did a closure passed to any generic function, a `sub` observer (a trait REQUIREMENT, not a default body), an inherent `SignalCell::update` view, and a `str` parameter — the "scalars are fine" control was an illusion of numeric defaulting grounding `next + 1` by a different route. A chain of rebindings resolves through the same walk, as does one inside a nested closure. The RUNNING half is why this is a miscompile rather than a refusal: an untyped binding reads as a scalar to the emitter, so it dropped the `__clone` that a `mut` rebinding of a List, a Map or a struct owes its caller. `apply(seed, |values| { mut next = values; grow(&mut next); next })` mutated `seed` in place and printed `2 2` where the annotated spelling of the same program printed `1 2` — a clean compile, silently sharing the value it was supposed to copy. Following initializers put the walk on a graph that can cycle (`let a = b; let b = a;` is writable, module bindings resolving in any order), so bindings already stepped through end it; the two module-level-cycle pins hung without that and are green with it. Found by the website migration's clean-build gate, whose four errors were all this one bug.

**A generic parameter on the right of a native operator is refused now, whatever it is bounded to — the last square of the `+` family, and the same hole in every one of its siblings.** `fun bump<T: Add>(total: i32, value: T): i32 { total + value }` compiled, and `bump(1, Point { x = 1, y = 2 })` printed `11,2`: a string, typed `i32`. B169 had closed the UNBOUNDED parameter in that position and B176 the bounded one on the right of a `str`, and this was the square neither covered — a bound was read as a promise worth keeping, and the pre-ruling message steered the author straight into the program that miscompiled ("Bound it (`<T: Add>`)"). What closes it is a ruling about operand ROLES rather than about generics: the `+` belongs to its LEFT operand, so the right one has to be a MEMBER of what the left's `add` accepts, and a bound can prove membership only where some trait names that set. `str`'s set has one — "everything with a string form" is `Display`, which is exactly why B176's render bound can route a bounded operand through the impl — and a number's does not: `i32`'s `add` accepts `i32`, nothing names that set, and a bound promises a trait's methods rather than a type (`Add`'s `B` defaults to `Self`, which is the parameter, not the left operand). So every generic right operand of a numeric `+` is refused, bounded or not, with a message that names the spellings that work instead of the one that does not; `total += value` rides the same check, reached through the second registration site its desugar builds. The siblings had the identical hole with quieter garbage and close with it: against a `total: i32` and a `value: T`, `total - value` and `total * value` emitted `NaN`, `total & value` emitted `0`, `total << value` emitted `total`, and `total < value` and `total == value` emitted a plausible `false` — each typed as though the operator had been checked. B170 routed every left SHAPE through the check; this routes every right one, and `str` keeps its one exception because `+` on a string is the one native operator whose admitted set a trait can name. Two things deliberately stay open. `f64 * i32` — two grounded numerics that compute a correct answer — is still admitted, because refusing it is the numeric-strictness change with a migration of its own that b148 deferred, not this miscompile fix. And the generic LEFT operand is still pinned rather than closed: a trait default body writes `self.once() + self.once()` over the trait's own parameter today, so refusing it is a bound requirement on every such declaration.

**An operator whose left operand is a tuple, an array, a closure, a function reference or `void` is checked like every other operator now, instead of falling through to the host's.** The check b148 shipped keyed off the operand's SHAPE: the dispatch loop `continue`d unless the left operand was a struct or an enum, so those five shapes reached neither `+`'s admitted set nor the "does not implement the `Add` operator" refusal, and the anything-goes emission b148 removed survived intact for exactly them. `(1, 2) + 1` printed `1,21` — b148's own miscompile, entered from the left instead of the right — `nothing() + 1` was `NaN`, a closure concatenated its SOURCE TEXT, and `let v = if false { 1 }; v + 1` printed a plausible wrong `1` rather than anything a reader would notice. **`Option::replace` declared the value it KEEPS as a loan, so a resource moved into a slot was destroyed twice.** `external fun replace(&mut self, value: T)` spelled its new value BARE — a loan under R3, which changes no ownership — and then stored it. The consequence was visible in three lines of accepted code: `mut slot: Option<Res> = None; let r = Res { .. }; slot.replace(r);` printed the destructor twice, once for the slot and once for the caller's binding, which the compiler still believed owned a value it had handed away. The same hole left `r` READABLE after the move — `print(r.tag)` compiled, where the identically-shaped `List::push(own item: T)` has always rejected it — so the move checker was silent on a program with two owners of one resource. The honest declaration is `own value: T`, and that is the whole fix: a declaration that says what the callee does, in the one std surface where an `external` has no body for the move-clean check to read. A sweep of std for the same shape ("a bare parameter the callee stores") cleared two more and left one open: `Shared::new(value: T)` stores, but R10 refuses a `Shared<resource>` at every site, so nothing reaches it at a resource; `Context::run(self, value: T, body)` binds its value for the dynamic extent of `body` and hands ownership straight back, which is exactly what a loan says. The third, the internal `NativeMap::insert`, is genuinely broken — the caller frees the value at the insert statement while the table goes on holding it — and is pinned `#[ignore]`d rather than fixed, because the declaration fix would buy a redundant deep copy on every `Map`/`Set` insert in the language to close a hazard reachable only by importing `std::native_map` directly; the zero-cost fix is adding the internal head to R10's rejecting list, which is a ruling of its own. **With the declaration corrected, C11's temporary predicate goes back to its ruled width.** The statement-temporary rule shipped narrowed to `&` / `&mut` views and a bare `self` receiver *because* of this defect — recording a temporary in a bare parameter would have destroyed a value `replace` had stored — and the narrowing is now lifted to the rule the spec has stated all along: only `own` moves, so a resource temporary in ANY loan position is its statement's to destroy. `peek(Res { .. })` on a bare `handle: Res` parameter used to leak on every path and now releases at the statement, at a vilan function and at an `[extern]` alike. One callee is exempt, and the exemption is new spec text: a `[extern(…, retains)]` host keeps what it is handed past the call, and a temporary has no binding whose scope could hold it open, so such an argument is left to leak rather than freed under a host still reading it — the direction these rules always fail toward. Six pins, each red-first: the double destruction and the readable-after-move, the widened predicate at both callee kinds proven by re-planting the narrowing, the retains exemption proven by removing its guard, and the pre-existing `option_replace_returns_the_old_resource_for_the_caller_to_own` pin, which goes red on the widening WITHOUT the declaration fix — the two had to land together. No corpus golden moves. (backlog B153, found by Order 19's lastuse-s3 lane; docs `spec/memory.md` §6.8 and `std/option-result.md`)

**A resource held in an `if` arm, a `match` leg, a loop body or any nested block emitted a `try` that trapped a name read after it: accepted vilan that throws `ReferenceError` the moment the scope runs — live in v0.39.0.** S3 moved disposal from scope end to last use by wrapping the statements between an acquisition and its last read in a `try`/`finally`. That region lowers to a JS block, so every `const` a statement inside it declares dies at the closing brace, and the region must therefore be WIDENED until it covers the last read of every name declared within it. That rule shipped, was pinned, and worked — at a function body's top level, and nowhere else. The widening asks the dataflow, once per statement of the region being emitted, *what names does this statement put into the block I am about to wrap?*, and the answer arrives as a map the liveness pass keyed on the OUTERMOST statement enclosing each declaration. At a body's top level a declaration's statement chain has ONE element, so outermost and direct are the same id and the lookup hits; one level down they are different ids — inside an `if` arm the chain reads `[the if, the let]`, the transformer holds the `let` and the map holds the `if` — so every lookup missed, the fixpoint never ran, and the `try` closed over a `const` whose read followed it. `if flag { let r = Res { … }; let value = 7; print(r.tag); print(value); }`, with one ordinary statement after the `if`, emitted `const value` *inside* the `try` and `console.log(value)` after it. The differential that isolates it is one statement long — the SAME `if` written as the function's TAIL widens correctly, because a tail is never pushed onto the statement chain and the arm's declarations key themselves, and adding a single `print("after")` after the `if` breaks it. The fix is the keying, moved on the map's side: `declared_binding_extents` now keys the INNERMOST enclosing statement, which is the coordinate its one consumer holds at every depth. That is the side that was wrong, not a second lookup bolted beside the first, because only a statement's OWN declarations can put a name into the block the region becomes — a name declared inside a nested construct is scoped to it and cannot be read outside it — so the direct statement is the only key that ever answers, and the outermost key answered at exactly one depth by coincidence of chain length. The three shapes that were already correct stay correct and are pinned or probed as negatives: a closure body is its own walk region, so its chains start at the closure; the function body is the one-element case; and an `own` resource parameter keys nothing at all, declaring at its body's entry with an empty chain. Six pins, five of them red first with a genuine `ReferenceError` — a compile-only pin cannot see this class, since the bad JavaScript is well-formed — covering the `if` arm, the `match` leg, the loop body, a block two deep, and the tail-versus-statement differential with both spellings in one program so neither can be fixed at the other's expense; the sixth is the closure-body negative. No corpus golden moves. (tracker B159, audit run 5's F1; docs `spec/memory.md`)

The check is its own constraint rather than a line inside the inference, and it runs LAST: unlike `match`, whose resolution *types* the expression every dependent then reads, the arm check produces nothing anything consumes — the `if`'s type still comes from inference, which folds the identical merge without a voice to report with — so it can wait until every value-typing kind has landed and read settled arm types instead of deferring on each of them. The fix is not a second check beside the first — a second check is how the two doors came to disagree in the first place. The assignment side is a constraint (`FieldAssignment`) rather than a post-pass, because the target is a *place* whose field type is not known until the field accessor resolves — it defers until the target lands, is vacuous when the target turns out to be a local or a tuple position (those places are checked by the kinds that own them), and reads the field type off the TARGET, which the accessor already recorded with the receiver's type arguments substituted in, so a field reached through `Wrap<Doubler>` is checked against `Doubler` and not against the struct's abstract parameter. Compound assignment needs no second site, and that is the point of registering the constraint on the value that LANDS: `s.f += v` desugars to `s.f = s.f + v`, and it is the sum, not the written `v`, that the field ends up holding — a `str` field `+= 5` is well typed and still runs, where checking the written operand would refuse it. No compound shape can land the wrong type today, because every overloadable operator's trait returns `Self`; the door is covered regardless, so it stays covered when one can. **The estate census came back at zero.** Every entry of every project — vilan's corpus and examples, kolt, the website, the playground, 149 checks, std riding along on each — was checked with the fix on and against a base binary, and not one site newly refuses; the corpus goldens do not move. (The estate had to be shadow-migrated past this cycle's `std::print` removal first, or the census would have been reading eight first-error walls instead of the code behind them.) The kolt site that prompted the report is already written `Some(handler)` in the working tree — the owner reached the same conclusion by hand, which is the refusal this now gives him at compile time. Nine pins, each proven red-first by re-planting the removed check: str-into-numeric, scalar-into-scalar, a bare value into an `Option` field, the owner's closure-into-`Option<closure>` shape, the nested and indexed places, the compound form (red under the wrong-operand registration, which is the mistake it exists to catch), the well-typed store whose `is Some` does match, and the literal-door control, which must and does stay exactly where it was. (backlog B166, the owner's kolt find generalized by probe; docs `spec/types.md` §5.11)

**`if stored is Some(let f) { f() }` compiled to a call on an `f` nothing ever declared: a `ReferenceError` at run time, from a program the compiler accepted.** An `is` capture has no declaration of its own — that is the lowering's design. It is ALIASED to the subject's payload slot (`$a[1]`) and substituted at each use, which is why a capture costs nothing and why `match`, whose legs really do declare their captures as `const`s, takes a different path. The alias table had one reader: the arm that turns a local into a JS value. There are TWO places a local becomes JS, and the second — the call arm's named-callee fast path, written for functions and reached by every `Expr::Local` subject — never consulted it and emitted the binding's SOURCE NAME as the callee. So the defect selected precisely the payloads whose uses are calls, which is to say closure-typed ones: an `i32` payload was read as a value and had always worked, a struct payload read through its fields had always worked, and the same closure through `match` had always worked. Three green neighbours around one shape that threw. It was found in kolt's `interact.vl`, where a stored drag handler is exactly an `Option<|| DragHandler>` pulled out with `is Some(let …)` and called. The fix is a guard, not a new path: the call arm no longer claims an `is` capture as a named callee, so it falls to the value-call arm it should always have taken — which walks the subject and finds the alias by the same lookup a READ does. One alias table, and now every place a local becomes JS consults it. `$a[1]()` is the emission, which is what reading the capture and then calling it has always meant. Nine pins, every one of them RUNNING the bundle — the program compiled before, so only execution can tell the difference — and every one proven red-first by removing the guard: the direct call in the arm, the call captured by a closure created in the arm, two closures deep, a capture called with arguments whose result is used, an `else if` chain where each arm must alias its own subject, the shadowed spelling that the first (and wrong) diagnosis blamed, and the three controls — `i32`, `match`, struct payload — which stay green under the planting and are pinned so they keep doing that. No corpus golden moves: a program that called an `is` capture could not have had a working golden. **The first diagnosis was wrong and the probes are why.** It was filed as an alpha-rename that lost a shadowed binding inside closure bodies, on the strength of a `drag_handler_2` in the emitted output; the owner could not reproduce the shadowing trigger, and four discriminating probes — the same shape with and without a shadow, with an `i32` payload, and through `match` — put the boundary exactly on the payload's type and nowhere near the name. (backlog B167, the owner's kolt find; diagnosis corrected mid-lane by probe)

**A call through a bound no longer inherits the context requirements of a same-named member on an unrelated trait.** The context-coverage check refines its candidate set per call, but the set it refines is keyed by member NAME — every trait in the program declaring that name, and every impl of those traits. For a bound call that is far too wide: `v.bind(..)` under `V: MyTrait<str>` can only reach an impl of `MyTrait`, and never some other trait's `bind`. Two traits in one program spelling a member the same way was enough for each to inherit the other's context reads, and the refusal that came out named a `run` the author's own code had nothing to do with. The refinement now narrows a bound site to the impls providing the bound's own traits, with their supertraits, and widens back exactly as before wherever the constraint names no trait or the filter selects nothing. Found building std's `MaybeSignal`, whose blanket subject matches every type: without this, its `bind` was a candidate for every receiver in every program that loaded `std::reactive`. (backlog A32)

**A trait may now declare associated functions — a `fun` with no `self`, with a default body — and `Trait::func(..)` calls that body.** A trait's members were all methods: something with a receiver, reached through one. That left the CONSTRUCTOR out. A type whose canonical construction belongs to a capability rather than to one struct — `Signal::new(value)`, where `Signal` is the capability and `SignalCell` the canonical cell — had nowhere to put it, and `Trait::static()` did not resolve at all, with or without a body on the declaration (the state B83 probed and recorded rather than built). It resolves now, and to a ruled answer: `Trait::func(..)` is THE TRAIT'S OWN default body, always — never an impl's override, which is reached through the implementing type's own path, `Type::func(..)`. That is not an arbitrary tie-break. A `self` method's `Trait::method(receiver)` form exists to name the trait a RECEIVER dispatches through; an associated function has no receiver, so there is nothing to select between, and the two spellings name two bodies rather than one dispatch. The trait's own generic parameters bind from the call like any generic function's (`Signal::new(7)` binds `T = i32`), and a supertrait's associated function is reachable through the sub-trait, as its methods are. Two refusals ship with it, from day one rather than as a later tightening: `Trait::func(..)` for a declaration with NO default body names a per-impl requirement with nothing behind it — the shape that used to reach the transformer's "please report this program" guard — and is refused naming both spellings; and `Type::func(..)` where the impl declares no such member is refused with the trait's spelling named, because a body with no receiver is not inherited onto a type's path the way a method's is. `spec/types.md` §5.5 states all of it.

The refusal it replaces at this one position is NARROWED, not repealed — a parameter, a return type, a struct field and every nested spelling (`&Display`, `List<Display>`) still refuse, which is what keeps a heterogeneous container impossible. The holes that refusal was built to shut stay shut, by the semantics rather than by the ban; the destructor case is the clearest, since `let handle: Named = Handle { .. }` once compiled, ran, and silently never dropped the handle, and today it compiles AND drops it, because the binding is a `Handle`. The `if` case needed no rule of its own: the arms unify first, and the constraint meets the ONE type that unification produced, so two arms of different concrete types are refused at the arms as an ordinary mismatch even when both implement the trait — there is no widening for them to meet in. **`impl type T with Trait<T>` is a real blanket impl now: it dispatches through a bound, and any constructor-headed impl outranks it wherever both match.** The form parsed, analyzed and compiled cleanly for as long as nothing called through it; the first dispatch died with an internal error asking the author to report their own program — "a call resolved to `MaybeSignal`'s requirement `bind`, which has no body". The cause was a divergence rather than a missing feature. The analyzer already resolves a blanket beside a specific impl by SPECIFICITY (B73's R3): `"x".show()` reaching `impl type T with Show` has worked for releases. But a call through a BOUND — `fun badge<V: MaybeSignal<str>>(label: V)` — cannot be resolved there at all, because the receiver is a type parameter until monomorphization binds it, so the transformer re-asks the question at emission — and it re-asked with a nominal head comparison that could not see a generic subject at all and ranked nothing. A blanket was therefore invisible to every bounded call, and, less loudly, a pair the analyzer DID rank was answered here in declaration order: `impl Box<type T: Marker>` beside `impl Box<type T>` ran the marked body at a direct call and the plain body at a bounded one, in one program, silently. Both are gone, because the two sides now ask one shared question (`crates/vilan-core/src/impl_select.rs`, following `dispatch_refine`'s precedent of a shared module owning a resolution its consumers merely ask), in three tiers the spec now states: **applicability** — the impl's subject PATTERN matches the concrete type, its binders read as holes and the type as rigid, and every binder's bound holds there; **instantiation** — where the caller knows which instantiation it wants, and a bound-directed call always does, an impl is kept only if the arguments it provides FOR THIS RECEIVER are those arguments; **specificity** — the impl whose subject the others match and which matches none of theirs wins, then, for subjects of equal shape, the one whose binders carry the stronger bounds. A blanket is simply the least specific tier, which is why nothing needed inventing: it is the order B73 already ruled, applied where it had never been asked. The pay-off is `MaybeSignal<T>` whole — one trait, one blanket static impl, one generic `Signal` impl, and a component parameter that takes `badge("static")` and `badge(signal)` with no call-site ceremony, static dispatch, and the signal leg reacting to a later `set`. It also keeps a case a negative bound would have deleted: under a `MaybeSignal<Signal<str>>` bound a bare `Signal<str>` is a legitimate STATIC value through the blanket, while the same value under a `MaybeSignal<str>` bound is the reactive source through the `Signal` impl — the instantiation is decided before specificity is consulted, so both readings of one type live in one program. That is the recorded argument for ruling `impl type T: (not Signal)` OUT of the grammar and not merely deferring it: the two impls provably never overlap at one bound (`T = Signal<T>` has no finite solution), so nothing needed excluding, and a negative bound would have inverted the rule that adding an implementation is additive — implementing a trait for your type would newly EXCLUDE it from every `not`-bound in the ecosystem, making an impl addition a breaking change. **And the accept-then-ICE is closed as a class, not as an instance.** Every call through a bound now reaches one implementation's member, or the trait's default where the winning impl declares none, or the program is refused before it runs. Two impls with the same subject were already refused at the second declaration — so a second blanket for one trait never reaches a call site — and two the order genuinely cannot rank (`impl type T: Alpha` beside `impl type U: Beta`, met by a type that is both) were already reported at a direct call but reached the internal error through a bound; they are now reported at the call that made the binding, naming both subjects and the fix, in the same words the direct spelling uses. Ten pins, each proven red first by re-planting the exact defect it removes — blindness to a generic subject (seven go red, with the original internal error), the ranking itself (four), and the bound-side refusal (one) — plus a corpus program holding the whole recipe. Const evaluation reaches trait dispatch, so it reaches the blanket, and is pinned to select the same body a runtime call does at both tiers. No corpus golden moves. **A package now declares its own ambient scope: `print`, `Option`/`Some`/`None` and `Result`/`Ok`/`Err` are in scope with no import, `prelude = "std::web"` swaps in an application set, and the whole thing is the weakest binding in the language.** The argument is one probe. `list.get(1)` hands you an `Option` — a lang item, manufactured by a construct you wrote without naming a type — and the compiler then refused to let you take it apart, because you had not imported names you never wrote. `?.` has the same shape. A language that can *manufacture* a value at a use site should be able to *name* it there, and that is what closes here. This is not a new mechanism: the spec's §4.7 already made the primitives and `List` ambient, `macros.rs` already made every std macro ambient with the shadowing rule written into its own doc comment, and `world_prelude_nodes` already made ten `meta` types ambient in every macro body — ordinary std values and types were the one namespace left out of a pattern the language applies three times. **std ships TWO preludes**, which is the census's own finding turned into the design rather than an observation about it: `print` is not the most-imported name in real vilan code, `Signal` is (21 of 42 application files against `print`'s 15), and nine of the top sixteen application names are the style/UI cluster — so no single fixed set serves both a test corpus and an app. The base set is seven names, each admitted by a rule and not by rank: universal (base layer, every target), language-level, unambiguous, and top-of-census in more than one corpus. The web set adds `Signal`, `view` and `View` as members and `style` and `ui` as **modules**. **Ambient module names are the design's real addition.** A member entry costs one ambient name and buys one; a module entry costs one and buys a namespace — sixteen style enums behind `style::`, for the price of one qualifying segment. It also cannot collide, which is how the census's one self-collision dissolves rather than being adjudicated: `std::display::Display` (the `to_string` trait) and `std::style::Display` (the CSS enum) both exist in the base layer and could not both be bare, so bare `Display` is the trait's alone and the CSS one is `style::Display`. **The enum never renames and nothing in the estate moves.** No new precedence rule was needed for any of it — `std::style::style` is a function whose name equals its module's and the estate calls it bare 60 times, and every one of those files carries `import std::style::style;`, which is an explicit import and therefore outranks the ambient module. The other half of that is pinned too: a file which imports the function no longer reaches the module, so `style::Display` stops resolving *there* — one name, one binding, the ordinary rule rather than anything the prelude adds. **The key is `prelude`, on `[package]` and `[library]` alike**, because std — which must declare `prelude = false` — is a `[library]`. Its value grammar is one rule: a module path, or `false`. `"std::prelude"` and `"std::web"` are not set names the compiler knows, they are real modules in std whose exports ARE the ambient names, written in vilan in the same mechanism a user's custom prelude uses — so there is no built-in list in Rust to drift out of sync with the docs, and a reader can open the file. Omitting the key means the base set, which makes it additive to every existing manifest with no edit. A custom prelude REPLACES rather than extends, and extension is spelled by re-export — one mechanism, no merge rules, and std does not get a mechanism its users lack (`web.vl` re-states the base seven rather than deriving them). `prelude = "std"` is refused by name, because after the alias sweep std's root exports nothing and accepting it would mean a silently EMPTY prelude; `prelude = true` is refused because an untagged string-or-bool accepts it syntactically and the affirmative is spelled by omitting the key. **Per package, never inherited** — not from a consumer to a dependency, not from a dependency to a consumer, not from a `[project]` root (which has no such key), not per platform layer. Two packages that disagree about what `Signal` means both keep compiling in one build, which is the property that makes this safe to ship before a registry rather than after. **The implementation is a resolution scope, and that was the one thing this feature could get catastrophically wrong.** In this compiler an explicit import BEATS a same-file declaration, silently — `world_prelude_nodes` says so in its own doc comment ("imports overwrite hoisted function bindings, so the exclusion is how the prelude yields") and filters every name a macro world declares out of its synthesized text for exactly that reason. So a value prelude spliced in as file-head imports would have *replaced* `vilan/test/match-patterns.vl`'s own `enum Signal` and `vilan/test/default.vl`'s own `trait Default` with std's — turning two non-events into miscompiles. Instead the prelude's bindings are copied into a scope with `or_insert`, in the one window where both halves hold: after the import fixpoint (so a prelude module's re-exports point at real definitions, and an explicit import is already there to yield to) and before any name resolves (so nothing has memoized a lookup the prelude would change). Items overwrite it during the walk, imports overwrite it just before — the weakest scope by ORDERING rather than by a precedence table. `record_reference` is deliberately not called for a prelude binding, or Organize Imports would start pruning real imports because "the prelude already references them". The pin that holds this is not the obvious one: the entry file is seeded before its walk, so ordering alone protects it and every entry-file shadowing pin stayed green with the fix removed — it took a *module* file whose own `print` has a disagreeing signature to turn the miscompile into something an analyze-only harness can see. **Tooling was half the feature and mostly fell out.** Completion and go-to-definition needed no code at all: prelude names are ordinary entries in `name_to_id_map`, so `scope_completions` offers them undecorated, `auto_import_completions` stops offering them by its existing "already in scope" filter, and go-to-definition lands in the std source exactly as an import does. Organize Imports gained one line and now **strips an import the prelude covers**, matched on the DEFINITION rather than the name — so `import std::io::print;` goes and `import my_lib::print;` beside an ambient `std::print` stays. `vilan fmt` is untouched, by its own standing rule that pruning is the editor's job. The unresolved-name diagnostic gained the arm the two-set design makes necessary: a base-prelude package reaching for `Signal` is told `` `Signal` is in the prelude of the web set — set `prelude = "std::web"` `` rather than being steered toward an import, and that index is read out of `std/src/web.vl` itself on a cold path so the steer can never drift from the module. The base seven are excluded from that arm, since both sets carry them. One defect was found and fixed by a pin rather than by review: the base-cache key did not include the prelude, so a stored `std::web` world was served to a base-prelude program — the key and the workspace fingerprint now carry the entry package's and every dependency's. Twenty-nine pins across the manifest, resolution and editor surfaces, the shadowing ones proven non-vacuous by planting the bug they remove. (backlog B156; proposal/prelude.md; docs `spec/names.md` §4.4/§4.7, `spec/appendix.md` §A.4, `tour/hello-vilan.md`, `tour/projects.md`, `appendix/errors.md`, `appendix/editor.md`, `appendix/glossary.md`)

The bundles are also *smaller*: the widening puts the nested `effect`/`observe` instances under the enclosing monomorphization's memo key, so two instances that used to be emitted twice now hit it once — 285 bytes off the reactive-ui example, 274 off the walkthrough client. Pinned red-first from three directions: a browser app built by the real CLI and run against a DOM stub, where a user `Source` drives all eight widened bindings and then a write through it reaches the DOM (reverting the signature reddens it; keeping the signature and making the binding read ONCE reddens it too, which is the half a compile-only pin cannot see); compile pins for both twins, including the SSR twin's rendered markup; and the refusals for the write-back pair and the two trait arms. <!-- family: feature -->
**`window` is a listen target now, `listen` hands back the `Subscription` that unhooks a DOM listener, and an `Event` will tell you where the pointer is.** `std::dom` bound element listeners and nothing else, so anything needing a window-level event hand-rolled its own `external fun` — `std::router` had one for `popstate`, the website had a third, and a `message`, `resize` or `storage` event was a thing std simply could not deliver. The live exhibit is a sidebar-resize drag in the dogfood app, which had to hand-roll all three of the gaps at once, and a drag is the canonical case for why element-local `on_event` cannot carry it: the pointer leaves the element the moment the drag starts moving. **`window()` is a handle, not a suffix.** The obvious sketch was an `on_window` free function, but taken as written it grows a parallel vocabulary — `on_window`, `on_window_event`, then a `listen_window` beside `listen` — where the only difference from the element forms is *which object* is being listened to. That is a target, and vilan already spells targets as handles, so `external struct Window` carries exactly the three verbs `Element` does and the surface never has to answer why one of them is spelled differently. It also gives the next asks somewhere to land: window `resize` plus `innerWidth`/`devicePixelRatio` is what the canvas proposal's DPR path wants, and those are accessors on a handle rather than three more free functions. Nothing beyond the listen verbs ships, deliberately — an accessor no delivered event has a caller for is dead surface, which is the trap this gap was filed with. Acquiring the handle costs one runtime helper, because a global property has no function form; that is the same reason `location.pathname` has needed one since routing shipped. **Removal is a `Subscription`, and it is a new verb.** `on_event`'s signature does not change: it is the chaining form, it is what `on:click` lowers to, and it is fire-and-forget by design, because an element listener dies with its element and that is usually the whole answer. Nothing about the window ever dies, so removal has to be expressible — and the vocabulary already existed, since `Source::sub` has always handed back a handle whose `dispose` unhooks it. So `listen` is that shape on both targets, `[must_use]` exactly as `sub` is, over a new `Subscription::teardown(release)` constructor: a subscription over no signal, whose `dispose` runs the hook once and nothing else, riding the same one-shot release cell a remote source's lease decrement already uses — which is what makes disposing twice safe, and a drag disposes twice by construction. Two tiers, one rule: `on`/`on_event` are fire-and-forget, `listen` is the removable form. Making `on_event` return the handle instead would have turned every existing zero-ceremony call site into a `must_use` warning, and `View.on_event`'s chaining return has no room for it at all. Ownership stays the caller's, as `sub`'s is and unlike `effect`'s, and that asymmetry is the point: a drag arms two window listeners per `pointerdown`, so auto-registering with the ambient owner would push two dead cleanups onto the enclosing boundary on every drag, forever — the leak the owner model exists to prevent, entered from the other end. `get_owner().take(window().listen(…))` is the one-line idiom, and an owner-tied twin is recorded rather than built. The whole design rests on one host fact worth stating: `removeEventListener` is **identity-matched**, so `listen`'s teardown has to hand back the same closure the host was given, and that was probed against the real emitter before anything was built — a closure bound once, passed to a std function, used as an argument and captured by the returned teardown, emits as a single JS `const` referenced twice. **`retains` marks registration only.** `addEventListener` retains, because the host stores a vilan closure and calls it later; `removeEventListener` keeps nothing past the call and is left unmarked. The exhibit's hand-roll marks both, which is the over-marking a golden caught on `appendChild` during the retention audit, and this surface deliberately does not inherit it. **The coordinates are named for the pointer, not for the DOM's coordinate space.** `clientX`'s "client" means *viewport* for reasons that are pure history, and the mechanical transliteration would teach that history to every reader forever, so the accessors are `pointer_x`/`pointer_y`. The family objection is real and answered: if `pageX` lands later its name is `page_x` — where the pointer is *in the document* — which is self-explanatory on its own terms rather than as the second row of a coordinate-space table, and two good names beat four uniform ones. Page, offset and screen variants wait for a caller, as does `setPointerCapture`, which is worth designing alongside and is not a substitute: it retargets a drag's events to the capturing element, but `resize`, `popstate`, `storage` and `message` still have no element to hang on, and capture is its own surface with its own disposal question. `std::router` folds onto the new verbs and deletes its own hand-roll, which is one of the three the gap was filed over and the only one that lives in std; the split fixture's golden moves by exactly the two lines that says — the helper, and `window.addEventListener` becoming `__dom_window().addEventListener` — with every chunk byte-identical. Its `popstate` handler keeps its explicit `turn` wrapper, because the window verbs are raw exactly as `element.on` is. The acceptance test is that the exhibit rewrites onto std surface **alone** — its `impl Event` block and both window externs deleted, its `mut dispose` closure becoming two `Subscription::dispose` calls — and that rewrite is pinned end to end under a DOM stub whose `removeEventListener` matches by identity like a browser's, so a teardown that reconstructs its handler removes nothing and every negative assertion fails. Four browser-runtime gates, a fifth over the markings themselves (a declaration gate, because retention is not observable through a listener at all — a closure cannot capture a resource, so no drop order could move), two compile pins for the types, and the formatter and analyzer retention pins extended with the marked/unmarked pair this surface is declared in. Four plants, each watched red and restored: coordinates crossed, listener identity broken, the flag dropped from a registration, and the flag added to a removal — the last being exactly the exhibit's own over-marking. (backlog A27, kolt.local 037; proposal/router.md §5; docs `std/browser.md`, `std/reactive.md`, `guide/ui.md`)

**A file can now be read a chunk at a time — `Reader::of(File::open(p))` and `next(size)` — and every open mode has a scoped form whose close is awaited, which is the one that matters when you are writing.** These are the two halves the filesystem arc had left: the owner's vision named *"files can be opened, read incrementally"*, and until now the incremental half did not exist — `read_bytes` materializes the whole file, so a 2 GiB log had to be fully resident, and the only chunked reader in std read HTTP bodies. `Reader` is that loop, and the interesting thing about it is what it is built ON. Node's `FileHandle.read` keeps an implicit position when you pass none, and binding *that* as the primitive would have put mutable state under a loan where the move checker cannot see it: two loans of one handle, each reading, would silently move each other's position. So the handle stayed positional and stateless when it shipped, and the cursor arrives now as an ordinary vilan value layered on top — `next(size)` reads at a position this program owns and advances it, `position()` reads it, `seek()` moves it. A cursor can always be built from a position; a position can never be recovered from a cursor. The payoff is visible in one program: `reader.file.read_at(buffer, p)` reads anywhere in the file **without disturbing the cursor**, so a header probe and a sequential scan share one open file — the property the host's hidden position would have destroyed. A chunk is shorter near the end and **empty at end of file**, which is the loop's terminating condition and the one trap the docs state twice: stop on empty, not on short. That is `std::fetch`'s `BodyReader` loop with the mechanism swapped rather than copied — `BodyReader` answers `{ done, value }` because a `ReadableStream` may legitimately yield an empty chunk mid-stream, so emptiness cannot carry the end there; a file's read cannot, so a second field would be one the caller could always derive. Each `next` allocates and hands back a slice of exactly what was read, so a chunk is never a window on memory the next call overwrites — the reuse is what `read_at` is for. `Reader` declares no teardown of its own and needs none: it is a resource **by containment**, which buys the whole R-rule surface unmodified — it moves, no closure captures it, no `List` holds it, and dropping it closes the file it owns. One shape is deliberately absent and the reason is recorded rather than assumed: the position is a `Shared<i53>` rather than a plain field behind `&mut self` because the language *forces* it — `next` awaits the read, and an async function cannot take a `&mut` parameter, since the view would be held across the suspension. The sketch had guessed right for a reason it did not know it had. **The other half is the scoped form, which shipped read-only and was therefore available in exactly the mode where it matters least.** `with_file(path, |file| …)` awaits its close, so a close failure is a failure of the call — but a close failure is information almost exclusively on a *writing* handle: a write that resolved was handed to the OS, and the OS is entitled to report its failure at `close(2)` rather than at the write (a full disk, a quota, a network filesystem that defers), which is why POSIX warns that ignoring close's return can lose data you believe you wrote. Under the destructor that error goes to stderr and your program carries on. So there is now one scoped form per constructor — `with_file_create`, `with_file_create_new`, `with_file_append`, `with_file_modify` — the suffix naming the constructor it opens with, for the same reason five named constructors replaced node's flags string in the first place: a mode is a name here too, and threading an untyped one through `with_file` would have reintroduced what the constructors exist to prevent. All five delegate to **one** implementation, so the close-before-return ordering that IS the idiom is written once and a form added later cannot quietly drop the await; the emitted shape is `try { body; await close; return } finally { drop }`, so a throwing body still releases the handle through the safety net, and what it wrote before throwing is on disk. Nothing was needed from the compiler for any of it. Fifteen pins, against real files and against the emitted bytes: the chunk loop over a size that divides neither the file nor any prefix of it, a file shorter than one chunk, an empty one, the interleave, R1/R5/R9/R10 and the coloring refusal on the new type, the four writing modes proved by what each does to a file that already exists, the exclusive claim refusing an occupied path without touching it, the throwing body, and the descriptors coming back — plus a corpus program holding the emitted shape. The behavioural ones are plant-proven: a cursor that advances wrong reddens the three reading pins, a shared form with its `await` removed reddens all five scoped forms, a close taught to swallow reddens the seam pin, and the wrong constructor behind `with_file_append` reddens the mode pin. One honesty note the fd instrument earned: the descriptor counts prove release, not ORDERING (measured with the await removed, they still read zero, because the counting call itself awaits), so the ordering stays pinned on the emitted bytes, where the await is. (kolt.local 031 S5; proposal/filesystem.md §3.4's build note and §5.3; docs `std/process.md`, `guide/persistence.md`)

**A static estate is now three lines of vilan: `asset::read_dir_all` enumerates it, `asset::bundle_as` places each file at a url its path does not spell, and `asset::digest` mints the content-hashed one.** `bundle`'s rule has always been *the path IS the url*, which is what makes it impossible for two files to claim one output name and impossible for anything to be renamed behind your back — and also what forced a path-pinned name (`/favicon.ico`, `/robots.txt`) to sit at the package root, and what made an estate a hand-written list of calls: the dogfood app spells twelve of them. Both costs come off without giving the rule up, because the rename is spelled AT THE CALL. `bundle_as(path, url)` is `bundle` in every other respect — same registry, same copy, same tracked build input, same `chunks.json` row, same `serve_build` route, same `--watch` recopy — so `bundle(path)` shares one implementation with it rather than sitting beside a second one, and is exactly `bundle_as(path, i"/{path}")` for any path free of `.` segments — the one divergence is that `bundle` skips a `./` in the SOURCE spelling when minting the name, where the target grammar refuses one, because the target IS the url. What the target must be is stated and refused with the fix named: it starts at the site root, it is `/`-separated on every host (a backslash is refused, never translated — kolt.local 017's ruling, since the target becomes an output name, a manifest row and a golden), and every segment must be a name, so an empty segment, a `.` or a `..` is a compile error. The reason is that the value returned IS the url the copy answers on: `/a/./b` is a different url to a browser while being the same file on disk, so a target that is not already the url it promises would be a lie the caller cannot see. The target passes the build-owned-name fence `bundle`'s does by reaching the same check — `<leg>.js`, `<leg>.css`, `<leg>.chunks.json` and the route-chunk namespace, for every leg, because `dist/` is one directory — and gains the one refusal the identity rule used to give for free: two files bundling to one url is a compile error naming BOTH sources, because a collision is a statement about a pair and naming half of it sends the reader to the wrong call. That check is per compile, so the same collision across two legs of a workspace — separate compiles into one `dist/`, where the second copy would silently have won — is caught at the copy instead, naming both again. Enumeration is the other half. `read_dir(path)` lists a directory's immediate files by bare name and `read_dir_all(path)` every file beneath it by a path relative to it, both `/`-separated on every host, with two deliberate divergences from `std::fs`'s versions and each forced by what a const result is. Entries are **byte-sorted, always**: a const result is compiled INTO the output, so host iteration order would make one source tree produce two builds, and determinism here is the property the whole const feature rests on rather than a nicety. And only **files** are listed: nothing in this channel consumes a directory — `read`, `bundle`, `bundle_as` and `digest` all take a file — and there is no compile-time `stat`, so a directory entry would be one the program could neither act on nor filter out, and the estate loop would break on the first nested folder. A symlink is classified by what it points at, so a link to a file is bundleable; the walk never follows one into a directory, so it cannot loop. The listed directory is a **tracked build input** on `read`'s doctrine, recorded per directory walked, which is what makes it compose: a file appearing or disappearing anywhere in a listed tree moves exactly one recorded key, so both directions invalidate — you drop a file into `static/` and the next build ships it with no source edit at all. The re-hash the per-leg watch skip performs learned one arm to match (a recorded directory re-hashes as its listing, not as a file's text), so an unchanged tree can still be skipped instead of disqualifying the leg by failing to read. `digest(path)` is the last piece: the file's sha-256 as lowercase hex, 64 characters, over the BYTES — a fingerprint of a font or a `.png` must be a fingerprint of the file and not of a decoding — tracked exactly as `read`'s input is, so an edit re-mints the url. It closes a recorded exhibit: the dogfood app's fingerprints were minted OUT OF BAND because `asset::read` is text-only and no digest was in const reach, and `bundle_as(p, i"/static/{stem}.{digest(p).substring(0, 8)}.{ext}")` is now spellable in the language that ships the file. Fuel prices are argued rather than picked: a listing charges 1,024 per entry (the directory itself counting as one, so an empty listing is not free), a quarter of `bundle`'s 4,096, because an entry costs the walk a listing row and the stat that classifies it where `bundle`'s charge prices a whole-file read on top of both (the count is the files returned plus one for the listed directory; the directories a recursive walk descends are not individually charged, a recorded open question) — which leaves the dominant per-entry cost to what the program does with the entry and keeps the binding fence on the work that copies bytes; and `digest` charges one per eight bytes, an eighth of `read`'s rate, because `read`'s rate prices the arbitrary-length `str` the program then computes over while a digest is 64 characters whatever the file weighs, so the charge bounds how much a build hashes rather than how large a value it holds. Nothing about plain `bundle` moved: the corpus goldens are byte-identical, which is the negative this slice is checked against. Why the const channel and not a manifest key or a build hook is the owner's own argument, recorded in the paper: a toml key walls off programmatic logic, and a hook exchanges no values with the program, has no manifest contract to serve through, needs the whole freshness machinery to approximate tracked inputs, and is first-party-only arbitrary execution where the const channel is fenced interpretation a library can safely ride. Fifteen behaviour pins in the inference suite and eight end-to-end in the CLI (the served target, the sorted listing, the tracked directory in both directions, the fingerprint against sha-256's canonical `abc` vector, every url-shape refusal, both collisions, the owned-name fence), plus a corpus program holding the whole recipe. (kolt.local 035; proposal/const-eval.md §3.1; docs `std/misc.md`, `spec/const.md`, `std/process.md`)

<!-- family: feature -->
**`db.migrate(steps)` carries a schema forward — the thing `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` cannot do.** An idempotent schema *ensure* is right exactly until the first schema *change*: add a `description` column and the clause is a no-op, so the deployed database keeps the old shape while the code querying it has the new one, and the choices left are hand-run SQL against production or deleting the file. `std::db` is batteries-included by doctrine and had no third answer. It does now: `Migration { name, sql }` steps applied **in list order**, the applied ones recorded in a `vilan_migrations` table the migrator owns (`name TEXT PRIMARY KEY`, `applied_at_ms INTEGER`), and the names it applied returned — so a boot log reads `applied 2 migrations` the first time and `applied 0` on every restart after. The design is one invariant and everything else follows from it: **a step is recorded if and only if its SQL committed**, because the record insert rides *inside* the step's own transaction. There is no window where the schema moved and the record did not, so a process killed mid-migration leaves a database whose recorded set exactly describes its schema and the next boot resumes there. The transaction is per STEP and deliberately not per run — all-or-nothing sounds safer and is worse, because a failure in the fifth step would then re-run the first four, and a first step that is not re-runnable (a `DROP`, a backfill that doubles) could never recover. Three conditions stop the boot loudly, all of them *before* a single statement is applied, so a database this refuses is a database it did not touch: a step whose SQL FAILS, named alongside SQLite's own diagnosis (`migration '002-bad' failed and was not applied: no such table: taks`) with nothing recorded for it and its half-applied DDL rolled back; a RECORDED step absent from the list, which is a rolled-back deploy about to run its old queries against a newer schema; and an UNAPPLIED step ordered before an applied one, which is two branches merged into an order no fresh database could ever reproduce. Names must be unique and non-empty, but they need NOT sort in order — the list's order is the authority, and the second refusal already catches every misordering an ascending-name rule would, on a fresh database vacuously and on one with history exactly. Deliberately absent from v1 and stated as such: down-migrations (roll forward with a new step, which is what production does anyway), locking beyond SQLite's own file lock, and diff-GENERATION, which wants the declared-schema question answered first. One documented requirement the surface does not check: a step must never contain `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` of its own — that commits the migrator's transaction out from under it, landing the schema change permanently while its record is still unwritten, the one way to break the invariant — and it is not checked because substring-scanning SQL is not parsing SQL (a comment, a string literal and a `commit_sha` column would all be refused wrongly, and a line break evades the scan). How an app COLLECTS its steps stays the const channel's business: `const asset::read("migrations/001-create-task.sql")` compiles each file's text into the bundle, so the deployed app is still `dist/` and every migration edit is a tracked build input. Five pins drive real SQLite files in per-test temp directories across two boots each, every one proven red first. (proposal/db-migrations.md, kolt.local 036; docs `guide/persistence.md` and `std/process.md`)

**`str::index_of` and `str::last_index_of` — locating text, and three diagnostics that finally name their cause.** `contains` answered *whether* and `substring` cut, and nothing in between computed a bound, so text was taken apart with `split` and put back together — which is exactly what writing a real generator in vilan turned up. The name is the house one rather than a new coinage: `List::index_of(value)` already returns `Option<i32>`, and in this vocabulary `find` takes a PREDICATE, so `str::index_of(needle)` is the spelling that was missing rather than a second one. **Absence is `None`, never `-1`** — the whole reason this is not the host method renamed, and the same doctrine `substring` states: `-1` is an index nothing in the type system tells apart from a real one, and it would be reported one call later, by `substring`, about a number this call produced. The empty needle sits at each end, as it does in the host. Both live in `std::option` beside `strip_prefix`/`parse_i32`, so the always-loaded core `str` stays off the `option` chain. That last one is not a papercut for a generator: a CSS rule, a JS body or a JSON object writes braces on nearly every line. Pinned per case with the negatives beside them — `pub` still an ordinary identifier where it is one, the escaped brace still printing a brace, the misleading messages proven GONE rather than merely joined — and the std pair proven non-vacuous by planting the `-1` leak. **A `type` binder may be written inside an impl head's bound, and is in scope for the whole head.** `impl type S: Source<type T> with MaybeSignal<T>` — "for every `S` that is a `Source` of some `T`" — reported `cannot find type 'T'` at the `with` clause and again at every member signature that named it. **`Signal<T>` is a trait, so a signal can be your own — a clamping setter, a persisted cell, a debounced write.** `Source` reads (`get`/`sub`/`effect`) and `Signal` writes: `set` and `notify` are requirements, `set_with` a default of exactly the line std used to carry, and `new` a default-bodied associated function returning the canonical cell. **A module of a fullstack package is coloured by the entry that REACHES it, in the editor and in `vilan check <file>` alike — not by the manifest's default.** A `[entry.<name>]` package builds one leg per entry, each over the modules that leg loads, each under that leg's target; but a single file addressed by path took the `node` default, and the language server took its own imports' inference. Neither is what the build does, and the platform decides more than which functions may run: it selects `std`'s layer overlay, so it decides what the file's types ARE. Under the process overlay a browser module's `View` is `{ tag, attributes, children, text }`, `self.element` is a field that does not exist, and every browser-only module of a fullstack app was reported broken on correct code while `vilan build` was clean — the report this closes, against an app whose `default-entry` is its server. Reachability answers it: `platform_color::file_platforms` walks the loader's own `pkg::` import graph from each entry (`analyzer::package_modules_reachable_from`, the same `collect_module_refs` seeds and the same resolution the load loop uses), and a module reached by exactly one leg takes that leg's platform. Reached by SEVERAL, it takes each: a shared module is compiled once per leg and must type-check under every one of them, so `vilan check` on it reports the union its legs would and the editor publishes the union too, deduplicated to one squiggle per mistake — the mirror lie, passing a file the package check refuses, is now closed in the same place. Reached by NONE, the designated `default-entry` answers, which is the old behaviour kept where it is the only thing left to say. The two surfaces take one answer from one function: G20 had already unified them, on the manifest's default rather than on reachability. Found fixing it and fixed with it: file mode compiled every path it was handed as if it were the program, so `vilan check src/widget.vl` on a clean module answered "Cannot execute program without a main function" — a demand no module can meet, and the reason the fix could not be verified until it went. An ENTRY still gets the demand, because an entry without `main` is a build that cannot succeed.
