<!-- family: tooling -->
**The parser refuses a too-deeply-nested file now instead of dying on it, and the stack margins that were standing in for that bound have come down with it.** Every recursive family in the *analyzer* was bounded in v0.36.0 and v0.37.0 (B138, B139), and each time the 256 MiB compiler-thread spawns and the wasm build's 64 MiB `-zstack-size` kept their values, because measuring the whole pipeline rather than the analyzer alone kept naming the same remaining consumer: the **parser**, which recurses once per level of source nesting with the largest frame in the pipeline and had no limit at all. It also runs first, so it reached the stack cliff before any analyzer bound could refuse — which is why the existing 5000-level pin had to use a method chain, a shape that is deep to the walk and flat to the parser. Nest the source syntactically instead and the file died with a stack overflow and no diagnostic whatsoever, the one outcome the depth work exists to prevent.

The bound does not live where it looked like it should. `parse_atom` is where the depth instrument was first hung and where the bracketed forms — `(…)`, `[…]`, a call's arguments, an index — all re-enter, so a limit there would have looked complete; it would have covered four doors and missed the rest. Within expressions the block-bearing forms (`{ … }`, `if`, `for`, `match`, a closure body) reach a nested expression without ever touching an atom, and so do the unary prefixes and the `const` prefix, which recurse into themselves. Past expressions there turned out to be five more recursive grammars, each a closed cycle that reaches no expression rule at all and so could not have been seen from anywhere in the expression grammar: types (`& & & … i64`, `[[…; 1]; 1]`, `L<L<…>>`), binders and patterns, items (nested `fun`, `mod`, `impl`, `trait`, and chained `export`), `import`/`use` paths, and nested elements. These were not theoretical. `fun a() { fun a() { … } }` at 5000 levels overflowed a 64 MiB worker outright, and the other four parsed 5000 levels clean with no refusal at all. So the guard sits on a shared funnel that all six grammars call through, and it counts **one** budget of 500 rather than six of them: what a stack margin needs bounded is the parser's total recursion depth, and six per-family counters of 500 would have admitted 3000 nested frames between them, which is no bound at all for the purpose.

Two details are load-bearing and were each arrived at the hard way. The refusal is held **off** the error list until the parse ends, because the backtracking combinator truncates that list whenever a branch declines — and refusing hands the enclosing rule a hole where it wanted an operand, so that rule's `)` goes missing, it declines, and the refusal would have been rolled back with it, leaving a file that was refused for depth reporting only a puzzled "expected `)`". How deep the input went is a fact about the input, not a claim by whichever branch happened to be exploring when it got there. And past the bound each grammar hands back a stand-in rather than declining, because declining sends 500 open frames back through their remaining alternatives: measured, refusing that way took nested `fun` at 505 levels from 9 ms to not finishing in 25 seconds. The two funnels whose callers loop on success consume a token as they refuse, which is what keeps those loops advancing instead of spinning. The refusal fires once per parse, not once per level — a 5000-level file gets one sentence, not 4500.

The number is 500, the same as the analyzer's walk, and it is now backed by a sweep rather than a guess: across all 211 compilable corpus entries the parser peaks at 23 levels with a median of 14, so the bound is 21.7× the deepest real file. What it buys is a finite worst case where there was none — measured through the CLI on the worst plant, a bounded parse peaks at depth 501 and 35.2 MiB unoptimized, about 10 MiB optimized — and, because the parser will not descend past the limit, it cannot *build* a tree deeper than it either, so every later walk over the AST is bounded by construction rather than needing a bound of its own. On that basis the **compiler-thread spawns drop from 256 MiB to 128 MiB** (the CLI's and the language server's), roughly 3.6× the measured worst case with room left for a macro-world compile, which nests a whole pipeline inside the running analysis. The **wasm build's stack drops from 64 MiB to 16 MiB**, and that one was measured under the profile that actually ships rather than extrapolated from native frame sizes: the `wasm-release` artifact (`opt-level = "z"` plus fat LTO) was built at a range of stack sizes and run under node against the same pathological plants, where 8 MiB compiles every one of them and 4 MiB traps on the two worst. That is 48 MiB of linear memory the playground page no longer reserves before it can do anything.

Pinned per door: twenty-one plants, one for each way source can nest a level deeper, each confirmed to overflow or hang before the bound existed and each asserting the same three claims — a tree still comes out, exactly one refusal, and it steers toward the flattening that fits the construct. The formatter's own parse mode is pinned separately, since it is a second entry into the same parser and a bound wired into one entry point would have left `vilan fmt` overflowing on a file `vilan build` refuses cleanly. (backlog B142)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**The release path stops trusting mutable tags, and the installer stops installing what it cannot verify.** Two independent holes in the supply chain, both found by the first security audit run, both closed the same way — by removing a place where the toolchain trusted something it had not checked. Every third-party action in `ci.yml` and `release.yml` rode a mutable tag: `actions/checkout@v4`, `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable`, `taiki-e/install-action@v2`, the artifact pair, `azure/login@v2`, `actions/create-github-app-token@v2`. A git tag is a pointer its owner can move, so each of those was a standing grant of arbitrary code execution to whoever could move it — and in the release workflow that code runs holding the release token, next to the npm trusted-publishing exchange and the Azure OIDC login. All 32 `uses:` lines are now pinned to full commit SHAs with the tag in a trailing comment (`uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a… # v4.4.0`), which is the form that stays readable while being immutable. Every SHA was resolved from the real upstream and cross-checked two ways, against `git ls-remote` with tags peeled and against the API with annotated tags dereferenced; none was taken from memory. `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable` deserves its own note, because pinning it looks like it should freeze the Rust version and does not: `stable` is a branch, and its `action.yml` defaults the `toolchain` input to the literal string `stable`, which is a rustup channel name resolved at run time — so the pin freezes the action's code and rustup still installs whatever stable is that morning. That was verified by reading the branch's `action.yml`, not assumed.

A pin with nothing tending it is only a frozen dependency, and a frozen action stops receiving its own security fixes, so `.github/dependabot.yml` lands with the pins as one measure rather than two — Dependabot reads the tag comment beside each SHA and rewrites both when it opens a weekly bump PR, grouped into a single reviewable diff. Separately, `scripts/install.sh` failed open: when neither `sha256sum` nor `shasum` was on `PATH` it printed a warning, skipped verification entirely, and unpacked the download anyway, exiting 0 with the full success banner. That put the weakest verification on precisely the machine least able to notice, and an installer that only sometimes verifies makes a promise it does not keep. It now refuses, in its own voice on stderr with a non-zero exit, naming the fix — every supported platform can satisfy it, since `sha256sum` ships with GNU coreutils and `shasum` with macOS and with perl — and "skipping" is no longer an outcome it offers on either stream. Note the limit of what this buys, recorded rather than glossed: `sha256sums.txt` is produced and consumed from the same release page, so it authenticates the transfer and not the pipeline that produced it. Signing and provenance are a separate, larger piece of work and stay open. The same sweep is owed to the two sibling repositories and goes with it: the proposals repo's `hygiene.yml` declared no `permissions:` block and so inherited the default token grant for a job that only reads, and the website's `deploy.yml` plus `fetch-wasm.sh` piped the playground's WebAssembly compiler straight from `curl` into `tar` with no checksum at all — bytes that then execute in every visitor's browser. Both now carry the same discipline. (backlog L14, L15's S half, N18, K19)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**Inferring a return type through a long call chain is bounded now, and no longer quadratic.** When a function declares no return type, working out what it returns means working out what the function it calls returns, and so on down the chain — one level of recursion per call link, carrying a large frame (~12.8 KiB per link unoptimized, ~2.2 KiB optimized). Nothing bounded that: the guard in place caught *cycles*, not depth, so a long enough chain of unannotated returns could exhaust the stack. Two things change. The chain is now **bounded at 500 links**, 25x deeper than any real code reaches, and a program past it gets one clean diagnostic — "declare a return type on one of them to end the chain", which is the actual fix, since a declared return is read off the signature and ends the recursion — instead of an overflow. And the answer for each function is now **reused** rather than re-derived: an exact answer was already being recorded, but only a read-only coercion path ever read it, so every link in a chain re-walked every link beneath it. A 500-function chain went from 390,984 inference entries to 14,730, and the cost is now a straight line in the chain's length rather than a curve. In the common case where a function is defined after the ones it calls, the recursion now flattens away entirely: the same 500-function chain went from 502 levels deep and 6.26 MiB of stack to 6 levels and 0.07 MiB. **The stack margins still do not shrink, and now say exactly why.** The 256 MiB compiler-thread spawns and the wasm build's 64 MiB `-zstack-size` were waiting on this bound; with it landed, every recursive family in the *analyzer* is bounded (~3.4 MiB together at release frame sizes). But measuring the whole pipeline rather than the analyzer alone — `VILAN_DEPTH_STATS` now covers the parser too, and anchors before the parse instead of after it — turned up a deeper consumer: the **parser** recurses once per level of source nesting at ~20.3 KiB per level optimized, four times the bounded expression walk's cost, with no depth limit at all, and it runs first, so it reaches the cliff before any analyzer bound can refuse. That is what the margins are now standing in for, and each site says so. The depth line also reports a per-family call count, which is what made the quadratic behaviour visible. (backlog B139)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**Deeply nested expressions no longer take exponential time to parse.** `(1 + (1 + (1 + …)))` at 22 levels of nesting took 35 seconds to compile, 60 levels never finished, and nested array literals behaved the same way — a size a generated file or a macro expansion reaches without trying. The cost was in the PARSER, and it doubled with every level: an assignment (`place = value`) is tried before ordinary expressions, and the only way to know whether one is present was to parse the whole left-hand side speculatively and throw it away when no `=` turned up — after which the ordinary-expression path parsed the identical text again. Every bracket level therefore paid for its own contents twice, which is 2^n. The parser now works out up front, in one pass over the tokens, which positions could still be followed by an assignment operator — a place is a balanced run of tokens, so its operator always sits at the bracket depth the place began at — and skips the speculative parse where none can be. 20 levels went from 9.0s to 0.24ms; 320 levels now compile in a quarter of a second, and the cost is a straight line in the nesting depth. Nothing about what parses, or what any diagnostic says, changes. The measurement that found it is worth recording, because it was mis-filed as a type-inference bug: the analyzer's own phase clocks stayed flat near 200ms while the whole analysis took 8.4 seconds, and the recursion depth never moved — all of it was spent before analysis began. A pin holds nested expressions to a constant number of parses per level, counting parser work rather than wall-clock so that a regression to merely quadratic is caught too. (backlog B140)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**Organize Imports models usage as what the file actually resolved, so it stops removing imports the build needs and stops keeping ones it doesn't.** Both reported failures were the same defect seen from opposite sides: "used" meant *syntactically mentioned somewhere in this file*, which is neither necessary nor sufficient.

Not sufficient, so it **over-pruned**: `import pkg::helper;` where the file's only debt to it is an `impl` method it calls — `n.doubled()`, with the module's name never written — looked entirely unused and was removed, and the file stopped building. That is now answered from the analyzer's own provenance: a whole-module import is kept when this file resolved *anything declared in the file that import reaches into*, methods included. The question is asked of the reference index, so a method call, a constructor, an enum variant and a type annotation are all one query rather than four hand-written scans.

Not necessary, so it **under-pruned** — and the real culprit is sharper than reported. `Ok` and `Err` on their own were pruned correctly all along; the leaf that never pruned was `self`. An import path's segments resolve to the very definitions its leaves bind, so in `import std::result::Result::{ self, Ok, Err };` the `Result` written in the path counted as a use of `Result`, and the `self` leaf could therefore never be removed no matter what the file did — an import that justifies its own existence. References written by the file's **import list** are now excluded from the accounting, so an import must be earned by the code.

The pin the item asked for is in place: a build-preservation corpus that starts green, requires organize to actually change the text (a case organize no-ops on would pass vacuously and prove nothing), and requires the organized text to analyze green again — over a module import reached only through an impl method, an unused module import beside a used one, a brace set with one live and one dead leaf, an unused variant import beside a used one, and a shuffled run where everything is used. Over-pruning surfaces there as a diagnostic and under-pruning as an unchanged text, so one pin holds both directions. (kolt.local tracker item 004)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**Rename is a thin layer over the reference index, and refuses with a reason rather than emitting a partial edit.** The two reported symptoms turned out to be **two distinct bugs sharing one root class**, and their different wording was the clue. Renaming a struct field *failed outright* — "Rename failed to apply edits" is the client's message, not the server's, and it meant the request had succeeded and returned an inapplicable `WorkspaceEdit`: a cursor on a field's declaration resolved to the enclosing *struct*, and a struct's constructor sites were emitted twice over, once from the type-reference table and once from the initializer table, so the client rejected the whole overlapping edit. Renaming a static method was merely *"problematic"* — that edit set was perfectly applicable and simply wrong, because a `Type::method()` call's recorded span is the whole path and the declaration it paired with was the whole `fun … { … }`, so accepting the rename overwrote the entire function declaration with the new name. One class — occurrences reconstructed span-by-span per symbol kind — two failure modes, one inapplicable and one destructive.

Both are gone with the reference index behind them, and rename now adds only what rename needs beyond finding: that the new name is spellable, that every reference sits in a file the project may edit, and that nothing is known to be missing. It **refuses, with the reason, rather than emitting an incomplete set** — a half-applied rename does not fail loudly, it leaves a program that no longer builds and an editor that reported success. Renaming into a keyword or a non-identifier is refused (checked against the lexer's own keyword table, so it cannot drift from the language). Renaming a symbol declared in the standard library or a dependency is refused by name — reaching a `std` function through an import used to hand the client edits for files under `$VILAN_STD` without a word. A reference in `[derive(..)]`-generated code, which has no file on disk to edit, is refused rather than skipped, and so is any occurrence that cannot be resolved to a location. `textDocument/prepareRename` is now answered too, decided by exactly the checks the rename itself runs, so the editor can refuse before the user types a new name instead of after — and the two cannot disagree.

The per-symbol-kind matrix the item asked for is pinned: struct, field, instance method, static method, free function, enum, enum variant in expression and in pattern position, local, parameter — each asserting that rename rewrites *exactly* what find-references reports, that every edit replaces one identifier and never a declaration or a path, and that no span is ever emitted twice. (kolt.local tracker item 002)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**Find References answers every symbol kind, from one reference index.** It used to return nothing at all for an enum variant — clicked on its own declaration, or in a match pattern — and nothing but the declaration for a free function or a static method, while a cursor on a struct field's declaration silently answered with the *struct's* references and a cursor on a return-type annotation with the *enclosing function's*. Those look like six bugs and were one: the query guessed what the cursor named by asking which syntactic node contained it, and a node's span is the whole `fun … { … }` or the whole `struct { … }`, so a coarse declaration swallowed the precise probes underneath it. Having guessed, it then rebuilt each occurrence's span separately per symbol kind, out of whichever analyzer table sat nearest — which is how renaming a static method from its call site came to emit the entire function declaration as one span to overwrite, how `Enum::Variant` came to be rewritten whole rather than at its last segment, and how a struct's constructor sites came to be emitted twice, once from `type_references` and once from the initializer table.

Both halves are now one table. Each analysis builds a **reference index**: every identifier occurrence in the program, each a span covering exactly an identifier and the definition it names. The cursor is resolved by looking its offset up in that same table, so resolution and enumeration cannot disagree — a kind that can be found is necessarily one that can be enumerated, because both directions read one set of rows — and there is no coarse span left to shadow anything. Two invariants carry it and both are pinned: every row's text *is* its definition's name, and no two rows share a span. The first subsumes the whole whole-span class in a single assertion; the second is what makes an edit set applicable rather than overlapping. Where a `::` path carries no span for its member, the span is derived rather than searched — the parser ends a static-accessor node at the member's own end token, so the final `name.len()` bytes are the identifier exactly — and a span that cannot be *proven* to cover an identifier is dropped and counted, never emitted wrong, so an incomplete answer can be refused instead of quietly returned.

One gap in the analyzer had to close for this to be honest: the key `x` in `Point { x = 1 }` names the field, but it is not a field access, so unlike `p.x` it had nowhere to be recorded — the analyzer computed the span for a diagnostic and dropped it. Renaming a struct field therefore missed every construction site and produced a partial edit that broke the build. Those spans are now kept (`struct_initializer_field_spans`), and a field answers with its declaration, its accesses and its initializer keys alike. A per-symbol-kind matrix pins the lot — struct, field, instance method, static method, free function, enum, enum variant in both expression and pattern position, local, parameter — each from every end it can be clicked from, alongside a consistency pin that edits, queries, edits again and queries, so an answer tracks the buffer both ways.

One limit is now recorded rather than merely suffered, as an `#[ignore]`d pin: the query still answers over the open file's own program — its entry file plus everything it imports — so a symbol clicked in the file that *defines* it does not see the files that import that file. In a multi-file app that is most of the time, and it is the other half of what "intermittently returns nothing" described. Closing it means a definition key stable across programs and a union over the open set; the index makes that a lookup per program rather than a redesign. (kolt.local tracker item 003)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**The HMR dev channel now requires a per-run token on every route.** Dev-only, and never a network surface: the channel binds `127.0.0.1` alone, and its artifact routes always refused anything but a bare `<name>.<ext>`. What was open was the *browser*. While `run --watch` ran, any other page the developer happened to visit could reach the fixed default port `35917` and read `GET /bundle/<leg>.js` (the compiled app), hold `GET /events` open and watch every compile failure arrive as it was typed — the overlay payload carries `file:line:col`, the diagnostic text, and requirement-trace hops — and fire `POST /refresh` for a reload flood. `run --watch` now mints 128 bits per process and substitutes them into the browser shim exactly as it already substitutes the port; `/events`, `/bundle/`, `/asset/` and `/refresh` all refuse a missing or wrong token with a bare `403` that says nothing about which it was. The legitimate page has the token because the bundle carrying it came from the page's own origin; a hostile page cannot read that bundle and so can neither fetch nor forge. `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` deliberately stays — the app's origin is the user's own server and genuinely unknowable, and an origin allowlist would not have closed the refresh flood anyway, since a simple cross-origin POST needs no CORS permission. `std::watch::force_refresh()` is the one legitimate non-browser caller and learns the token from `VILAN_HMR_TOKEN`, inherited at spawn beside `VILAN_HMR_PORT`; its behavior is unchanged. Nothing to configure. One visible consequence: a tab left open from a previous watch session carries that session's token, so after restarting `run --watch` you reload it once. Docs `guide/dev-loop.md`. (backlog E93, N16 audit run 1)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**`vilan fmt` puts a `style()` chain's links in a canonical order — Tailwind's, with your own methods held in place.** A long builder chain read differently in every file, and the order carries no meaning of its own: a chain merges last-wins per property slot, so links on independent slots may be written in any order at all. `vilan fmt` now settles it — Tailwind CSS's category sequence (layout, flexbox/grid, spacing, sizing, typography, backgrounds, borders, effects, filters, tables, transitions/animation, transforms, interactivity, svg, accessibility), with every condition combinator after every property method in the axis order the selector already nests them (`md`, `dark`, `attribute`, pseudo-class). This is the only place `fmt` reorders code rather than re-laying it out, so it is correct by construction rather than by table lookup. A method the formatter does not know — one of your own `impl Style` extensions, or an escape hatch whose slot is an argument (`raw`, `with_length`, `with_color`, `with_border`) — is a **barrier**: links sort only within the runs between barriers, nothing crosses one, and a chain of nothing but your own methods is left exactly as written. Methods whose slots are entangled share a **family** and keep their written order, because `padding` then `padding_x` means something the reverse does not (`proposal/ui-styling.md` §0bis) — `padding` over its edges, `size` over `width`/`height`, `border` over `border_color`. Only independent slots ever cross, and the proof is the corpus itself: every tracked style source builds to a **byte-identical** stylesheet before and after the reorder, with the same slots resolving to the same declarations. The order table is derived from `std/src/style.vl` and gated against it in four directions, so a new style method is a red test rather than a link that quietly stops sorting. Docs `appendix/cli.md`. (kolt.local 006)

**The analyzer's recursion depth is measured now, and its deepest path is bounded.** The stack margins around the compiler were sized by incident, not measurement — the v0.36.0 gate SIGABRT'd when a modest server program's analysis outgrew a CI worker's ~2 MiB stack. `VILAN_DEPTH_STATS` answers the question that incident left open, the `VILAN_PHASE_TIMING` way: set it and every top-level analysis prints one stderr line with, per recursive family (`infer`, `type-walk`, `expr-walk`, `pattern`), the peak recursion depth and the stack consumed at that peak. What it measured: every realistic fixture — both walkthrough entries, the std twin-parity and release-emission corpora, the incident's own server program — peaks at 20 levels, and the deepest path by bytes is the phase-1 expression walk at ~36 KiB per nesting level unoptimized (~4.5 KiB optimized), one frame per level of syntactic nesting, unguarded. That walk is now depth-bounded at 500 levels — 25× the deepest realistic fixture — and an expression nesting past it gets one clean diagnostic steering toward `let`-flattening instead of a stack overflow: a 5000-deep method chain that aborted a 64 MiB worker (SIGABRT) now refuses in under a second. The 256 MiB worker spawns and the wasm build's 64 MiB `-zstack-size` keep their values but lose their folklore status — each site now carries the measured rationale, and what keeps them generous is named precisely: cross-function return-inference chains (~12.5 KiB per call link unoptimized) are not yet bounded.

**An operator at an all-native binding no longer ICEs when the impl's body calls the trait method explicitly.** A conditional impl whose body spells the comparison `.eq()` instead of `==` — `impl Pair<type T: PartialEq> with PartialEq { fun eq(self, b: Pair<T>): bool { self.a.eq(b.a) && self.b.eq(b.b) } }` — died in an internal error at `Pair<i32> == Pair<i32>`: "a call resolved to `PartialEq`'s requirement `eq`, which has no body … please report this program" (B127's family, the OPERATOR half). Every corpus golden is byte-identical: the shared emission remains the emitted shape for every operator-only body. Warned, never swept: no record proves the build wrote the old file (pre-rename builds recorded nothing, which is also why a record-scoped sweep would ship blind to every dist/ already carrying the residue), and the output directory is not exclusively the build's, so user files are never touched. **The docs state the build-hook trust model.** `[build] run` hooks have always executed through the platform shell with the developer's own privileges — deliberately, the cargo-vs-make decision, reasoned out in the code — but no user-facing page said so. The strongest sentence in the whole corpus described capability ("pipes, globs and `&&` work") and never authority, while the spec's `[build]` bullet introduced `run` one sentence after "Build options never change program semantics, only the emitted text" (true of `preset`/`indent`/`spaces`, false of `run`, with nothing separating them), and the CLI appendix's one-rule-up-front scoped the reader's threat model to the network on the very page that documents `vilan build`. <!-- family: tooling -->
**Two closed items were under-pinned and six open ones had no pin at all — a sweep to make the test file say what the tracker says.** The standing rule is that "fixed" and "closed" require a pinned test *per case, not per example*, and that a known-but-unfixed bug is pinned as an `#[ignore]`d test that is un-ignored when it is fixed. An audit found gaps in both directions, and this closes them. On the closed side, **B139** was recorded as two halves fixed with only the DEPTH half pinned. Its TIME half — the memoized return chain — was evidenced by a prose measurement (390,984 inference entries down to 14,730) plus a green suite, which is precisely the evidence the rule refuses. It now has a COUNT pin in the shape B140 established one item later: `inference_entry_count`, a monotonic thread-local probe beside `atom_parse_count` and `buffer_parse_count`, asserted against a ceiling LINEAR in the chain's length. A wall clock was the wrong instrument for the same reason it was there: a ceiling generous enough to be stable across machines separates linear from exponential but *not* from quadratic, and quadratic is what this bug actually was, not some distant worse case. The constant term is measured in-run rather than written down, because it is std's own inference cost and std grows; only the marginal cost per link is a claim about this code. Disabling the memo read takes a 400-link chain from 4,202 entries to 245,200 and reddens every depth in the sweep. B139's second claim, that the fix is linear in *both* source orders, had been plant-tested caller-first only; a callee-first plant joins it — in its own test, not sharing one — and the flattening claim (502 frames collapsing to 6) is now pinned behaviourally, since a callee-first 1200-link chain must not reach the 500-link bound at all. **B140** had both its plants inside a single test function, so an arithmetic failure short-circuited the list shape and it was never reported; they are two tests now, which is what "per case" means.

One claim could not be pinned as asked, and the negative result is worth more than a pin that pretends otherwise. B139's `substitution_context.is_empty()` guard on the recorded-answer read is the correctness guard the tombstone singles out, on the reasoning that an answer shaped by a caller's generic bindings is that caller's and not the function's. The hazard is real and measurable: 1,157 records are written under a non-empty substitution context over the inference suite, and one generic enum's slot receives six different instantiations in a single run, so the map genuinely does collect caller-shaped answers. But **deleting the guard changes no observable behaviour today** — all 2,596 inference tests, the docs gate, and the byte-identical corpus are unaffected, because a wrongly-served answer is re-substituted downstream before it can reach codegen. Twelve candidate programs were built to find a wrong-typed one and none discriminates. So the pin asserts the guard *itself*, through a probe that counts what the guard forbids and must read zero; deleting the guard turns it red immediately (4 serves against an expected 0). It is a weaker claim than "a wrong type is served", and it is the true one.

On the open side, six defects that the tracker calls open had nothing in the suite naming them, so nothing would notice when they were fixed. Each is now an `#[ignore]`d test whose reason string names the item, and each was run un-ignored to confirm it fails for the stated reason rather than a harness mistake: **B142** (the parser has no depth bound — the existing 5000-deep pin uses a method chain, which is flat to the parser, so nesting the source syntactically instead aborts with a stack overflow and no diagnostic at all); **E94** (`asset::emit`'s kind reaches `with_extension` unsanitized, so `..` or a separator directs a write out of `dist/`, pinned under one rule with a green negative so the fence cannot be over-broad); **kolt.local 001** (the context-blind completion classifier, whose faults cut both ways — a `.` starting the next line offers nothing, a cursor in a string body offers the whole scope including functions); **kolt.local 007** (CSS hot-reload's added- and removed-stylesheet transitions); and **L15** (`install.sh` prints "skipping checksum verification" and installs unverified bytes when no sha256 tool is on PATH, where it must refuse). Two findings came out of the pinning rather than the audit. kolt.local 001's second listed face, `a.|.b`, does **not** reproduce — a call receiver, a trailing dot, a field or method after the cursor, and a partial name before it all resolve correctly — so it is pinned green rather than dropped, keeping the face covered by name; while a *third* shape of its first face turned up, a space between receiver and dot, which offers 80 candidates where three members belong. And **K18**, the playground's origin-blind `message` listener, has no honest home here at all: it is `vilan-website` code, that repo has no test harness of any kind, and forcing a pin into this one would have been a pin in name only.

<!-- family: tooling -->
**Member completion offers the methods a type inherits as trait defaults — `xs.iter().` used to answer `next` and nothing else, one method out of fifteen.** The gatherer walked `program.implementations`, matched the impls whose subject was the receiver's type, and offered what those impl blocks themselves DECLARE. A default-bodied trait method is declared on the trait, not on the impl, so nothing ever reached one: `impl ListIterator<type T> with Iterator<T>` writes out exactly `next`, and `map`, `filter`, `take`, `skip`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `chain`, `to_list`, `fold`, `for_each`, `count`, `any`, `all` and `rev` all live on `trait Iterator<T>` as defaults, invisible on every list in the language. This was never iterator-specific, which is the reason the traversal is fixed rather than the symptom: every default-bodied trait method was invisible on every implementing type, so `PartialEq`'s `ne`, `PartialOrd`'s `lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` and `Ord`'s `min`/`max`/`clamp` were missing too — a type implementing `Ord` offered none of the three comparisons a reader would go looking for — along with any user trait carrying a default body.

The admission rule is the analyzer's own, so the popup and the call site agree on what a type provides. For each impl of the receiver's type, each trait that impl provides and each of that trait's supertraits contributes its default-bodied instance methods, which is how an `Ord` implementor reaches `PartialOrd`'s comparisons and not only `Ord`'s own three. A member with no default body is never inherited, because conformance forces the impl to declare it and the declaring pass has already found it there. A `[trait_only]` default stays off the concrete surface, as it does at a call site. And one name is offered ONCE: a declaration wins its name outright, which is what makes an impl that overrides a default offer the override rather than both spellings of it.

Hover and go-to-definition were checked for the same blind spot in the same pass and do not have it, for a structural reason rather than a lucky one. They read the target the analyzer already resolved AT THE CALL SITE — whichever resolution tier answered, the wiring records the member's own declaration id behind the call, and for an inherited default that id is the trait's. So hovering one shows the trait's signature and jumping lands on the trait's default body, both correct, and both now pinned so the finding stays a finding. Completion is the one surface that cannot borrow that answer, because it has to speak for a member nobody has typed yet, and re-deriving the member surface is exactly where the tier was missing. Docs `appendix/editor.md`. (kolt.local 033)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**Completion asks once where the cursor actually is — so a `.` that starts the next line completes, and a string body completes nothing.** The engine read the two bytes immediately before the cursor and dispatched on them, which left it blind along two axes at once; each face reported against it was one of those axes. Trivia was the first: `p.` was a member position but `p .` was not, so a space before the dot fell through to the bare scope position and offered the whole enclosing scope — measured at eighty candidates where three members belonged — while a `.` that started the next line, the ordinary way a long method chain is written, resolved no receiver at all and offered nothing whatsoever. The difference between code and text was the second: a string body was not distinguished from an expression, so typing a caption offered every function in scope.

Rather than a third branch on the same byte pair, there is now one cursor-context model that every completion path consults, computed once and dispatched on: no code (a string body or a comment), a macro name, an element head, an import path, a member position, a `::` path, or a plain expression. Two mechanisms make it answer the faces above. The member test reads TOKEN space, so the lexer's own notion of what is significant decides where the receiver and the dot are — `p.`, `p .`, a dot alone on the next line, and a dot with a `//` note between it and its receiver are one position, the receiver is the token before the dot rather than the byte before it, and what FOLLOWS the cursor never enters the question, so completing between two links of a chain works too. The string test reads the same tokens and takes the NARROWEST one containing the cursor, which is what keeps an interpolation hole a code position: an i-string's wrapper tokens all carry the whole literal's span while a hole's tokens carry their own, so `i"now {ma|}"` still offers the scope where `i"ma| now"` offers nothing. A comment leaves no token at all, being trivia, so that one case scans bytes — and the token spans are still what rule out a `//` sitting inside a string, which opens no comment.

The boundaries around it are held rather than redrawn. The element-head work's two deliberate refusals stand: an attribute NAME is still not offered, because the desugar is name-blind on purpose and there is no table to complete from, and a head item's argument, a `.` outside any markup, and an element's child position are all still ordinary expression ground rather than head ground. A cursor ON a delimiter is code and not text, so `|"a"` and `"a"|` both complete. The item's second face — completion between two dots, `a.|.b` — does not reproduce and never did: six shapes were probed and all resolve correctly, so it stays pinned green rather than shipped as a passing pin for an open bug. The three faces that do reproduce are pinned by name and their `#[ignore]` markers are gone, alongside a context matrix that pins each class of the taxonomy in its own test, so the next regression is caught by the class it belongs to rather than by whichever face happens to get reported. Docs `appendix/editor.md`. (kolt.local 001)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**CSS hot-reload was decided by one bit, so adding a stylesheet did nothing and deleting one brought it back.** The watch round asked `old.css != leg.css` and called every answer a `css` hot-swap. That bit conflates three different transitions, and only the middle one is a hot-swap: a sheet whose TEXT changed is a sheet the page already loads, and replacing its text is a complete description of the round. A sheet that **appeared** or **vanished** changes which stylesheets the page has at all, which is a change to the browser's output, not an edit to a loaded sheet — and calling it a hot-swap produced two silent failures and one that was worse than silent. A first-ever stylesheet was announced to a page with no `<link>` to supersede: the shim walked the page's links, matched none, injected nothing, and made no request at all — a completely successful-looking round in which nothing happened, and, since a client-only round never restarts the server that rendered the page, nothing ever would. A deleted stylesheet was announced too, and **that push landed**: the dist writer only ever wrote `dist/<leg>.css` inside `if let Some(css)`, and the one thing that deleted anything swept `<leg>.<arm>.js` and `<leg>.chunks.json` only, so last round's sidecar sat there, the dev channel served it with a healthy 200, and the browser re-injected the stylesheet the developer had just removed. Deleting styles reasserted them, with no 404, no warning and no failed round anywhere in sight.

A third face was hiding behind the rank rule. When a bundle and its sidecar both change, the round pushes `swap`, on a reason recorded in S1: "a reload subsumes the stylesheet refresh". That reason died when S2 made a swap a MODULE swap instead of a document reload — nothing about re-evaluating a bundle refreshes a stylesheet — so every round that touched code and styles together, which is most rounds in an app whose styles live in its source, refreshed the code and dropped the styles on the floor. That is the reported "CSS reload sometimes does not apply at all", and no amount of fixing the presence transitions would have touched it.

One corrected classification covers all three: the css axis is decided by TRANSITION rather than by a difference. `Some` → `Some'` stays a `css` push naming the changed sidecars. `None` → `Some` and `Some` → `None` become `swap`, carrying the version bump every other browser-output change carries — and a `swap` now DECLARES the round's complete stylesheet set on the wire (`"sheets":["client.css"]`, or `[]` when the round emits none), which is what lets the browser reconcile rather than guess. The shim's apply layer became that reconciliation, keyed by sidecar name rather than by `<link>` element: a declared sheet with links to supersede is superseded exactly as before, a declared sheet with no link is this leg's own and joins `<head>` on its own, and this leg's sidecar missing from the declaration is the round's statement that it emits none, so the page's copy is withdrawn. Superseding also stopped moving a sheet to the end of `<head>`: the injected `<style>` now takes the `<link>`'s place in the cascade instead of quietly re-deciding every tie. On disk, `sweep_stale_sidecar` extends the doctrine the chunk sweep already enforces — the leg's dist namespace belongs to its LAST build — to the style sidecar, so a build that emits no stylesheet leaves none behind and the manifest's `"styles": null` and the directory finally agree. That half applies to `vilan build` too, where the same file used to outlive the source that emitted it.

Two invariants were load-bearing and are unchanged, deliberately. Asset matching still holds: a named event touches only the `<link>` whose file it names, a nameless one refreshes every stylesheet the page links, each by its own basename — and a page can now be told, and pinned, that a nameless event cannot reach a sheet with no `<link>`, which is why the CLI always names its sidecar. And the **never-reload discipline is untouched**: a 404 or a network failure still warns and leaves the stylesheet exactly as it was. A failed fetch is ambiguous and is never read as a removal; only the round's own declaration withdraws a sheet, which is precisely why the swap carries the set instead of the shim probing for it. Another browser leg's sidecar is left alone entirely — every leg's page receives the same broadcast, and injecting the admin leg's stylesheet into the client leg's page would be a new bug. The recorded limitations stay: an app that inlines its CSS gets a full swap, and a sidecar swap still replaces the whole stylesheet rather than a rule.

Pinned as the matrix the item asked for rather than as three patches: the classifier's transitions as unit cells (including the empty one, the node-leg axis, and the wire's `sheets` shape), and the apply layer's **(new / changed / removed) × (named / nameless) × (link present / absent)** as 46 named cells across two documents in `hmr_css_matrix.rs`, driving the real shipped shim. Two end-to-end pins hold the wiring against a running dev channel: a first-ever stylesheet reaching a page a boot-time-rendered server built before it existed, and a removed one leaving no sidecar on disk and declaring none on the wire. Verified live as well as in the suite — a real `run --watch`, a real SSE connection, the real bundle: adding a stylesheet to a page with no `<link>` landed it as a `<style>`, changing it updated that same element in place, and deleting it took the element back out and the file off disk, with the app's own hand-written sheet untouched and no reload at any point. Docs `guide/dev-loop.md`. (kolt.local 007)

---

<!-- family: tooling -->
**`AGENTS.md`'s repo map is gated against the workspace it describes, after a crate spent five days missing from it.** `crates/vilan-ide` — the completion engine and line index the language server and the web playground share — landed on 2026-08-22, and the map at the top of `AGENTS.md` went on saying "five crates" and listing five bullets, through two later edits to that same file and several work orders after. It is the first thing a coding agent reads and the only place the workspace is described in prose, so the cost was not cosmetic: an agent briefed from it had no reason to think a completion behavior belonged anywhere but `vilan-lsp`, which is the one crate `vilan-ide` exists to keep protocol-free so it can build for `wasm32`. Nothing noticed, because a stale sentence still compiles.

The gate is the shape this tree already uses for the generated grammars and the book's deep links: one side of a hand-written pairing is held to a machine-readable source of truth on every suite run. The truth here is the root manifest's `members` list — the only list that decides what actually builds. Three pins: every member has its own bullet, no bullet names a path the workspace does not build (so a rename cannot leave a ghost behind), and the count word in the map's lead sentence is the members' count. Deliberately nothing about what a bullet *says* — that is prose no test can judge, and pinning it would turn every honest improvement to the map into a red suite. Membership is the half with a right answer. Found by the recurring codebase audit (backlog N16).

## v0.36.0 — 2026-08-24

<!-- family: breaking -->
**`std`, `pkg`, and `macro_std` are reserved package names; the manifest now refuses them.** They name the three import roots themselves, and until now nothing defended that: a dependency declared as `std = { path = "…" }` silently shadowed the entire standard library — every `import std::…` in the package resolved into the dependency, so `import std::print` failed with "cannot find 'print' in the imported path" while `std::whatever_the_dependency_has` quietly bound — a dependency named `pkg` was accepted and then silently unreachable (the self-package root always wins, so the declaration did nothing), a dependency named `macro_std` shadowed the macro world's std and satisfied the macro-body hermeticity check by spelling alone, and a `[package]` could name itself `std` without a word. Now a `[package] name` or a dependency key in `[package.dependencies]`, `[library.dependencies]`, or `[project.dependencies]` claiming one of the three is a manifest error, at the same layer every manifest problem reports: `` `std` is a reserved package name: the standard library owns it (`std`, `pkg`, and `macro_std` are all reserved); rename the package `` — the CLI refuses before any dependency work, and the editor publishes it on the `vilan.toml`. The dependency fix is free: the key is the import name and yours to choose, so rename it; the library it points at keeps its own name. `[library] name` is deliberately exempt — the standard library itself is the `[library]` named `std` (likewise `macro_std`), and a library's own name, unlike a dependency key, never binds an import root. Spec §4.2/§11.4, tour "Projects and dependencies"; the ruling is `proposals/proposal/std-shape.md` §4 (L12, RULED 2026-08-22).

---

<!-- family: breaking -->
**std no longer ships the reflexive `Into` blanket.** `std::into`'s `impl type T with Into<T>` — the identity conversion every imported `Into` gave every type — is deleted (B127, `proposal/method-resolution.md` §14; ruled 2026-08-22). The `Into` trait, the module, and the import path all stay, and every corpus program emits byte-identical JavaScript. The census that preceded the ruling measured the blanket selected by resolution at zero sites in the entire tree, and its one unique affordance — `fun accept<T: Into<Foo>>(x: T)` fed a `Foo` itself — dying in an internal compiler error ("a call resolved to `Into`'s requirement `into`, which has no body … please report this program", live in released 0.34.0), because the emitter cannot see a generic-subject impl on the bound path. If you called the identity `.into()`, write the reflexive impl yourself: `impl Foo with Into<Foo> { fun into(self): Foo { self } }` — three lines, already legal, and strictly more functional than the blanket it replaces: it satisfies the `T: Into<Foo>` bound *and* runs, where the blanket crashed the compiler.

What deleting buys: the common case stops paying an annotation tax. One type, one conversion — `let s = foo.into()` beside a single `impl Foo with Into<str>` — used to be a two-home ambiguity demanding an annotation, because std's blanket made every `.into()` receiver an overlap; now it just runs and prints the conversion you wrote. An `Into` overlap is now something only your own impls can create, and the bound-fed-its-own-target shape is a clean refusal naming the missing impl, with a note at the bound's declaration, instead of an internal error.

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**A call landing on an impl overlap the compiler cannot rank is now reported, not answered by declaration order.** The shape takes both halves at once: one trait at two instantiations on one receiver, and — inside the instantiation the call selects — two impls neither of which is more specific. `impl Box<type T: Display> with Conv<Bar>` and `impl Box<type U: Ord> with Conv<Bar>` beside an `impl Box<type T> with Conv<str>`: the annotation on `let b: Bar = box.conv()` picks which *instantiation* the call means (that shipped with B73), but the unrankable `Conv<Bar>` pair was represented by its first maximum, so the program compiled clean and ran whichever of the two was declared first — swap the blocks, change the program. The selection now carries each instantiation's ranking verdict, and landing on an unrankable one reports the same "neither impl subject is more specific than the other" ambiguity the pair would report alone, naming both subjects with their bounds. An annotation selecting a ranked instantiation beside an unrankable pair still runs, exactly as before. (`proposal/method-resolution.md` §13.8's deferred residue, B128; no program in the tree had the shape — the probe was built to pin it.)

---

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**An unannotated function's return positions now reach the memory-model seams — and its tail no longer hands back live storage.** The compiler's one list of "places a function returns from" (the tail, and each `ret` — the join that feeds borrow inference, the resource-crossing scan, the view-escape check, and the pass that decides which returns must copy) was built only for functions with a **declared** return type. With the annotation left off, `fun grab(&self) { self.inner }` returned the receiver's field **without the copy** its annotated twin gets: mutate `h.inner` after the call and the "returned value" changed with it — this exact program printed `99` where `fun grab(&self): Inner` printed `3`. The `ret` spelling had the opposite defect: an unannotated `ret &self.inner` was refused outright with the generic `a view cannot escape its scope`, where the annotated twin compiles and copies; an unannotated `ret &self.g` of a resource drew the same generic refusal instead of the move scan's precise `cannot move a resource field out of a live aggregate; loan it with `&` / `&mut`, or make the field an `Option` and use `take``.

The join now carries every return position of every bodied function, annotated or not — the last release made an unannotated function's `ret`s typed, so the seams can finally see them. An unannotated function has no return annotation to declare a view with, so its return is **by value in both spellings**: a returned loaned place is copied (a scalar view is read), at the tail and at each `ret`, exactly as the annotated twin; a resource crossing is named by the move scan at either position; a view of a local still cannot escape either way. Tour "Memory model" (the projection-or-copy box), `proposal/ret-checking.md` "Rule 3, amended" Q2 (B134).

Note plainly: programs that RELIED on the aliasing change behavior on upgrade. An unannotated method or function returning a field of a live receiver used to hand back the storage itself — mutate the receiver after the call and the "returned value" moved with it; it now gets the copy the annotated spelling always got. And an unannotated `ret &self.x` that was refused outright now compiles and copies. No program in the tree had either shape; a program that did was depending on a miscompile.

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**Iterating or indexing an unannotated closure parameter no longer commits it to `any`.** `let items = Signal::new([Todo { .. }]); items.map(|list| { for todo in list { if !todo.done { .. } } })` failed with `cannot access field 'done' on type any` — blamed on the un-annotated `let`, and worked around by annotating it (the todo example's last annotation). The `let` was incidental: the `for` loop resolved before the `.map` call had typed its parameter and committed the item to `any`, where every other use of an unannotated closure parameter waits. Iterating or indexing a closure parameter now waits the same way; the inline chain and the plain nested-list forms, which failed identically, compile; the todo example drops its annotation. One edge reports where it used to be accepted: a closure that is never called and never annotated, iterating its parameter, used to compile with the item typed `any` and now reports — as one refusal at the parameter naming the cause (the entry "A closure that is never called says so, at its parameter"), where this change first surfaced it as `could not be resolved` at the use.

<!-- family: feature -->
**`std::markdown` — a strict markdown parser with mdBook-exact heading ids, the first package-shaped std module.** `parse(source)` returns `Result<Doc, ParseError>`: a plain-data AST (two enums, two structs — no `Shared`, no `View`, no closures, const-eligible by construction) covering the docs book's measured grammar — ATX headings, backtick fences with verbatim info strings and bodies, paragraphs, flat lists whose items carry real block bodies, recursive blockquotes, pipe tables with `\|` cell escapes, inline code/strong/emphasis/links, autolinks, and the `<a id>` passthrough (`proposal/markdown.md`, RULED 2026-08-24). The parser is **strict**: every census-zero construct — images, footnotes, setext headings, nested lists, indented code, reference links, thematic breaks, hard breaks, stray HTML, and friends — is a loud `ParseError` naming the construct and its line, so the first page to write one fails the docs walk instead of rendering wrong. Heading ids are a pinned compatibility surface: bit-exact mdBook v0.5.4 parity (per-whitespace hyphens, entity drops, Unicode lowercase, per-page `-1`/`-2` dedupe), held by an adversarial unit corpus and a book-wide golden of all 456 rendered anchors generated from a real mdBook build (`scripts/regen-markdown-golden.py`). The whole 56-page book parses in ~55 ms on the process leg; the largest page in ~0.9 ms. New docs page: `std/markdown.md`.

<!-- family: feature -->
**Lists compare with `==`, and a struct with a `List` field can derive `PartialEq`.** `std::List` carried only the inherent `T: PartialEq` methods (`contains`, `index_of`) — the type itself never satisfied a `PartialEq` bound, so `[derive(PartialEq)]` on a struct holding a `List<…>` field was refused ("type 'List' does not implement the `PartialEq` operator") and the first real site wrote its `eq` by hand, hop by hop (I4, found by E80's lane). `impl List<T: PartialEq> with PartialEq` now compares element-wise, length first; the impl is conditional, so nested lists (`List<List<i32>>`) compare through their elements and the derive on a `List`-holding struct just works. The hand-written impl and its helper can be deleted wherever a struct was carrying one.

---

<!-- family: feature -->
**`Document` gains `description(text)` — `title`'s twin.** The first real site put its `<meta name="description">` through the `head()` hatch and interpolated the text raw, so a `"` in a description would have ended the attribute and turned the remainder into junk attributes a browser tolerates — the page looks right and the search snippet is wrong (E85, the §10.1 review's first graduation; `proposal/fullstack-dx.md` §16.13, ruled 2026-08-22). `Document::of(build).title("Notes").description("A tidy list.")` now writes `<meta name="description" content="A tidy list." />` beside the `<title>` in the generated prefix, escaped the way an attribute value must be; a document not given one carries no description meta at all. The ruled bound moves with it: rung 2 is the intersection of the shells in the tree, **plus the identity lines the document is the sole author of** — `title` and `description` — while everything naming a second party the build cannot see (a file, a host, an address, a palette) stays a `head()` call. Like `title`, it shapes the generated document only: a supplied shell's identity lines are the shell's own.

<!-- family: feature -->
**`data-*`/`aria-*` attributes in element heads are a documented, pinned guarantee.** `<div data-foo-bar("x") aria-label("y")>` has always parsed, checked, and emitted its attributes verbatim — the name-blind desugar never cared that a name has hyphens — but nothing said so, and nothing pinned it (E87, the owner's question, probed 2026-08-22). Now the guide says it (hyphens are ordinary attribute-name characters, exactly as in HTML — no `data:` marker family, no `.data("foo-bar", v)` method twin) and a compiler test pins the probe end to end, so the spelling can never silently regress into needing one.

<!-- family: feature -->
**Repeated `head()`/`body()` calls land one per line.** Consecutive hatch calls used to concatenate with no separator — two `head()` calls put two items on one line of the served page — which is why the first real site wrote its own `joined()` helper and called the hatch once with everything pre-joined (E86, `proposal/fullstack-dx.md` §16.13, ruled 2026-08-22). Consecutive calls now join with a newline at the hatch's indent, on the generated document and the supplied-shell splice alike, so the hatch is usable per item and the written page still reads in View Source — the §15.1 promise, kept for both spellings.

<!-- family: tooling -->
**A bare scope-position completion no longer costs twenty member completions.** K9's measurement (`proposal/playground-completion.md` §9) had members and import paths answering in ~3 ms but a bare scope position at 51 ms for 131 items — in the language server and the playground alike, since both drive the same engine: the E54c auto-import path called `formatter::insert_import`, a full re-parse of the buffer, once per surviving candidate (the cap is 20), and every candidate's `///` doc re-read — re-cloned — its module's text through `read_source`. The buffer is now parsed once per completion request and shared across every candidate's edit (`formatter::ParsedSource`, a parsed-input twin beside the string `insert_import`, both pinned to answer byte-identically), and module texts are cached per request on the `Analysis` — per query, never global, so an overlay edit still lands in the next query's reads. The pins hold the *counts*, not the time: a completion request pays exactly one whole-buffer parse and one text read per docs module, each plant-proven red by restoring the per-candidate call. Re-measured on §9's folded walkthrough scenario (release wasm under node, median of 20): the scope position 60.8 ms → 5.8 ms for the same 136 items, with member completion (2.7 ms) and the worker round trip (3.0 ms) unchanged; the completion wire is byte-identical. Record: `proposal/playground-completion.md` §9 (amended 2026-08-24).

---

<!-- family: tooling -->
**Editing a file that another open document imports no longer grows the language server for the session.** The compiler's module parses are cached process-globally by content — right for std and dependency files on disk, whose contents recur across every compile — but an open buffer's content is a keystroke's, which never recurs: with `helper.vl` open and edited while a `main.vl` importing it was also open, every landed keystroke re-analyzed the dependent and left one immortal copy of the edited file's text and parse tree in the cache (one per distinct content — on an 8.7 KB file, 8.7 KB of text plus the tree per keystroke, for the rest of the session), and a buffer that was mid-edit and did not parse clean left its text **twice** (`leak-soak.md` §7.5, §7.9.1). During a language-server analysis, module loads served from the open-document overlay now bypass the process-global caches and parse into allocations the analysis itself **owns** — text, tree, and rendered errors — reclaimed when the analysis is superseded or the document closes, the same discipline the entry's own text and tree have followed since M7. Outstanding module bytes are bounded by the open set, and distinct-content growth is zero at every cache site. The deliberate, bounded costs: a dependent's re-analysis re-parses each overlay-resident import (≈0.8 ms end-to-end on an 8.7 KB module in release, unmeasurable on a small one — parsing is the cheap phase), and a base world is never stored for an analysis that loaded an open buffer (a stored world must not borrow analysis-owned memory), so base-world caching pauses while a std or dependency file is open in the editor and resumes when it closes. The CLI, the wasm playground, and transient editor queries keep the shared caches byte for byte. Record: `proposal/leak-soak.md` §7.10.

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**The context-coverage error treats a dependency package like std: your call is the primary, the package's read is the note.** The unprovided-context refusal has anchored at the user's call since E74 — but only when the strict read sat in *std*. A read inside a dependency package (a git or path dependency's function your code calls) anchored at `current.get()` **in the dependency's own file**, and the package's internal frames — calls you never wrote and cannot fix — rendered as trace hops beside your own. The owner's ruling (diagnostics-standard.md C3a, 2026-08-22) makes the contract explicit: code the user did not write — std or ANY external/linked package — demotes and traces the same way. The coverage walk now keys on the loader's package classification (a new `Program::dependency_sources`, fed by the same `Origin::Dep` seam that namespaces a dependency's modules — never a path heuristic): the primary anchors at your earliest call into the package, the read demotes to the cross-source C3 note (`the read is inside `deep_read` here`, in the package's file), package-internal calls are traversed but never labeled, and the injected-call flavor (`the injected call is inside `call_it` here`) demotes identically — its first library-internal incidence, previously unprobed even for std. Your own code is untouched, and **your own code includes your workspace**: a `pkg::` sibling's read still anchors at the read, and a package listed in the enclosing `[project]`'s `packages` — a workspace MEMBER, path-linked like `common = { path = "../common" }` — never demotes at all (E90, the owner's 2026-08-24 ruling): its reads anchor at themselves in its own files and its internal calls label as ordinary hops, exactly like the entry's modules. Only genuinely *external* packages demote — git checkouts, and path dependencies the workspace root does not declare — decided by the root manifest's `packages` declaration, never by where a directory happens to live. An overlaid dependency buffer (open in the editor) keeps anchoring at itself, by the same disk-only rule std has. On every surface: the terminal leads with your file and sub-reports the package's, the editor publishes the primary and hop diagnostics in your files only with the read as related information into the dependency, and the overlay/playground inherit the trace channel unchanged (E80). Record: `proposals/proposal/diagnostics-standard.md` C3a (E84; the member carve-out is E90).

---

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**An unannotated function's `ret` now counts toward its inferred return type.** `fun f(x: bool) { ret 1; }` — no declared return type, a body that leaves only by `ret` — was `void` at every call site, so `let y: i32 = f(true)` reported `Expected i32, but got void instead.` at the call, the one line with nothing wrong on it. The return type was read from the body's final expression alone, and a `ret` was invisible to it. Invisible was worse than missing: `fun f(x: bool) { if x { ret "s"; } 2 }` compiled clean and handed a `str` to an `i32` binding at runtime, a bare `ret` beside a value tail handed back `undefined`, and an exhaustive `if`/`else` of `ret`s typed as `never` and let `let y: str = f(false)` through.

The return type is now inferred from every return position — the final expression, when the body can reach it, and each `ret` — and they must agree. A `ret` that disagrees is reported at that `ret`, naming its type, the inferred type, and where that came from (the tail, an earlier `ret`, or the body ending without a value), with a note at the origin: `this `ret` returns str, but the function's return type is inferred as i32 from its tail; make every return agree, or declare the return type`. It is the only diagnostic — the function's calls stop reporting the mismatch a second time. A bare `ret` is a void return and is refused beside a value tail. A final expression the body cannot reach is not evidence, so `{ ret 1; }` is `i32`; one it can reach is, so `{ if x { ret 1; } }` is refused rather than typed `i32` and handed `undefined`. A call the function makes to itself contributes nothing, so `fun count(n: i32) { if n == 0 { ret 0; } ret 1 + count(n - 1); }` infers `i32` where a `ret` that was nothing but a self-call used to be "could not be resolved". The same answer now serves a named function passed where a closure is expected, an unannotated `next` driving a `for` loop, and an unannotated impl member checked against its trait — `fun area(self) { ret "wide"; }` against `: i32` used to pass conformance and print `wide`. Closures keep their existing rule (`ret`s are checked against the closure's tail). Spec §5.6, tour "Functions & closures", `proposal/ret-checking.md` rule 3 (amended).

---

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**A closure handed to a generic method is checked against what the call site expects, where it is written.** `let widths: List<i32> = points.map(|point| { point.x * 2; })` reported `Expected List<i32>, but got List<void> instead.` across the whole call: `map<U>`'s `U` was bound from the closure's own (void) body first, and the annotation could only disagree one level out. The annotation was available all along — it is recorded before any call resolves — but the call never read it for its own type parameters. It does now, after the receiver and the non-closure arguments and before the closure is typed, so `U` is `i32` when the body is checked and the report lands on the closure's closing brace: `` Expected i32, but got void instead: the `;` discards this body's last value. `` — the same one-character steer a plain `|value| { value * 2; }` under `let scale: |i32| i32` has had since S3. Once, not twice: the `let` no longer repeats it. The same holds for a call in tail position, under a `ret`, in a block or `if`-branch tail or a `match` leg, through a free generic function (`apply<U>(xs, |x| { .. })`), and on `Signal::map`. A generic an argument binds is never overridden by the annotation (`xs.fold(0, ..)` under `let s: str` still reports at the `let`, as before), and an unannotated `let` still takes the body's type.

---

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**A closure that leaves only by `ret` now infers its return type, like a function.** `|x| { ret x * 2; }` was refused with `the closure's body ends without a value, but this `ret` returns one; make the ret'd value the body's tail` — the conservative rule closures kept when functions got return-position inference. The refusal blamed a "body without a value" that no execution ever reaches: a body whose last statement is a `ret` has a dead final position, and dead code is not evidence. A closure's return type is now the unification of its **reachable** tail and every `ret` — the same rule, the same machinery, and the same one-refusal-per-disagreeing-`ret` reporting an unannotated function has had since the last release, notes at the origin included. So `{ ret 1; }` is `|| i32` and can bind a caller's generic (`Iterator::from_fn`-style callbacks that leave by `ret` now type), an exhaustive `if`/`else` of `ret`s agrees with a `|i32| str` slot and runs, and `async { ret 1; }` settles as a task of `i32` instead of refusing. What stays refused stays refused where it was: a value-`ret` beside a body path that can actually end without a value keeps the "make the ret'd value the body's tail" steer (now with a note at that path), a `ret` disagreeing with a reachable tail or an earlier `ret` reports at that `ret`, and a bare `ret` beside a value tail is still an error. When the closure's return type is already known — its own annotation, or the call site's expectation binding a generic (`let widths: List<str> = points.map(|point| { ret point.x * 2; })`) — the `ret`s check against that type, once, at the `ret`; neither the call nor the `let` repeats it. Spec §5.6, tour "Functions & closures", `proposal/ret-checking.md` rule 4 (amended).

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**A bare-expression closure body reports its type disagreement on the expression.** `let widths: List<str> = points.map(|point| point.x * 2)` reported the closure as a whole value — `Expected |Point| str, but got |Point| i32 instead.` — while the same body written as a block reported at its closing brace in the element's own terms. The block-vs-bare split was an anchor artifact: the return-position route was scoped to bodies with a closing brace to point at. A bare body now takes the same route, anchored on the expression itself: `Expected str, but got i32 instead.` on `point.x * 2`, still exactly once, with the same wording family as the block spelling — a void-valued body says `Expected i32, but got void instead.`, and a bare `if` with no `else` says so. The refinement applies wherever the closure's return type is known ahead of the body — an annotated `let` through a generic call, a receiver- or argument-bound generic (`twice(seed, |x| ..)` with `step: |T| T`), a free generic function, or the closure's own return annotation.

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**A derive refusal points at the derive, in the file that wrote it.** `[derive(PartialEq)]` on a struct whose field type does not implement `PartialEq` refuses inside the generated `eq` — an `==` over each field, checked by the post-fixpoint operator pass. That pass never attributed what it pushed, so the refusal kept the generated template's offsets while claiming the entry file: `vilan check` drew its label over whatever text the entry held at those offsets (a comment line, in the report that filed this), and for a struct in an imported module the editor published it against the wrong file and showed nothing at all in the one with the mistake. The gap was the whole pass's, not the derive's: every diagnostic it raises — the operator refusals, the non-`bool` condition and `&&`/`||`/comparison operand checks, the string-backed-enum ordering refusal, the uniterable `for` subjects, the numeric-literal suffix and range checks, and the post-solve "could not be resolved" residuals — claimed the entry while its span indexed the file that wrote the code. Each now anchors the way every other diagnostic has since the E1/E16 fixes: in its own file at its own text, and, raised inside generated code, re-anchored at the attribute that generated it with the provenance said in the message — `in code generated by this attribute: type 'List' does not implement the `` `PartialEq` `` operator; add `impl List with PartialEq` providing `eq`` — where the language server now publishes it. (E82.)

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**A closure that is never called says so, at its parameter.** `let walk = |xs| { for x in xs { print(x); } };` with no call to `walk` anywhere: nothing can ever type `xs` — inference fills an unannotated closure parameter from the closure's first call, and there isn't one — so every use of the parameter stalls, and the program reported the stall in the residual sweep's voice, `type of function call arguments could not be resolved` at `print(x)`: the right refusal, two hops from the cause (the edge the entry "Iterating or indexing an unannotated closure parameter no longer commits it to `any`" accepted as the cost of the fix). It now reports once, at the parameter, naming both facts that starve it and the fix: `` `xs` is never given a type: this closure is never called and its parameter is unannotated; annotate it (e.g. `|xs: List<i32>|`) `` — and the residuals stay silent behind it, one diagnostic per root cause. A closure that is called keeps inferring from its call, and one whose call merely fails to resolve keeps the residual report rather than being called "never called". (B131, filed by B125's lane.)
